About this work

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum — "On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks" — is Trithemius's ascetic guide for monks, charting interior progress through three "regions" or stages of discipline: purification, illumination, and union with God — a Pseudo-Dionysian scheme adapted to Benedictine observance. He finished it in manuscript in 1497; it was first printed at Mainz by Peter von Friedberg on 8 August 1498, and it is one of the central texts of his Sponheim reform programme.

This is the 1498 Mainz edition (e-rara witness) — printed by Peter von Friedberg, one of three witnesses of the De Triplici Regione in this corpus: this 1498 Mainz first printing, the 1498 BSB witness (prdl-24385), and the 1516 Leipzig reprint (prdl-24386). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known;

English translation

On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks

Book on the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks: no less useful and necessary for all religious.

[unclear] Baptista Mantuanus, On Patience.

I HAVE RESOLVED.

Letter of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, concerning the little work On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents, definitors, and the other abbots of the annual chapter of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Bursfeld Union and Observance: Brother Johannes Trithemius, called abbot in Sponheim, of the same order and congregation, in the diocese of Mainz, sends reverence and charity.

I have regarded your commands, most honored fathers, as small, and I undertook to correct the little work On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, together with the spiritual exercise of monks, lately published by the venerable father lord Johannes, abbot of Bursfelde, as you instructed me. And indeed, unless your authority had compelled me, I would never have dared to set my hand to the distinguished work of so great a father, who is known to have written excellently and to be far more learned and holier than I. For what should I correct, where everything is found most approved? A good and devout man wrote no otherwise than as he lived and as was fitting.

Nevertheless, to satisfy both your command and the prayers of the author himself, I rendered the whole little work in briefer, though not fewer, sentences, and, while serving its emphases, reduced it as far as I could into my own manner and style of writing. I kept the order and matter of the earlier volume, but completely changed its form and customary mode of expression. I added many things that seemed useful to me in almost every place; I removed a few; in individual passages I altered the words, not the sense. Your command gave me the courage to do this, and the insistent request of the aforesaid father persuaded me. For you wished me to make a new work from old material: to add whatever seemed suitable to me, to cut away superfluities, and to alter what needed changing. I did what I could; I obeyed your mandates; by rewriting, I completed the work enjoined upon me according to the powers of my intellect, which are slight.

Now therefore receive, most beloved fathers, a work not mine but yours, not composed by me, but rather rewritten. If the labor of the aforesaid father pleases you—

A ij If it pleases you, praise the author’s talent; but if it displeases you because of its worthlessness, correct my imperfect work. For I had excellent material for a spiritual building, supplied at another’s expense, but through my own inexperience I have constructed an unskilled structure. If I have become a fool, you compelled me. Therefore, whether the work pleases or displeases, it was easier for me, by writing ineptly, obediently to undertake your command than, against obedience, to keep silence. Yet I trust not in my own powers but in the merits of others, for a work that charity has produced will displease no one who loves God. I pray that your paternities may always remain happy in Christ. From Sponheim, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1497.

Here begins the book on the threefold region of cloistered persons, and on spiritual exercises

When I recall to mind the state of the monastic life in this time, I grieve deeply over its calamity, because the fervor of spiritual exercise, which once produced the richest fruits in the order of our holy father Benedict, has now largely failed among monks. For we see cloistered persons returning in their ways to the world; we see the institution of regular observance being despised by many; and religion, which from the beginning had been instituted for contempt of the world, is now being recalled again by wicked monks to the pomps of the world. The crown has fallen from our head; the integrity of regular discipline has been corrupted; and the former fervor of holy life has perished. We see many monasteries of our order lying buried in the worst deformity, and very few restored to the purity of the rule.

The cause of this destruction of regular institution is negligence of spiritual exercises. For as soon as the spirit of fervor has grown faint in the minds of cloistered persons, the flesh, formerly dead through denial of itself, has revived; and the world, which before seemed dry and contemptible to devout hearts, has begun again to flourish in carnal minds. Indeed, the thought of the human heart, prone to evil from youth, unless it is daily spurred on to fervor of spirit by the bridle of spiritual exercise, soon falls back into its former negligences and grows lukewarm from its holy purpose. For just as fallow land, deprived of the careful attention of the cultivator, quickly returns to its former wasteland as thorns spring up, so the human mind, however pure or holy it may be, is quickly reduced to thickets of vices unless it is daily renewed to fervor of spirit by the exercise of devotion.

Led by this consideration, the fathers of our Bursfeld observance, devoted cultivators, commanded us and posterity by word and example that, since because of our frailty we cannot remain constant in fervor of spirit, at least by an evening recollection after Compline, accusing our daily negligences, we should renew the state of our mind to the fervor of our purpose.

Whoever neglects the exercise of daily institution falls into a deep torpor, as the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “If you do not hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house will soon be overthrown,” which is understood as a good conscience. The rule of our father Benedict seems sufficient for a monk, since it is agreed to contain all material for exercises, both spiritual and bodily, necessary for guarding regular discipline among monks. And therefore all exercises of monks must be humbly submitted to the constitutions of the rule, because whatever is commanded either by us or by others for the instruction of monks is wholly assigned to the observance of the monastic norm.

For the sum of our entire religious life, which is acquired by the continuation of spiritual exercise, is contained in compendious form, as in a root, in the rule of monastic tradition. Therefore every exercise of monks, whether spiritual or bodily, by which the mind is led from love to a humble abasement of itself, is conformed to the institutions of the holy rule. The more it is known to present the monk to God as good, humble, and very near, the more it opposes the zeal of proud contempt.

The holy mysteries of this exercise direct the mind of their cultivators by an invisible teaching toward the love of God, as toward their proper end, along a secure path; they wonderfully obtain the grace of inward devotion; and they make the monk despise all earthly things as nothing, and burn sweetly with every time of the lower spirit [unclear]. The animal man does not grasp this wholesome exercise of devotion; the vain and curious monk does not understand this pursuit; the proud man does not admit this knowledge, to be preferred to all things. Happy is he who has learned to penetrate the secrets of this exercise; happy is he who has deserved to receive from the Lord this gift of holy compunction. Whoever has once perfectly obtained it will fear no adversities of this world.

But that exercise which, lacking its proper end, does not direct the minds of cloistered persons to observance of the commandments of the rule does not pour in the holy spirit of discipline, because where the obedience of subjection is despised, no gift is accepted by almighty God.

On the first region of the soul, in which carnal monks dwell with beasts: disordered by many passions, living sensually in the lowest region

The first region of the soul, then, is called sensual, lowest, and animal; in it the roots of all evils are contained. Persons placed in this dark region share with beasts in their own kind, since they observe, so to speak, beastly habits, while they defer either not at all or only a little to reason, but yield everything to sensuality like beasts. For in this lowest region three sensual powers of the soul preside. The first, the sensitive power, is poured out upon the objects of each of the exterior senses; the second, the concupiscible power, takes delight in carnal things; the third, the irascible power, pursues by fleeing the pleasures contrary to the flesh.

And this lowest region is compared to the airy heaven, because, just as hailstorms, snows, lightning, and various tempests are generated in the air, so also in the minds of carnal persons inhabiting this dark region, various storms of vices rage. Woe to carnal monks who inhabit this dark region, in which there is frequent movement of crimes and a continual tempest of pleasures. These are monks given over to animal passions, who subject reason to sensuality, who live according to the flesh in beastly desires. The works of the flesh dwelling in this lowest region are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, luxury, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; concerning them the holy Apostle proclaims that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. These are the marks of the works of the lowest region; these are the deadly tempests of the minds of carnal monks, who live irreligiously in religion, who despise the traditions of the holy fathers, who with ruinous presumption scorn the precepts of their elders.

These are the unclean cultivators of the lowest region, given over to vices and carnal desires, who do not care to have God in their knowledge, who serve the pleasures of the flesh, who contumaciously break the vow of holy religion that they have professed, who, despising the salvation of their souls, refuse to follow the grace of God when it calls. Therefore he delivered them over to a reprobate sense and to false judgment, so that they judge evil to be good, and falsely suppose that things which are in truth the worst are the best. These are the carnal monks about whom the holy Apostle prophesied: whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, abusive, proud, haughty, inventors of evils, disobedient to superiors, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy, filled with every iniquity, malice, wickedness, contention, deceit, and malignity. For those who do such things are worthy of eternal death, and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, and those who, by duty of office, do not in the least oppose the pursuits of the wicked. Indeed, A ruler of souls who does not correct his offending subjects entangles himself, to his own damnation, in the crimes of others; by keeping silent he becomes the companion of those whose faults damnation will follow. For whoever, having been appointed a shepherd of souls, neglects to reform sinners according to the canonical rule, even if he is free from any fault of his own, will nevertheless be condemned before the strict Judge for another’s offense. For the supreme Shepherd says to the prophet: “Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall indeed die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand.”

And our blessed father says in the Rule: “Let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd will fall upon him if the master of the household has been able to find any lack of profit in his sheep.” O judgment ever to be feared by all shepherds: by it not only is the wicked conduct of subjects charged to the rector, but he is also held guilty before the inward Judge for their lesser progress. O what shall we wretched shepherds say in that strict examination, we who neglect to reform according to the Rule the monks entrusted to us when they offend in many ways; who do not call those lying in the lowest region to higher things, but, carnal among the carnal, grow numb in the shadow of death through destructive idleness?

Woe to all who remain in this dark region, for unless they do penance they must be assigned with those who inhabit the outer darkness, where no order dwells but everlasting horror. For just as monks who walk according to the Rule in spirit are to be happily crowned without end in heaven with the holy angels, so those who persevere until death, against the norm of monastic institution, in this lowest region of the flesh are worse than pagans and are to be tormented eternally in hell with demons. For that blessed man spoke truly: “Just as I have never seen better men than those who have made progress in the monastery, so I have not found any worse than those who have failed in the monastery.” For monastic profession demands the perfection of the spiritual life, and tends toward the height of the virtues as toward its proper end. But the more anyone established in a monastery falls away from this effort to make progress, the farther he withdraws from the purpose of a monk.

How carnal monks, citizens of this lowest region, are disordered in many articles

Although the description of this lowest region applies generally to any carnal human beings who dwell with beasts in sins and crimes, nevertheless, to attend to our own concerns, we intend to speak of lukewarm and carnal cloistered men, doing no injury at all to the good and devout. For always and in all things we wish the character of good cloistered men to remain untouched and unharmed whenever we discuss the evil pursuits of the wicked. Thus we rebuke wicked cloistered men and corrupt habits, while everywhere honoring the good and praising them as is fitting. And what else can we say of the wicked except evil, since in them we find no good things to speak of? They live disorderly lives in a holy order; they despise the traditions of the elders; they do not admit the words of salvation.

So great, indeed, is the disorder of the monks of the lowest region that, in my judgment, it would be easier to convert a publican than to recall a disorderly monk to penance. We include this disorder of carnal monks under eight articles, although we are not unaware that they are disordered in many matters.

First, then, the citizens of this lowest region, beastly monks, are disordered toward God; then toward their prelate; third, the prelate toward his subjects; fourth, the members toward one another; again, fifth, they are disordered toward themselves; then toward the property of the monastery; seventh, toward contempt of the world; and finally, toward penance for sin. These are the principal disorders of the citizens of the lowest region; these are the beastly affections of carnal monks, who dwell in the depths in mind and body and do not hasten to advance toward the heights. I shall therefore take care to set forth briefly, in order, these disordered conditions of the lowest region, and to demonstrate, so far as I can, how far carnal monks are from God. For as the prophet says: salvation is far from sinners. [unclear] How the citizens of this lowest region are disordered with respect to God.

Article 1

Therefore carnal monks, the mad cultivators of this lowest region, are in many ways disordered with respect to God. They never taste the sweetness of his love; they admit no compunction from divine fear. In their affections they are bestial and proud; in their carnal pleasures they are always unclean.

And first, their disorder toward God takes its origin from ignorance: while, given over to animal passions, they do not care to hold God in their knowledge, nor do they allow the mind to think on those things that lead to fear of him; but, blinded by evil desires, they vanish away in their own thoughts. But what does Scripture say? “He who is ignorant shall be ignored.” They are unwilling to understand so that they may act well; they do not tremble before the face of the strict Judge; without penitence they continually persevere in evils. Indeed, after the manner of beasts, they do not fear to rot in their pleasures; they do not heed the patience of God calling them to penitence; they seek nothing except the conveniences of their own flesh. At all times they walk in the greatest sins without any fear; they stubbornly refuse to know the ways of the Lord. Concerning the future judgment they think either little or nothing; they do not fear the punishments prepared in hell for sinners; the grace of compunction never pierces their hearts, whose minds the love of God does not inflame. They have no care for God; no dread of death. They obey the belly rather than God; at all times they desire to live according to the flesh; they shamefully neglect their own salvation in the Lord; they descend to hell with the demons. For indeed, those who, forgetful of God, badly keep the vow of holy monastic conduct do not attain the rewards of heavenly life to be given to the just.

Second, carnal monks are disordered with respect to God through foolish profession, because they promise to live according to the Rule, yet do not truly care to fulfill what they promise. And what is more disordered than to promise holiness of life to the Lord God and to remain in the foulness of one’s former life? He is a mocker of almighty God, not a monk, whoever lives in a monastery otherwise than the monastic Rule teaches.

And we discern that many among cloistered men today live in a worldly manner; we see that many neglect the purpose of their profession; many violate the observance of regular discipline in various ways; many knowingly ignore the goodness of God; many refuse to do penitence.

Third, many cloistered men of this lowest region are disordered with respect to God through neglect of the service they owe: they serve their own affections and carnal desires in various ways, and always approach the service of God with a distracted mind. Some of them hurry lukewarmly to choir without any devotion; others come unwillingly, compelled by necessity; certain men, scattered among outward thoughts, are present at the divine offices in body, but in mind wander outside through various workshops. Others do not fear to seek false excuses by which they may be able, as if lawfully, to absent themselves from choir. Now they pretend to have a severe headache; now they mendaciously allege this, now that; and while they deceitfully withdraw from the service owed to almighty God, they incur the reproach of eternal malediction owed to the negligent.

Fourth, there are very many disordered with respect to God through the operation of habit: even if they sometimes escape the malediction of the negligent, still they never draw near to the fruit of eternal devotion. For they approach the service of God from habit alone, and are not moved to any good work by devotion. Others, placed under grave necessity, obey the commands of their superiors quite unwillingly, and they fear temporal punishments rather than the judgment of God. These carry the cross of the Lord with Simon under compulsion; like Ephraim, a heifer trained for the threshing floor, they apply themselves to good works by habit alone. But they do not do the good well who approach the service of God with an intention that is not right. They also perform the deed of the just without the reward of the just, because in good and just works they do not assume a good will.

Fifth, the citizens of the lowest region are disordered with respect to God through the vice of ingratitude, which is a very great crime of disordered will. And often, indeed, he who is found ungrateful to the Lord for the benefits he has received is exposed, by his own desert, to be scourged by various and most grievous temptations. And therefore he deserves to lose the benefit he has received, who does not show himself grateful for so great a to show himself grateful to his benefactor. And what greater ingratitude can there be than to live irreligiously in religion: to break one’s vow, and shamefully violate the purpose solemnly undertaken? For the monk who entangles himself in carnal vices, who neglects to live according to the Rule he has professed, voluntarily incurs the greatest vice of ingratitude.

In what way the monks of this lowest region are disordered toward their prelate. Article II.

Carnal monks are disordered in many ways toward their prelate: they tear apart his life with continual slanders; with a stubborn heart they disparage the pastoral office; they refuse, according to the Rule, to show the affection of filial love to their shepherd. For, blinded by various pleasures of the flesh, the monks of this lowest region disdain to look upon the abbot as one who holds Christ’s place in the monastery; and the one whom they ought humbly to have venerated as Christ’s vicar, they regard as like themselves in weakness and worthy of no honor. Under the snare of this disordered conduct the ancient enemy deceives carnal monks, whom he leads in various ways into displeasure with their shepherd. For very great power to rage against the monastic flock is granted to the devil when the one who presides is hated by his subjects. For just as a sick man cannot be healed if, by detesting the physician, he does not allow him to approach, so a monk cannot be saved if, because of aversion, he is unwilling to disclose his temptations to his shepherd. For how will a weak sheep be able to escape the teeth of a ravening wolf, if it cannot endure the presence of the shepherd?

First, therefore, disordered monks disparage the life of their shepherd; they obstinately accuse both his deeds and his words, because, when they see the rector proceeding according to the traditions of the holy fathers, they fear being corrected in their own depravity. For among reprobate minds the life of the good is always drawn into suspicion; envy is always tormented by the virtues of others; and the monk who voluntarily subjects himself to vices and sins always hates a shepherd of purified conduct.

Second, the citizens of this shadowy region are disordered toward their prelate when they disparage his office, though they know that he was ordained by God to preside in the monastery. They murmur against him on any easy occasion; they do not observe his commands; and those who long ago, for the love of God, had submitted themselves with the weapons of holy obedience now, after despising obedience in the manner of Sarabaites, usurp for themselves the pernicious mastery of their own wills. They desire to have an abbot suited to their depraved habits; they reject one who is holy and useful. If they find a lax and idle shepherd, they poison him with many venoms by flattering him, calling him a most excellent and most loving father; and they subject themselves to him not humbly but gladly, since they fear no correction of their depravity from him.

Third, carnal monks show themselves disordered toward their shepherds when they withdraw from them the affection of filial love and scorn to obey according to the Rule. Yet since a monk is bound to love his abbot with sincere affection as Christ’s vicar, he will not be able to hate him without a very grave crime. Indeed, whoever does not love his shepherd for the love of Christ is not a true lover of God. For Christ, who wills that even enemies be loved, how would he permit his vicars to be hated? Therefore attend to him who wished the abbot to be over you in his stead, and from now on there will be no cause for displeasure against him.

Fourth, the disordered citizens of the shadowy valley disparage the reverence owed to their shepherd when they scorn to show him the honor due from the Rule; and, what is worse, they do not fear even to inflict insult upon him. For the Rule declares that the abbot holds the place of Christ in the monastery, and all monks ought humbly to obey him as Christ himself, because the obedience shown to superiors is shown to Christ. But perverse cloistered men, always ungrateful for the presidency of their prelates, do not fear obstinately to resist the divine ordinance; they scorn to obey the commands of the holy Rule; and they dishonor their abbot, to whom they ought to show every reverence, tearing him apart with hatred and slanders. Whatever he does, whatever he ordains, [unclear] whatever he has ordained, whatever he has said, displeases them as though badly done, since they detract from his way of life at every time and, despising his office, seek nothing more, like sickly sheep, than the confusion of their shepherd. From these, some judge and despise their abbot in secret; others contradict him to his face. And while they neglect to show reverence to their shepherd, they throw the whole observance of discipline into confusion. Pride is always familiar to them, and shamefulness, the friend of the flesh; for those who voluntarily withdraw themselves from affection for their shepherd fall into abominable temptations and the worst crimes. For whoever despises the vicar of Christ in the monastery hands over to the devil the power to rage against him, and disrupts the union of the mystical body.

Fifth, carnal monks, disordered toward their shepherd, derogate from his authority, when they think that nothing is permitted to him in the monastery unless they themselves have consented. With neck held high they despise the virtue of humility; they spurn regular subjection; they disdain to yield to their betters. They wish to thrust themselves into all business and causes, and to usurp for themselves the chief place in counsel, so that the abbot dares to do or arrange nothing unless the matter first proceeds from their consent. But what does the lawgiver Benedict say in the Rule? “Let the abbot,” he says, “after hearing the counsel of the brothers, consider it within himself, and do what he has judged more useful.” And again: “Let the brothers give counsel with all humble submission, so that they do not presume insolently to defend what has seemed good to them; rather, let it depend on the abbot’s judgment, so that all may obey what he has judged to be more salutary.” And again, concerning the appointment of the prior, he says: “We have thought it expedient, for the preservation of charity and peace, that the ordering of his monastery depend upon the abbot’s decision.”

This ordering indeed concerns the appointment and removal of all officials of the monastery; it requires not the consent of the brothers but the counsel of those who fear God. Finally, the Rule commands that all things be done according to the will of the abbot, and that absolutely nothing be presumed which has not been enjoined by him. Carnal monks, rash usurpers of their own will, try in various ways to break this authority of his and to disturb the order and charity of the whole monastery, since they think the rector should do nothing except what they themselves consider right. But tell me, proud cultivators of the lowest region, you who always establish your own will, you who usurp for yourselves another’s right: is this the virtue of obedience, to refuse to yield to the command of a superior, but to cling obstinately to your own judgment? The holy father did not establish in the Rule that you should live in this way, for he commanded you in all things to follow the will of the abbot. For obedience is the monk’s greatest virtue, which our divine father wished to commend to such an extent that he said a good work lacks merit without the abbot’s will. Hence, giving command, he concludes thus: “Therefore let all things be done with the abbot’s will, and let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart.”

But if the prudence of the rector does not seem sufficient for the ordering of the monastery, this must be imputed to the carnal monks, who voluntarily set over themselves someone unfit. Folly always hates prudence, and wicked monks detest a wise abbot. Therefore those who knowingly set a fool over themselves will necessarily be subject to his ordering and will. Finally, no incompetence of a shepherd ought to extinguish the obedience of subjects, since the Rule orders us to obey even an unprofitable one. For it says: “The commands of the abbot are to be obeyed in all things, even if he himself, which God forbid, acts otherwise.”

But when we rebuke disobedience, carnal monks object: “We do these things with a right and good intention, since we see the substance of the monastery perishing through bad governance.” But the Apostle contradicts you, since evils are not to be done so that good may come, nor is the subjection of humility to be abandoned because of damage to a temporal thing. For where one must undergo either the loss of temporal substance or danger to regular obedience, it is better for the substance to perish than for the purity of obedience to be harmed. For God will not require money from our hands, but souls. Indeed, one who prefers [unclear]. But the citizens of this lowest region, carnal monks, tear apart the virtue of obedience in various ways and They attack the weapons of holy humility, so that it seems easier to me to make a new monk from the world than to be able to correct the sloth of these men. But from their fruits we know plainly what sort they are: namely, they violate peace and charity in the monastery; they disturb concord and unity; they sow discord between the brothers and the abbot; they stubbornly refuse to obey the commands of the rule. These are the works of evil cloisterers; these are the signs of the citizens of the lowest region: as most wicked defenders of their own will, they cast away the weapons of holy obedience; they live by the flesh, not by the spirit; they show either no deference, or little, to the statutes of the fathers; they do not acquiesce in sound counsels. Their condemnation is just. For just as it is impossible that a flaming fire should not rise upward, so it is impossible for a monk without obedience to penetrate the secrets of heaven.

How the shepherds of this lowest region are disordered toward their subjects

Article III

Since, then, we have shown that very many monks of the lowest region are disordered toward their shepherds, shall we not also show the disorders of prelates toward their subjects, as though sparing ourselves? Neither does the name of abbot sanctify anyone, nor does the eminence of pastoral care save the undeserving. Therefore, since many among the prelates dwell with the beasts of the earth on the mountain of the lowest region, they must by no means be passed over by us in silence. For very many rulers of cloistered communities show themselves disordered toward their subjects: they not only neglect to feed according to the rule the souls committed to them, but tear and kill them in various ways. Whenever someone from the lowest region is taken up as shepherd, the pursuits of the wicked are strengthened for the worse. Therefore the man to be promoted as abbot should be good and devoted to God, one who has long since overcome this lowest region, who has learned to tame the passions of the flesh, who both wills and is able to ascend to that highest region of the spirit. For the abbot of monks ought to be of higher merit than the monks, since whoever is appointed ruler of souls must necessarily be adorned with many virtues. For if the shepherd, still weak, dwells in the lowest region with the sheep, he kills the feeble by neglecting them; he does not strengthen them. For if a blind man offers guidance to a blind man, he must necessarily fall with him into the pit. But the shepherd who does not show himself ordered toward his subjects according to the rule should be called not a shepherd but a hireling, and he will not remain in the house of the Lord forever. There are, moreover, many disorders of carnal prelates, which do harm all the more because they are more rarely corrected.

First, then, a ruler is disordered toward his subjects if he is a hireling: if, neglecting the sheep, he seeks his own advantage of flesh or soul; if, so that he may be able to obtain his own will, he denies nothing contrary to the rule to those who ask. For he who is a hireling does not truly love the sheep; he seeks his own glory; he desires to be over others; he does not care to profit them according to the rule; he rejoices to be called abbot, but does not know how to show himself a shepherd. Therefore he receives the empty reward of his vanity, who seeks not God’s glory but his own; who would sooner allow the souls of his subjects to perish than resign his abbacy to a better man. He is a hireling, and it does not belong to him to care for the sheep. He is not a true monk, not a good shepherd, not a sincere lover of God, who, when presiding over monks, is unwilling to yield if, by the counsel of those who fear God, it should seem expedient to do so. The care of ruling souls rejects a proud man; it requires one humble and resigned to God in all things. Therefore, if you wish to be found a good shepherd and a true monk, remember that your intention must at all times be formed in such a way that you are ready, from love of God, humbly to feed the souls committed to you according to your strength, and ready also, at the judgment of God and of good men, to resign the pastoral office from the integrity of your heart. If you always keep this intention abiding in your mind, you will be a good shepherd both to yourself and to others. But if in pastoral care you love your own honor, if you prefer your own advantage to the usefulness of your subjects, you still dwell with the beasts in the lowest region, and you make manifest how disordered your heart is.

Second, a pastor of souls becomes disordered toward his subjects if his mind is too greedily occupied with temporal affairs, if he has greater concern for secular business than for the souls committed to him. This excessive care for temporal things holy father Benedict forbids in the Rule, and he rightly judges rational souls to be preferred to all the things of the world. “Above all,” he says, “let the abbot not, by neglecting or making little of the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, have greater concern for transient, earthly, and perishable things; but let him always consider that he has undertaken to govern souls, for which he must render an account.” Then, when the pious father gives assurance about bodily necessities, provided that he loves God with a pure mind, he says: “And lest perhaps he complain of lesser means, let him remember what is written: First seek the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you. And again: Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.”

But a disorderly pastor of monks is seduced by the desire of greed; blinded in mind, as though without perception, he casts the fear of the Lord away from himself; with Ahab, sold under sin, he runs to the aid of wickedness. He is deprived of confidence in the necessities promised by the holy father as consequences; he is occupied in external things more than befits a monk. Driven henceforth by the goads of greed, he despises the commandments of God and of holy mother Church; he does not observe feast days; he is wholly immersed in earthly affairs; he meditates on nothing except temporal things. Foolishly, with Saul, he transgresses the commandment of God; foolishly, contrary to obedience, he thinks himself expiated by sacrifices. Finally, grown gross and enlarged either by secular possessions or by secular cares, he commonly slips into every kind of wantonness and dissolution; he detests the observance of regular discipline; and, while he fears being restrained from evil pursuits by the authority of the chapter, he seeks the dissolution of holy union. Then, made reprobate with Saul, he calls upon the counsel of the pythoness; he declares the obedience of reform damnable for his monastery; he desires to be absolved as quickly as possible from submission to the holy confederation; to this end he tells many things falsely and mendaciously. But when the authority of the annual chapter is despised with impunity, it remains B ij that monastic observance suffer shipwreck, since the love of God regularly keeps the good within discipline, and fear of correction restrains the wicked from evil works. Whoever strives to evade the unity of the chapter imitates the devil. Thus the emperor of the Bulgars forbids the Christians subject to him, on pain of death, to hold an assembly in church, although he grants them license to believe whatever they wish. For that crafty man knows that the sincerity of Christian faith cannot long endure if the office of public exhortation happens to be absent. The disorderly and carnal abbot strives, as far as he can, to imitate this adversary of the Christian faith, for he resists the authority of so necessary a synodal chapter. For the authority of the chapter alone is what maintains in the order the observance of regular discipline; if it is despised, no integrity of monastic life will remain.

But the inhabitant of the lowest region, the disorderly abbot, devises innumerable excuses against regular observance: he falsely claims that the conditions of his monastery are contrary to it; he complains of ancient privileges of his own; he is indignant that his monastery should be subject to anyone. But woe to disorderly men through whom even one monastery should happen to be lost from this most holy congregation. Finally, this plague of greed makes an abbot not only disorderly toward his subjects, but also opposed to himself and wholly turned away from God. For cupidity is the root of all evils; taking away the servant of Christ, it makes him a minister of the devil. Therefore the abbot who has submitted his mind to this vice shows himself to be not a pastor but a hireling.

He always pants after earthly profits; he cares nothing for the progress of souls. A book of sacred reading is rarely, or never, seen in his hands; registers of revenues are turned over more often. He joins field to field; always burying gold and silver in a chest as he gathers it, and while he desires too greatly that his monastery abound in temporal goods, he prepares plunder for robbers. Often [unclear] devours the monies of monasteries, which the excessive greed of the monks brings into the cenobium. Woe to you, greedy pastor of cloisterers, who have greater concern for brute animals than for those entrusted to you souls. A horse falls ill, and at once you prepare a remedy; a soul perishes, and you think no danger is imminent. An ox and an ass fall sick, and you show them compassion; a brother is swallowed up by sadness, and you do not come to his aid. You, then, are a hireling, not a shepherd: you despise the infirmities of your brothers with a stubborn heart; you do not help those set in bitterness. Do not suppose that you can escape the hand of the Lord, whose sheep you permit to perish so wickedly.

Third, a ruler is disordered toward his subjects when he places outside, not without danger, those whom he ought carefully to have kept within the enclosures of the monastery. For truly, when a weak cenobite is exposed to the governance of nuns or to secular churches, the integrity of regular observance is violated, because one who, still dwelling in the lowest region, has not learned to subject the flesh to the spirit does not know how to preside over others without danger to himself.

But the disordered shepherd who, for the sake of some advantage in temporal affairs, is not afraid to expose his monks to so great a danger is guilty of all the souls struck down on such an occasion, and before the inward judge he is bound to make restitution for all of them. It does not belong to a monk’s profession to govern secular churches; it is not expedient for a weak cenobite to preside over nuns. But what then? Ought a monk to oppose the command of his shepherd if he wishes him to reside with nuns or in secular churches? For the Rule commands that nothing is to be preferred to obedience. I truly do not know what I should answer to this question, so that I may not incur the danger that is seen to threaten on both sides. For if I speak the truth, I shall seem to weaken the subjection of obedience; if I consent to exposing monks to danger, I confess that I sin. Yet I shall say briefly what I think, although I know that the truth will give birth to hatred. Just as a monk, by the necessity of his profession, is simply bound to obey his shepherd in all things that are according to the monastic Rule, so a prelate cannot compel a monk, without that monk’s own will, to things that are beyond the Rule, especially when danger to salvation intervenes. But to govern churches, to preside over women, to reside outside the monastery: this is not to have obeyed according to the Rule. Do not be angry with me, fathers, if I have spoken the truth; do not contract your brows if I have expressed what seems right to me. You, nevertheless, will do what seems right to you, even if I protest. Yet I beg you: do not expose your monks to dangers to chastity; do not violently compel anyone to the governance of nuns and parish churches, since you can find many who ambitiously seek these offices. Obedience is indeed good, but it must in no way be preferred to truth and to the salvation of the soul. For when danger to salvation is at issue, it is better to set obedience aside by humbly excusing oneself than to suffer shipwreck of chastity. Woe to the prelates of monks who incorporate secular churches into their monasteries, who widen the bosom of desire with the torches of avarice, because while they think they are benefiting posterity, they damn many through the occasion.

Fourth, a ruler of monks becomes disordered toward his subjects if he is found turbulent and anxious. In a shepherd of souls, pious and prudent discretion is very necessary, lest either zeal for discipline be excessive or the measure of compassion be relaxed by too much laxity. But a disordered ruler sometimes, through indiscreet fury, considers himself a tyrant of monks and does not know himself as the father and companion of the humble. What can be more savage than this kind of rule, what more criminal than this kind of power, where not God, not reason, not understanding, but a beast holds sway? For truly, where God and understanding govern authority, the judgments of those who preside do not depart from the rectitude of the law of nature. But a disordered and anxious ruler is infected by the various passions of beasts; he always suspects evil of the monks, and while he directs the manner of his rule wrongly, he is always anxious and, with Herod, greatly fears losing his kingdom.

Fifth, a shepherd of cloistered men is said to be disordered toward the monks if, in dispensing the goods of the monastery, he is considered either excessive or obstinate. He must be called excessive if, in distributing, he has been prodigal, or too lavish through indiscreet generosity. But he is called obstinate if he does not give at the proper time the things that ought to be given does not give what ought to be given, or grudgingly dispenses necessities to his subjects. He is also to be called obstinate who casts aside the fear of the Lord; who trusts too much in his own judgment; who, in any matters to be done, admits no counsels of the wise. And indeed, among pastors of souls, very many are disordered by this sickness of mind: they either spend the resources of the monastery too improvidently, or preserve them with too much tenacity. For their flatterers they prepare the most sumptuous feasts; but to others, to whom they are averse, they deny even the smallest things. In the guesthouse or in their abbacy, pastors depraved by disordered conduct sometimes eat to the point of gluttony and always drink the best wine; but to the poor monks, who by watching and singing bear the burden of the day and the heat, they scarcely and meagerly grant necessities.

Sixth, a prelate of monks is shown to be very disordered if, bold against God, he is lifted up in pride by making light of his judgments. For indeed, since the pastor cannot be corrected by his subjects, he is referred by the holy father Benedict to the judgment of God, as is found in many places of the Rule. “Let the abbot know,” he says, “that he must render an account to God for all his judgments.” And again: “The ordained abbot should always consider what burden he has undertaken, and to whom he is going to render an account of his stewardship.” And again he says: “As soon as vices begin to arise, let him cut them off with charity, not with tyranny.” And in another place he admonishes, saying: “Yet the abbot himself should do all things with the fear of God and the observance of the holy Rule, knowing without doubt that he will render an account of all his judgments to God, the most just judge.” But the disordered ruler of monks, like an asp with stopped-up ears, despises hearing this threat of the most holy lawgiver; he scorns the patience of God’s long-suffering; he thinks nothing of the examination to come, until at last the judge, angry with him, says to his face: “These things you have done, and I was silent. Now, therefore, render an account of your stewardship. Give back to me the sheep of my inheritance, and restore to me without delay the souls once entrusted to you in the body. Return their number entire. If even one of them has perished through your negligence, your soul will never behold my face forever.

What then will you answer to the supreme pastor, useless ruler, when not only is the blood of those who perish required from you, but an account is also demanded for those who made too little progress? Behold, now you walk in the worst security, despising God’s examination; you think that in the body all things that please you are lawful for you, and you never consider to whom you must someday render an account for all things. Soon the Lord of all will come, to whom you do not fear to show yourself an unfaithful minister, and whose honor you do not fear to usurp for yourself. Unless meanwhile you do penance, unless you amend your life for the better, you will burn without end with the demons in hell.”

Seventh, it happens that a pastor is disordered toward his subjects if, neglecting the common utility, he seeks his own advantage with a vicious intention; if, presiding in the monastery, he serves not God but his own interests, while he rejoices that he is prelate in order to obtain ruinous liberties of the flesh, and fraudulently provides for himself in the future from the resources of the monastery. This disorder is especially visible in those who resign their office on some pretext, to whom, as payment for their stewardship, just as if they had been bishops, an annual pension from the resources of the monastery is assigned. This is not the way of those who seek the Lord; this is not the path of the ancient monks. When you resign the pastoral office for God’s sake, resign it simply. Do not demand anything beyond food and clothing, if you do not wish to sin with proprietors. You are a monk; you were a monk before you became abbot; you will remain a monk after the office. Why, then, do you demand a pension, when you know that you are a monk? For just as the vice of simony is committed by buying prelacies, so by demanding a pension for the resignation of an abbacy, one sins against the Rule. What then? Do we condemn those who, resigning the office of pastoral care without fault, have received annual provisions from the resources of the monastery? Far from it. We do not forbid necessities, since we deny superfluities. Nevertheless, one who is a true monk and lover of God is content with the regular provision even after an abbacy.

How Monks of the Lowest Region Are Disordered Toward One Another.

Article 4

The inhabitants of the lowest region, monks and carnal men, are disordered toward one another in many and various ways. For since, stirred by animal passions like beasts, they do not direct themselves according to the right judgment of reason, it is no wonder if they pervert the order of brotherly life. For a savage, troubled conscience is always presumptuous, and an evil mind never has the joys of peace, but is continually shaken by vice and sorrow; inwardly it is tormented by the everlasting fires of crimes. And so monks who are inhabitants of the dark region, blinded by evil and disordered affections, do not consider the end of the monastic profession. They love nothing except the advantage of the present life; they neglect their own salvation; they do not rise up to the love of eternity.

First, therefore, they are greatly disordered toward one another when they cast aside the intellectual regard that should be had for brothers; when they do not take note of the image of God in man; when they do not think of the communion of grace and glory infused into human beings and to be granted in the future; nor do they take care to show one another the love of brotherly fellowship. They live together like horse and mule, in agreement according to the bodily frame, because they love whatever is pleasing to sensuality, and do not admit whatever accords with reason. One is loved by another not because he is a human being, but because he is like his lover in the affection of sensuality. For the carnal man loves in a human being not virtues, not religion, not, finally, nature itself, but flesh, blood, and bodily quality. Since therefore the love of carnal men is carnal, it is easily changeable at any occasion. For the inhabitants of this lowest region revere those whose habits they find like their own, and monks always embrace monks equal to themselves in affection. The disorderly cenobite persecutes the one whom God has loved from eternity; the one whom God himself spurns because of his demerits, this man venerates as a saint.

Second, cloistered men are disordered toward one another by reason of dissimilarity, when either the elders, stirred by austerity and pride, despise their juniors, or the juniors stubbornly set themselves against their seniors. And this disorder is proved to be very contrary to the holy Rule, which commands the seniors to love the juniors with fatherly affection, and instructs the juniors to obey their seniors humbly for God's sake.

But since the elders, inhabitants of this lowest region, withhold fatherly affection from the juniors, the younger men blaze up into grave hatred; and when they consider that as young men they are unjustly despised by them, they accuse their depraved habits every day. Therefore weak young men learn the crooked habits of the elders; and, as the proverb says, just as they see the greater ones sing, so too the lesser ones dance.

Third, monks are badly ordered toward one another when they cast aside good zeal and mutual obedience, and take up the evil kind of zeal forbidden by the Rule. In words and deeds they commit various injuries against one another. One, in his effort to rival the other, strives to watch him for evil; one is provoked by another to inflict insult. They mutually reproach one another with their infirmities; they are always panting for vengeance. Zeal for regular discipline is despised; the passion of indignation and bitterness rules. They meet one another with faces turned away; by clear signs they make manifest how much hatred lies hidden in the breast. Not so the wicked, not so: for whoever persecutes his brother with hatred is proved a murderer and unworthy of the kingdom of God. O always wretched condition of carnal monks, which is so much the nearer to hell as it has been alienated from the fear of God. For those who through evil zeal delight in being discordant in the school of peace imitate not angels but demons. For truly, just as a brute animal does not abandon the savagery of its nature, so a beastly monk does not withdraw from the worst zeal.

How monks who are inhabitants of the lowest region are disordered toward themselves. Article V.

The inhabitants of the lowest region, carnal monks, are disordered toward nothing more than toward themselves. For they cast aside every consideration of themselves; they do not attend to the end for which they were created, because while each one pollutes himself with the filth of vices, the depraved mind withdraws from the original rectitude of its condition. Nor is it any wonder if outside himself the cultivator of the lowest region becomes disordered toward others, since through various passions [unclear].

through the passions of the flesh, inwardly confused, is scattered away from himself. For Scripture says: “He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” The right order of the human condition established that the flesh should be subjected to the spirit; the spirit is commanded to be subject to him from whom it received the form of being. But among carnal minds the order of reason is perverted, since the flesh dominates the spirit; and reason, which according to the power of understanding implanted in it ought to have governed everything, is suffocated by the pleasures of the flesh and does not hasten toward uprightness of judgment through command.

Carnal monks, therefore, are disorderly toward themselves through the vice of curiosity, because by prying they curiously judge another’s life, and do not amend their own, stained with every vice. They do not know how to correct great crimes in themselves, although they proudly rebuke others who sin in the smallest things. They carefully consider the speck in a brother’s eye, and excuse the beam clinging in their own eyes as though it were nothing. They subject all their affections to sensuality, and, despising the judgment of right reason, live carnally like beasts; passion often stirs them to anger, and the fury of envy inflames them against their neighbor. With an anxious mind they always demand vengeance against the brothers; blinded by excessive rage, they often bring it back not without harm to themselves. But disorderly citizens cannot remain long hidden in secret, because the more they remain unknown to themselves through elation of mind, the more they are made manifest to others through blind judgment. For every proud and disorderly man is said first to be ignorant of himself, since if he truly knew himself, he would in no way be proud. Since, however, disorder of oneself takes its origin from pride, we cannot describe this plague better than if we take care to disclose its roots, descending by degrees to hell. For just as the perfection of the spiritual life is contained in twelve degrees of humility, so the source of all monastic disorder is contained in twice-six degrees of pride.

The first degree of pride, then, is called curiosity. By it monks badly ordered toward themselves neglect their own life and morals, and continually inquire into the deeds or words of others. At every time they accuse the negligences of the brothers and rebuke the life of the pastor, because the more curiously they desire to know external matters belonging to others, the farther they withdraw from themselves. But the vice of curiosity is most pernicious to monks, because once it has invaded their mind, stripping it of all virtues, it makes it a dwelling place of vices. It is the surest sign of infirmity to examine the deeds of others and, apart from the reason of one’s office, to be occupied with others’ affairs. For the monk who, according to the definition of his name, is commanded to care for himself alone, searches out the deeds of others not without manifest danger to his salvation. Whoever subjects himself to the vice of curiosity soon descends into the second degree of pride. For one always disposes a person toward another, and no single sin rules alone over proud monks.

The second degree of pride, therefore, is lightness of mind and the unstable occupation of a wandering heart. Carnal monks fall into this degree of disorderly conduct through various affections, which they have sensually contracted from the vice of curiosity. But the true cenobite must remain steadfast in his holy purpose, because when lightness of mind is admitted, the constancy of virtue is scattered in the heart. It is the mark of a disorderly mind’s judgment to run about among various images of things, and always to beget new forms of sensual affections.

The third degree of pride is called empty joy, which is begotten from the lightness of a disorderly man’s mind. Carnal monks compose for themselves various images of affections; when these occur pleasantly to sensuality, they rejoice, but when it turns out otherwise, they contract grave indignation and slip into various temptations. But that joy is not true which does not take its beginning from decorum, nor does a joy long persevere which does not have its source in the love of God. And therefore disorderly men, tossed about by vain joy, fall into foolish boasting, when they falsely ascribe great things to themselves.

The fourth degree of pride, then, as we have said, arises from empty joy; it is called foolish boasting. Carnal monks fall into this when they magnify and exalt themselves before others. If they have done anything good, they boldly bring it forward in public, often falsely inventing even things they have not done. They desire to seem holy, learned, prudent, and noble, and they invent many things by the craftiness of their wit, so that they may appear glorious outwardly to men, though inwardly they know they are empty of the merit of virtue. If anyone is praised before them if you begin, he at once rises up to the contrary: he says many vicious things against him, because, while they desire to show that only they themselves are worthy of praise, they do not allow anyone else to be praised in their presence.

The fifth degree of pride is taken to be singularity, which is generated from the swelling of boasting. Proud cloistered men fall into this degree, who, through boasting, have presumed that they surpass others either in merit or in knowledge. Hence, lest they should appear like the others in their manner of life, out of mere pride they make themselves singular in everything. But this singularity is reprehended in a monastery, where all are commanded by the rule to live in common. Proud monks, as Saint Bernard testifies, when they prefer themselves to others in virtues and wisdom, fall into such arrogance of rashness that they flatter themselves more over one fast while the others are eating than if they had fasted seven days with the others. Finally, one little singular prayer seems more suitable to them than the whole psalmody of one night. During the meal they often carry their eyes around the table; and if they see anyone eating less, they groan, and begin to grieve that they have been outdone, cruelly withholding from themselves what they had provided for necessary sustenance. These proud cloistered men are vigorous in their own singular practices, but sluggish in common ones. They keep watch in bed; in choir and at the regular reading they doze.

The sixth degree of pride takes its beginning from the fifth, and is called the arrogance of the proud. For indeed, when disordered cloistered men, through the pursuit of singularity, begin outwardly to appear different from others, they burn with a greater madness of arrogance; and whatever is said by men in their praise, the fools think true. O pitiable folly of the proud: since in all other matters they believe no one more than themselves, about themselves alone they believe themselves less than another. Whatever praise they hear about themselves from the inexperienced, they attribute not to the ignorance or goodwill of the praiser, but to their own merits. But whoever is agreeably fed on human praises is held before the Lord to be empty of every virtue and full of arrogance.

The seventh degree of pride is born from the preceding one, and is called the presumption of the proud. All the arrogant fall into this, who individually believe themselves to be something great.

Concerning these Bernard says: He who thinks that he surpasses others, how should he not presume more about himself than about others? He sits first in the assembly; in councils he answers first; he comes forward uncalled; he thrusts himself in unbidden; he rearranges what has been arranged; he rejects what has been done by others. Whatever he himself has not done or arranged, he does not think rightly done or beautifully ordered. He judges those who judge; he prejudges those who are going to judge. For the one for whom God is not enough in the heart seeks comfort in outward things in vain.

The eighth degree of pride is called the defense of sins, which is always generated from presumption. For a presumptuous monk, always thinking himself better than everyone, if he commits something either obstinately denies it, or, if he has been convicted, excuses it in many ways. For how will he be able humbly to confess his fault, who does not acknowledge himself guilty? If you wish to chastise such a man for his offenses, you always make him worse. Therefore whoever, when corrected for any matter, falls into malicious words; whoever opposes excuses for sins to the one reproving him: he falls into this descent of death, which is set opposite the fifth degree of humility. The presumptuous man who is found to have fallen into this degree of pride tries in various ways to excuse his sin. For he says either: I did not do it; or: I did it indeed, but I did well; or, if badly: not very badly; or, if very badly: not with evil intention. And if he has been convicted of malice, immediately in excuse of himself he does not fear to bring forward the counsel of another or of his abbot; and sometimes, contrary to the rule, he will reveal the secrets of his abbey. But when he comes to confession, he will cloak the truth with a feigned mind, because, so that he himself may escape confusion, he strives to bring the negligences of others into the open. Inwardly disordered, proud, and presumptuous, in confession he cloaks his own faults and confesses those of others. Always restless within himself, with one sentence he condemns the examinations and deeds of others; he complains that no one lives rightly in the monastery; he thinks that there is no charity among the brothers. But if vain presumption if it has been detected by the diligence of the confessor, he at once seeks another confessor; and if the abbot should begin to contradict him, or even gently to do so, the elated monk falls through restlessness of mind into the ninth degree of pride.

The ninth degree of pride is described as murmuring or impatience, which for the most part rules carnal monks. For truly, when a man whose confession is feigned is touched by one slight reproach or penance, he at once rises up into open pride; the deceit of feigned humility is uncovered, and the false mind can no longer hide itself, but is compelled to bring out into public whatever lies hidden within. From then on, having lost command of himself, the proud monk in the monastery murmurs at everything; he contumaciously accuses the judgment of the pastor, however just it may be; he gnashes with his teeth; when stirred, he grows angry; without reason, like a madman, he is thrown into disorder. But the proud monk, given over to murmuring, having despised the fourth degree of humility, falls into the tenth descent of pride, through which he runs toward hell.

The tenth degree of pride follows murmuring, and is called rebellion. Proud and carnal monks fall into this, who, still dwelling in the lowest region, devote themselves to murmurings. Hence Bernard says: Unless divine compassion looks upon the murmurer, so that at last, converted, which is very difficult for such men, he quietly acquiesces in the judgments of others, he soon becomes brazen and shameless, and falls the more disastrously into this degree, in proportion as, in despair, he does not restrain the movement of his soul. He always advances toward worse things; and he who before had arrogantly despised his brothers in secret now openly shows what is still more serious: that he despises his master.

But the censure of divine judgment does not allow this degree of pride to pass long unpunished. For monks rebellious against their pastors often apostatize from the order; others, because of grave crimes, occupy prisons; some, expelled from monasteries, wander and live as miserable exiles; many, horribly struck by the Lord, hasten in despair to the lower world. For it is written: He who resists authority opposes the ordinance of God.

And again the Lord says concerning the prelates of the faithful: He who despises you despises me. What will you say to these things, rebellious monks? Will you cite laws to me, by which you corrupt the truth? But I dare to say what perhaps you are not ashamed to hear. In the strict judgment of God, presumption of law will not save you, rebellious monk, who now proudly despise the obedience of subjection. Law commands obedience; it requires humble subjection in the order.

Rebellious monks consequently fall into the eleventh degree of pride, which is the freedom to sin: those who despise not only the corrections and exhortations of the brothers, but also those of the prelates. For truly, when rebellion is taken up against the teacher, boldness in sinning is generated, because one who despises the authority of correction now commits every crime as if by license. The love of God voluntarily restrains good monks in the monastery from sins, and fear holds back the weak. But where neither the love of God nor fear of correction penetrates a monk, the mind, through rebellion and the habit of sinning, is already approaching hell. For Scripture says: When the impious man has come into the depths of evils, he contemns. What does he contemn? He contemns God; he despises men; in despair he does not know how to seek the salvation of his soul.

Therefore they fall into the twelfth degree of pride who, through boldness in sinning, run into an evil habit. This is the nearest descent to hell; this is the path of hell; this is the swift road to the region covered with the darkness of death. Whoever has once fallen into this degree of the habit of sinning rises again only by the strong hand of God’s mercy, because when habit is not resisted, necessity of sinning is generated. For he always advances in worse malice, and always, falling, drops more deeply.

Behold, these are the twelve degrees of pride through which one descends to hell. Whoever desires to escape them should always strive to keep himself in the observance of humility. In these twelve evils every indignity of vices overshadows the monk in the monastery; it causes him to be disordered in himself; in his conduct it changes a man into a most savage beast. The end of these things is destruction; and unless, before the death of the flesh, the remedy of repentance intervenes, the progress of the evil degrees will leave the monk to burn without end.

condemns him. Whoever, already disordered in himself, has once fallen into the first degree of pride, unless he strives to rise again as quickly as possible through penitence, soon casts himself down into the second, and consequently into all the others in order. The full measure of the disorder of carnal monks in themselves is expressed in these degrees of self-exaltation, through which the disordered citizens of the lowest region are shown forth. What we have said about disordered and proud monks must also be understood of the prelates of the lowest region.

In What Way the Citizens of the Lowest Region, Carnal Monks, Are Disordered with Regard to the Goods of the Monastery. Article VI

Whoever, while established in the monastery, neglects to order his inner affections toward the purity of his holy profession, also frequently exceeds measure grievously in outward matters. For monks disordered toward God are consequently shown to be disordered toward everything. For just as the good cenobite, united by love to the divine will, considers everything with a simple eye according to the right order of reason, so one turned away from God through disordered affections sins even in good things when he uses them badly. Therefore carnal monks, inhabitants of the lowest region, are badly disordered not only with regard to the soul, but also with regard to the temporal substance of the monastery. For outward disturbance of the body follows the inner confusion of the mind, and the one is shown by the other.

First, then, the citizen of the lowest region is badly ordered with regard to the goods of the monastery when he demands that they be granted to him in an improper order, or in any way usurps more than the use of regular observance permits. For our rule, which commands that all necessary things be given to monks, utterly forbids superfluities.

Second, those who do not fear to give and receive against the prohibition of the master use the goods of the monastery badly; so do those who act unfaithfully, with deceit and fraud, in the things entrusted to them. For the monk who, at his own pleasure, without reasonable cause, against the rule, and without permission, dissipates the goods of the monastery in any way, sins against the rule like an unfaithful and false proprietor.

Third, monks or abbots show themselves disordered toward the goods of the monastery when they devote them to unlawful uses. Theft and sacrilege are committed together when the goods of the monastery are converted to illicit uses. For the substance of the monastery, dedicated to God, should be kept like the vessels of the holy altar, lest it be dissipated in any way through negligence. But whoever forbids the goods of the cloister to be spent uselessly would by no means grant that they be squandered sinfully on base uses. What answer will monks and rulers of the lowest region give to the lawgiver in the strict examination, when they do not fear to dissipate the goods of the monastery on parents, relatives, minstrels, and shameful people, as occasion and reward for sin?

Fourth, carnal abbots and monks sin more gravely in the goods of the monastery when they gather them with excessive greed, to the detriment of divine charity and of their own salvation. For those made subject to the tribute of avarice think of nothing but profits and money; violating feast days, they do not observe them; they always desire to increase temporal goods; they do not notice the losses of charity. They grieve more over a dying beast than over a sinner perishing. Indeed, all disordered cloistered men are so blind that they consider avarice prudence and think wealth is reform. They join field to field; they call gain piety; and where they see temporal things abound, there they say the best discipline is observed. They refuse to spend even small sums for the common good of the order, because they have truly lost the order of charity. They raise useless, curious, and damnable structures on high; they keep costly vestments and ornaments less necessary for divine service; they clothe sacred things in gold and leave the poor of Christ naked. This avaricious curiosity does not befit monks, since we are commanded to imitate the ancient saints and are ordered to sell these things for the support of the poor. But a covetous monk and an avaricious abbot are as far from the purpose of holy religion as the devil is from heaven.

Fifth, carnal monks sin in the goods of the monastery when they do not recompense them with prayers. Alms All receive the alms of the faithful cheerfully, but few bestow the support of prayers upon those who give them. From these things many citizens of the lowest region, when they have come to the order, serve not God but the belly. They desire more food, drink, and clothing to be given them than necessity requires; and those who in the world could scarcely have bread and vegetables for food, now, having become monks, refuse eggs and little fish. They importunately demand that large, varied, different, and delicate fish be given them. Murmuring from the concupiscence of the flesh with the children of Israel in the desert, they cry out to their leader, saying that they cannot eat eggs and peas; they always desire more delicate things.

How the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered toward contempt of the world

Article VII

The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Therefore whoever desires to enter the heavenly kingdom by the arms of holy obedience, whoever chooses to live for God under regular conduct, must do violence to the pleasures of the flesh and firmly contemn the world with all its vanities. But the carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, who are badly ordered both toward God and toward their neighbors, are also badly ordered toward contempt of the world.

And first, they are infected by concupiscence of the flesh, for they always burn with the fire of pleasure. In food and drink they are found excessive; in beds and baths, against the rules, self-indulgent; they prefer the desires of the flesh to the salvation of the soul; they do not seek the sweetness of inner conduct. They nourish their flesh too delicately, through which they continually burn in various concupiscences. For no one can truly contemn the world who neglects to restrain the appetite of the flesh even in the smallest things. If you eat to satiety, you do not truly contemn the world. For the first commandment imposed upon contemners of the world is grounded in abstinence alone. But if you fill your belly with food to the point of satiety, you at once incur either lust or grave acedia.

Therefore concupiscence of the flesh draws back the mind of the disordered cenobite, so that he cannot contemn the world.

Second, they are disordered toward contemning the world because of the vain concupiscence of the eyes. For the monk who forgets the true honor of faithful souls delights entirely in worldly pomps and curious ornaments. Indeed, what each person is inwardly, hidden within himself, his outward attire makes manifest. To carry rings on the fingers, corals on scarves, scent-vessels in the hands, and pleats in cowls does not show a monk but a soldier; it presents not a humble cenobite but a proud secular man. This ornamentation in monks cannot please anyone except the reprobate, and it is often found to have displeased even the proud. Woe to you, disordered cloisterers, who descend to hell through the double concupiscence of the eyes, while you desire to see in others what is not fitting, and present yourselves to be seen by others otherwise than you ought.

What have you to do with the trinkets of the world? What with worldly curiosities? All these beauties, as the divine Bernard bears witness, make a masculine soul effeminate; these outward honors quickly weaken a manly purpose. Such men are like ragged boys who, because of one thin red strip fastened to a torn sleeve, think themselves very handsome and elegant, and insolently mock others standing before them, though they are very well dressed, as if they were naked. These pompous cloisterers see others, walking in humble habit, contemn the world in the spirit of poverty, and for that reason please both God and human beings; but they see themselves despised by the wise and by princes, and sometimes not even admitted to conversation. Seeing these things, the proud, even if they grieve heavily as if over an injury, nevertheless utterly refuse to lay aside their arrogance.

Third, the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered toward contempt of the world because of pride of life, since they are not only infected by vain pleasures of the flesh, but also proud through swelling of mind. For all who follow the desires of the flesh are puffed up in spirit; they do not know how to endure equals; they do not admit superiors. These men rejoice that a great retinue of servants attends them.

they strive to sit first in councils; they desire to seem glorious to men; they walk pompously in public. Inflated by the spirit of pride, they boast that by foundation they possess distinguished monasteries, rich in temporal goods, remarkable for treasures, buildings, and privileges. With an exalted heart they despise poor monks or abbots of small monasteries; they are not ashamed to prefer themselves to their betters. The more they desire to hunt for glory in outward things, the more they withdraw from true glory with the foolish virgins.

In what way the citizens of this lowest region are disordered toward penitence.

Article VIII

Since man, born of woman, living for a short time and filled with many miseries, cannot remain long in the same state, it is necessary that with all zeal he turn himself daily, by reforming himself, toward his due end; for as long as anyone is permitted to live in this world, he is shown to be changeable in either direction. Therefore whoever, placed in this mutability, desires to come to the joys of immutability should humbly acknowledge his frailty, should always, after the fall of sin, flee to the remedies of penitence, and should fear to lie in crime even for a moment. For the life of a monk must always consist in saving penitence, and he must continually await the coming of the judge with holy fear. For blessed Jerome says: “A monk has the office not of one who teaches but of one who laments, who should mourn either himself or the world, and should await the Lord’s coming in fear.” But the disordered cloisterers of the lowest region despise this saving remedy; they consume the acceptable time in vanity; and because they do not fear to be badly ordered toward all things, they show themselves very disordered even for doing penitence.

First, indeed, they are badly ordered toward penitence through negligence of mind, when they neglect to understand how greatly sin displeases almighty God, against whom, by the decision of a depraved will, they do not fear to rebel. Just as black night is opposed to day, so the sinner, turned away from divine goodness, is opposed and hostile to it.

What a putrid corpse is accustomed to do in the sight of men, sin in its own way does incomparably in the sight of angels.
