But carnal monks despise the honor of God and therefore do not notice the disgrace of sin. They neglect to amend venial sins, as if they might lawfully commit mortal ones. For Scripture says: “He who neglects the smallest things gradually falls.” Hence Bernard’s sentence warns us, saying: “Let no one, brothers, say in his heart: These are light matters; I do not care to correct them. It is no great thing if I remain in these venial and very small sins. This, brothers, is impenitence; this is the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is unforgivable.” For no one can escape greater sins if he has disdained to amend the lesser ones. Nothing is worse than negligence of mind.

Second, the carnal monks, lovers of the lowest region, are exceedingly disordered toward penitence because they do not perceive the contagion of sin. For just as a healthy man is often infected by a contagious disease, so from one sin a man is inclined into another. For one sin is always said to dispose toward another, unless it is amended as quickly as possible through contrition. For the prophet says: “Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become unstable; let her be defiled still.” We have sufficiently shown the contagion of this disease in the degrees of pride; for just as we said that one always arises from another, so we perceive that through negligence a man becomes slippery from one sin into another.

Third, carnal monks, disordered toward penitence, contract a very bad sickness through the habit of sin, when they incur a pernicious blindness of mind. Every vice, often committed, is held cheap and is judged lighter through habit. Just as grace enlightens the mind, so the frequency of sin blinds reason. For it is written: “Blind the heart of this people and make its ears heavy, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest they be converted and I heal them,” says the Lord. For when the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises. No sin is so great that it does not seem light and small through habit.

Fourth, disordered cloisterers, through the habit of evil, ob Blinded by sin, they do not come to the grace of true compunction; they approach confession superficially, from habit alone; they do not abandon their depraved will; they do not truly take up a purpose of amendment. Woe to those who, buried in the habit of sin, do not fear the judgment of a strict examination; who do not withdraw from blindness of mind by the remedy of contrition. For just as they now despise the long-suffering of God’s goodness, so in that terrible hour they will undergo the sentence of eternal death. What can confession of the mouth profit where there is no true contrition of heart? Without contrition there is no saving confession, nor can there be contrition without a purpose of amendment. The test of contrition is to be unwilling to sin any more.

Fifth, the disorderly citizens of the lowest region, made contemners of almighty God through the habit of sinning, always fall into graver dangers of soul, since they always approach badly the most holy sacred mysteries of the body and blood of the Lord. They make a superficial confession from habit; they allow things that they think well ordered to run on in their consciences. And thereafter, as if confederates of hell, they do not fear God; they despise the paths of a more amended life; they think themselves well ordered; they do not care how many vices they are inwardly full of. Sometimes, sensibly affected by a fantastic devotion, they think that the Holy Spirit is now present; they affirm that they are beloved by God and holy. They also thrust themselves shamelessly upon the divine mysteries; not discerning the body and blood of the Lord, they take it to themselves for judgment and condemnation.

Finally, such people, communicating unworthily, are hardened more gravely, because, while they think themselves very secure and well conducted, they do not take proper care to cleanse their conscience of vices. Thus Judas the apostate, the evil of betrayal which at first, as someone says, he was afraid to commit against the Savior, after the morsel had entered and the devil had entered into him, did not fear to carry out boldly and without shame. O how many carnal monks are citizens of this lowest region: exalted, proud, envious, murmuring, and entangled in various sins, whose conscience is rarely or never made clean by true contrition, and who nevertheless are not afraid to approach the most holy altar almost every day.

Behold how evil is the society of all who dwell in this lowest region, whose end is destruction, for whom descent into hell is prepared through bodily death. This is the far-off region of beastliness and unlikeness, into which that prodigal son went away, who squandered the portion of his inheritance luxuriously with prostitutes. In this region the carnal citizens dwell, concerning whom the holy Apostle declares: The animal man does not know the things that are of God.

In this dark region, covered with the gloom of death, no spiritual good dwells. In it not peace but beastly discord reigns, as the prophet says: There is no peace for the wicked, says my Lord.

Concerning those who are neighbors to this lowest region and relapse into it rather often through inconstancy of mind.

Although between the first region of the bad and the second of the good there is properly no middle place, nevertheless there are some who often move between both, since from weakness they are at one time tepid, and at another time, from contrition of mind, seem to be devout. These are weak people. Although they are not submerged in the lowest region, nevertheless through negligence they are very near to it; and indeed they frequently fall into it through bad habit, since they do not withdraw, as far as they can, from the affections of the flesh.

Concerning them Bernard says in a certain sermon: Harmful tepidity, because it is dangerous, because it is most troublesome and full of misery and sorrow, and plainly nearest to hell, is rightly judged the shadow of death. Indeed, one may find fainthearted and remiss people, failing under the burden, needing the rod and spurs, whose joy is brief, whose sadness is fainthearted, whose compunction is brief and rare. Their thought is animal; their way of life tepid; their obedience without devotion; their speech without circumspection; their prayer without the heart’s attention; their reading without edification. Finally, as we see, fear of Gehenna scarcely restrains them; shame scarcely holds them back; reason scarcely bridles them; discipline scarcely confines them. But if people of this kind remain long under the burden, either they are crushed and fall, or in some way they are in hell, so that they never breathe fully under the sweet yoke and light burden. From this, however, so Now such pernicious lukewarmness flows from the fact that their will has not yet been purified, and they do not will the good as they know it, being drawn away and enticed by their own concupiscence. For in their flesh they love little earthly consolations, whether in word, or in sign, or in deed, or in something else; and even if at times they interrupt these things, still they do not break them off completely. Hence it is that they rarely direct their affections toward God, and their compunction is not continuous, but occasional. But a soul that is subject to these distractions cannot be filled with the visitations of the Lord; and the more it is emptied of the former, the more fully it will be filled with the latter. If much, much; if little, little. Or perhaps, if you prefer, these things will never be able to be mixed with those forever. For spirit and flesh do not dwell in one home, nor fire and lukewarmness, especially since lukewarmness itself is accustomed to provoke the Lord to vomiting.

Therefore whoever desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the region of the spirit, should always take care to drive torpor of mind away from himself, and in his holy purpose to burn continually through the fire of divine love. Nothing harms those wishing to serve God so much as lukewarmness of mind. It always arises at first from some small negligence, but unless it is immediately treated, it grows wonderfully by degrees. Moreover, one placed near the lowest region of religion often falls back into that same region, because the dregs of his former carnal way of life still subtly occupy his will, and by an easy occasion disturb the weak fervor of his devotion.

But no one can rise from the depth of hell with a lukewarm will; no one can overcome a habit without a contrary habit, because unless some violence intervenes, the habitual practice of sin will always strengthen vice. This lowest region is rightly called hell, for by a certain likeness of disturbance and aversion it is compared to hell. After this life there are three dwelling places of souls, which receive their citizens emigrating from this world from the three regions. The first dwelling place is called hell, and it is compared to the lowest region. For just as in hell no order, but everlasting horror, dwells, so in this lowest region all things are disturbed by the frenzy of a mind blinded by carnal affections.

In hell all are evil, and in the lowest region good people are nowhere found. Whoever falls into hell has come from the lowest region. For the lowest region always sends its citizens to hell, unless, led by repentance while alive, they have taken care to renounce dead works.

The second dwelling place is called purgatory, and it is compared to the second, rational region. For just as purgatory purges and perfects souls, and sends those purged on to the kingdom of heaven, so this second region, through continuous exercise, washes the citizens persevering in it from the stains of sins, and disposes them for the ascent of the third region, which is called spirit. In this dwelling place all are good, but still to be purged so that they may become better; and in the second region no evil people are found, but they must always be exercised so that they may be made better. This region sends its citizens who die in it to purgatory, because, even if all are good, they do not yet seem fit for the kingdom without temporal purification. For indeed, those who inhabit this middle region, although they seem to be very near the highest, have still not yet been entirely removed from the dust of the lower region.

The third dwelling place of separated souls is called the kingdom of heaven, and it is compared to the highest region of the spirit. For just as in that heavenly homeland there is the highest rest and eternal peace, so in the region of the spirit there is continual tranquillity of mind.

Here ends the first region.

Preface to the second treatise of the first part, which deals with the middle region, namely the rational region, of cloisterers

And now at last let us leave behind this dark region of the carnal, in which the whirlwind of crimes remains and the continual storm of vices. We have granted enough to it, and have lingered over it more than our purpose required. Let us therefore leave the dead to bury their dead; let us yield to the darkness; let us hasten toward the light of the spiritual life. We must go out from the Egypt of the dark region and hasten diligently to the highest summit of the spirit through the middle way of reason. Let us therefore now at last approach the middle region of the soul, through which one comes successively to the highest. This region of the soul is quite suitably called rational, since in it there is continual labor for the investigation of the highest truth. The fervor of mind of the citizens of this middle region always strives to raise them to higher things, but the weakness of the flesh, by the motion of a raging whirlwind, attempts to draw them back to the lowest things. From this comes continual labor; from this arise sighs and groans, because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and this earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks on many things.

This is the narrow way that leads to life, and few walk along it. In this region violence is laid upon the concupiscences of the flesh until the will is subjected to the spirit at its command. For the Lord says in the Gospel: The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. In this region the war of contest is declared against those who serve God, as the wise man bears witness, saying: Son, when you approach the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. How great the temptations are in this middle region we learn daily through the difficulty of spiritual exercise, when, driven in various ways, we cannot remain long in the fervor of the spirit. Now the weakness of the flesh recalls us from zeal for advancement; now the temptation of the ancient enemy troubles us; now the company of neighbors hinders us;

now the deceitfulness of the world leads us astray. Therefore those who wish to make progress in this region of labor need the greatest fortitude, because no one can resist his temptations to the end unless he strives daily to do violence to himself. Whoever thinks that he has come to this region should not presume upon his own powers, because just as the grace of God, in order to work good in us, requires the choice of our will, so the will necessarily requires grace. For no one is holy by his own powers. Therefore let no one dare to presume upon himself, but let him who stands take care lest he fall. The life of man upon earth is warfare, because through many tribulations one comes to the kingdom, and by the arduous labors of the virtues heaven is acquired. The prophet says: Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. For indeed those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. But if someone fails in the sowing, he certainly will not rejoice in the harvest.

Since, therefore, through the continual labors of spiritual exercise the mind must be cleansed from the dust of the first region, do not seek leisure in this middle region; do not love the repose of negligence, because no one is able to stand here except the one who firmly girds himself for continual labor. Whoever in this middle region does not always advance toward better things soon falls into the negligences of his former life, and there falls into the danger of failing where he has lost the desire of advancing. This is the place of continual contest; whoever neglects to fight in it retreats backward to be conquered.

Here ends the preface.

Here begins the second region of the soul, which is called rational, in which men are engaged amid many labors

The second region of the soul, therefore, is called rational, in which the mind is exercised with continual labor for the investigation of the highest truth; and the farther it separates itself from the lowest region, the more it approaches the highest. And this region is proposed to be likened in certain ways to the ethereal heaven, in which there is the position of the stars and their continual motion.

For just as motion itself is always ordered in heaven by the order of the first mover as its cause, so continuous labor is carried on in the middle region, so that each intellectual power may perfect its own object and in no way depart from the order naturally implanted in it. There are three powers of the soul of this kind: memory, intellect, and will.

Of these, memory gathers the likenesses of things and phantasms, and extends itself toward what is difficult. The intellect, by distinguishing those phantasms, considers them, and there investigates the true. The will embraces what has been approved and ordered by the intellect, and is occupied with the known good. When these three powers of the soul rightly preserve their own order, they lead the spirit in faith toward heavenly things.

This second region is compared to the ethereal heaven, in which, just as there is the continuous motion and position of the stars, so in this middle region there is continuous motion and labor against the struggles of vices. And just as the motion of the stars accomplishes the order of its office implanted in it by nature, so too in this region the equity of rightness requires that it be done: namely, that each power of the soul, when it is subjected to its own object, may be perfected toward the end appointed for it, so far as can befall wayfarers. Yet none of these powers can simply be perfected to fullness in this region, since no one in this pilgrim condition is so perfect that he cannot be more perfect in his own order. For even if memory, in its own object, which is the difficult, could behold the gathered likenesses and phantasms of all creatures, it would not be satisfied unless it could apprehend their principle, which is God. But this is altogether impossible for this region, in which we can form no phantasms or likenesses of God. The intellect too, the counselor, as I might say, of the blind will, extends itself toward the true; but however much it considers its object, it is not satisfied until it can apprehend all truth and come, without the opinion of fantastic speculation, to knowledge of eternal, highest, and infallible truth. But this perfection is possible for no wayfarer so long as he dwells in the body of mortality. The will also cannot be satisfied and truly delighted in its own object, which is the good, unless it reaches that immutable and highest good which no instability of change overshadows. The highest truth and immutable good is God, who said to Moses: No man shall see me and live. And the disciple of the highest truth says: No one has ever seen God. But the prophet too, addressing the Lord, says: Truly you are a hidden God. Although, then, the three aforesaid powers of the soul cannot perfectly comprehend their object in this life, nevertheless none should cease from its office, lest it run into the danger of failing precisely where it has laid aside the undertaking of striving.

Therefore the citizens of this middle region mortify evil affections in themselves, adorn themselves with continual virtues, direct all their works with a right intention, and do not depart in anything from the office of reason.

The citizens of this region are scholastic, contemplative, and active men, devoted to various and indeed honorable arts: those who subject the sensual or carnal powers to reason; those who do not neglect to cleanse these three powers of the soul from all unlawful objects; those who always raise their intention to the end of honorable usefulness; those who reform the will, in act or in habit, toward its proper end. Therefore the cenobite who loves this purification and desires to ascend to the third region of the spirit, while he remains in the middle region, ought to observe the following principal articles.

The summary of the truth of this middle region is expressed in seven principal articles.

Whoever desires to make progress in this middle region according to the vow of his profession should diligently take care to observe the following articles. If he has neglected to keep them, he shows that he is still a citizen not of the middle region but of the lowest. For, as we said above, no one can remain in this middle region without a continual effort to make progress; here, not to have advanced is to fail, and not to have ascended is to descend. Therefore the monk who, having overcome the region of darkness, has at last, with the Lord’s help, deserved to come to this middle region:

he should know that he must take care not to abandon, even for a little while, his effort to make progress, but should always stretch himself toward what lies beyond. He should remember the admonition of the wise man who says: Unless you hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown, that is, your conscience. For it is impossible for anyone to make progress in holy conduct if he neglects daily to renew, through fear of the Lord, the effort of making progress. The effect of this renewal is shown to be well ordered when the truth of the articles of the middle region is duly observed. The first article, then, is the diligent intention of the cenobite’s end; the second is the proper restraint of the sensual powers; the third, the faithful cleansing of the faculties; the fourth, the attentive reformation of the works of the lowest region; the fifth, the ordered establishment of the progress of a true cenobite; the sixth, the adaptation of the faculties for entry into the third region; and the seventh, exemplary or experiential certainty concerning all the aforesaid matters.

On the continual and diligent intention toward the end of cenobitic life. First Article.

Since the end is first in the intention of the wise person, and each thing in its own kind is judged the more perfect the more it approaches its own end, the monk who cultivates this middle region should always consider why he entered religious life. If he finds his intention well ordered, he should strive to continue it; but if he finds it corrupted, he should not fail to reform it according to the rectitude of the proper end.

But note that in spiritual exercises the end is described as twofold, and through it the virtue of monastic conduct is increased in merits. The first is charity, which is called the principal and ultimate end; toward it all monastic exercises are ordered as toward their first cause. Whatever good we do must always and principally be ordered toward this end, since no work of virtue receives merit unless charity always supplies the proper foundation.

God, says John, is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him. Everyone, moreover, who abides in God does not sin. The second end, as a dispositive end, is directed toward the first and principal end as though through some fitting means, and it is called secondary or less principal. The monk must always attend to this end and through it order his exercises toward the ultimate end. For no one can arrive at the principal end of charity if he neglects to observe the means.

This dispositive end directed toward the ultimate end, so far as it concerns cenobites, according to John Cassian in the Conferences of the Fathers, is to cast away from oneself all cares of the world completely, to mortify one’s own wills, to entrust every disposition and care of oneself to the superior, and to think nothing about tomorrow. For the cenobite who wishes to make progress in this middle region must wholly take up self-denial, and then resign himself totally into the hands of his superior, so that inwardly, within himself, he may be clean from every dust of self-will, and outwardly free from every secular occupation for serving the Lord. Indeed, unless our cenobite reaches this end, he is in no way a true monk, since he still sows corruption in corruptible flesh and by no means observes the virtue of his profession.

This monastic denial of self-will appears to consist principally in three things, without which no one can truly be said to have denied himself. First, the mortification of self-will requires in the monk the eradication of private judgment, since whoever relies on his own judgment or counsel disdains humbly to be subject to another. For the root from which the defense of self-will arises is called attachment to one’s own counsel or judgment. Whoever, being placed in a monastery, desires to cling to his own judgment, sins gravely against the rule as a usurper of self-will. For it is fitting for the cenobite to live by another’s command rather than by his own, if he [unclear]. According to Bernard, self-will is the greatest leprosy of the soul; it is the more pernicious the more hidden it has been, and the more [unclear] the more someone abounds in it, the sounder he seems to himself to be. Second, the mortification of the will requires the emptying out of one’s own affections, because no one can stand rightly ordered amid adversities and comforts, and truly subject to God, if he does not firmly restrain his carnal affections. Third, for the mortification of one’s own will that poverty of spirit is required, lest the monk’s affection be held captive by customary things, food, clothing, and the rest; for whoever loves these too much shows himself, against the Rule, to be a lover of his own will.

Therefore the true cenobite, as a cultivator of this middle region, must cling fervently to the teaching of holy humility, freely despise all worldly things for the love of God, and love absolutely nothing except God. If he has anything for use with the Rule’s permission, let him beware of setting the affection of his heart upon it, and let him be ready, at the judgment of his shepherd and for the benefit of the brothers, to surrender everything with a peaceful heart. Let him always choose what is simple and more lowly; let him give thanks to God in all things; and, placing his hope and sufficiency in him alone, let him say cheerfully: In you, Lord Jesus, possessing all things, I freely despise all things for your love; I shall care absolutely nothing for transitory things.

Therefore let our devout cenobite always direct the faithful eye of his intention, with consideration, toward this end of monastic instruction. Let him never withdraw from looking upon it, because whoever forgets the final end in his action wanders like an unskilled and blind sailor amid the storms of the sea, soon to perish. Therefore let the faithful monk imitate a sailor skilled in devotion: just as he, always keeping the harbor before his eyes, strives with intent solicitude to direct the ship there, so the mind of a good man should always be directed toward God as toward the shore and the final end. Archers set up for themselves some fixed mark, and, lest their sight be scattered from the appointed target, they close one eye. But just as the arrow of the shooter is directed toward the mark, so the intention of the good monk is always ordered toward God; in this too the eye of lower affection is closed, lest the sharpness of higher consideration be scattered by things that are empty. Therefore one must close the affection of earthly curiosity and the understanding of carnal wisdom as though not knowing them, if we desire always to lift the mind’s gaze toward its proper end. And just as the eagle is said to look at the sun with eyes undazzled, so the monk, serving God, contemplates without interruption the end of monastic instruction. Just as a prudent traveler, proceeding with delight, considers the lodging to which he is heading, so the good cenobite, in all that he does, always pants with fervent desire chiefly toward his own end, which is God. But foolish is the traveler who, set on the road, forgets the lodging toward which he is heading, and, wandering after other things, knowingly becomes entangled in various obstacles. And the monk who does not diligently consider the end of his destination is certainly blind and goes astray on the road.

Therefore the good monk and lover of his own salvation does not neglect his good striving in spiritual exercises, but, always reaching in affection toward higher things, lifts himself up by exercising himself in holy works. Now good striving is to omit none of the things that God has commanded; to obey the shepherd humbly in all things for the love of God; always to raise affection, removed from earthly things, to the memory of heavenly things; and through continual exercise in spiritual conduct to renew the holy purpose daily. Whatever good the devout cenobite does, let him always offer it with faithful attention to almighty God; let him despise all earthly things with a strong spirit; let him desire to please God alone.

Let the intention of the cenobitic life always be faithful, so that it wishes and desires nothing other than the praise and honor of God. Let its attention be diligent, so that it knows how to summon all the senses of the body and the affections of the soul to the service of God, in order that it may serve its Lord faithfully and seek his glory, not its own.

On the due restraint of the sensory powers. Article II

For I think that no one is unaware, especially among monks, how useful and necessary it is for us to restrain the forces of sensual passions. Indeed, whoever desires to reach, in this region, the due end of regular conduct that we have described must subdue his disordered natural habits and movements with prudent constancy, because no one is truly able to resign himself to another’s command who does not firmly restrain the forces of sensual passions. For one who desires to make progress must, with steadfast mind, abandon both the movements and the prudence of the flesh, and show himself to be a son of divine grace, not of flesh and blood. For Scripture says: “If you live according to the rule of the flesh, you will die.” Indeed, those who sow in the flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh. But flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. Yet what does the Savior say to us? “A man’s enemies,” he says, “are those of his own household.” And who are these household members, except the sensual powers that oppose the spirit? For concupiscibility and irascibility, our enemies, stir up every evil in us against the spirit, and continually disturb the house of conscience with various passions. For as long as these sensual powers pursue their natural movements and courses in a person, they do not allow him to ascend to the liberty of the spirit. Concupiscibility takes pleasure in delights through the sense of the flesh, while the contrary irascible power detests bodily hardships. Meanwhile, as long as this war of the flesh is being waged in a person, the monk is considered restless, carnal, and a cultivator of the lowest region. Therefore whoever desires to come to eternal life must firmly restrain these disordered powers of the senses in all things.

Therefore let the faithful coenobite take care to direct the force of concupiscibility toward hardships that are acceptable to God, and to reform all his affections according to God’s good pleasure. If he does this, he will confidently pray to the Lord: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times.” And that other verse, he will often cry out sweetly with tears: “As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Then, cleaving to God, he must prudently set the irascible power against sensual pleasures, and diligently reform it toward hatred of vices. Thus the soul, ordered toward its own principle, will not fear to endure any hard things for the love of God, and through the irascible power it will begin to struggle firmly against all carnal desires. And then the devout coenobite, as the spirit lifts him up, will cry: “My soul refused to be comforted.” And that saying of the Apostle: “I have counted all things as dung.” For the soul that truly loves God despises everything except him.

Now from these two powers every disordered affection arises; and, similarly, good affections are generated from these by way of opposition. For from the concupiscible power joy and hope take their beginning, and the irascible power gives birth to sorrow and fear. Saint Bernard speaks of these in this way: “The whole heart of man is turned about by four affections; if we bring these back to God, the whole heart of man is converted.”

On the faithful cleansing of the powers.

But we are by no means able to restrain the sensual powers unless we also faithfully cleanse the intellectual powers. For this cleansing great and continual diligence is needed, since the coenobite who is loosened by the sluggishness of negligence is never cleansed from vicious affections. For he carries corruption back from his own errors. Therefore the coenobite, a cultivator of this middle region, must correct his inner powers from every disorder, if he wishes to remain constantly in the pursuit of progress. These intellectual powers must be cleansed in this way.

First, the intellect must indeed be purged from every imagining of vain likenesses, so that it may withdraw itself from the one from all material things, raise itself upward, without any image of likeness, to its principle, and, prudently intent upon its object, turn itself wholly toward the ray of supreme truth.

Next, let our faithful cenobite not neglect to cleanse his memory from every occupation with unlawful things. Let him admit no forms of shameful or less useful thoughts, and let him strive to repel the phantasms of irrational passions by holy meditations, and, so far as can be done, to think nothing foolish.

The will also must be cleansed from every disordered affection, so that it wishes nothing except what right reason suggests should be wished, and rejects nothing except what reason, according to the judgment of truth, forbids it.

But this manly restraint and cleansing of the powers, as we have said, is granted to absolutely no one except through great, discreet, and continual diligence in a strong struggle, knowing that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and that no one can subject the enemy to himself unless he has chosen to fight against him fiercely and perseveringly. For, as blessed Bishop Augustine testifies, we know that a person does not die well unless he has first died to vices and concupiscences. But no one truly dies to these among human beings unless, resisting his own wills through continual labor, he sows in tears. Therefore the mind must be fortified with salutary teachings; the strength of patience must be taken up in all things. For just as someone unarmed and impatient of labor cannot overthrow an armed enemy, so a monk cannot cleanse his intellectual powers without spiritual weapons and a certain continual force in fighting. Although the weapons of spiritual warfare are very numerous in one’s progress, nevertheless three must chiefly be taken up by the monk.

First, indeed, vigor is necessary for the cenobite in everything he does, so that he may dare to attack courageously the things contrary to the flesh, and may never grow lukewarm in his holy purpose. For the exercises of the spirit are hard and wholly contrary to the flesh;

and no one is able to persevere in them constantly who refuses to put on the strongest armor of vigor. Therefore, if you desire to subject all your affections to the spirit, if you wish to fight successfully against the vices of the flesh, take care to do prudent violence to yourself and to arm yourself bravely against all things.

Next, a certain holy severity is set forth as something to be assumed by you; through it all contrary and adverse things of this world are borne as though they were nothing. For whoever, with a kindly lightness of mind, has once truly taken up anything for the love of God and for desire of heaven will thereafter fear no adversities of the flesh, but will be filled inwardly with so great a consideration of divine reward that he seems to delight more in adversities that occur than in prosperity.

But severity is by no means pleasing to the weaker unless it has been tempered somewhat with the sweetness of kindness. Therefore, consequently, kindness itself must be taken up with it, so that when, because of the weakness of the flesh, a person tempted in battle, or even wounded, sometimes falters, he may soon rise again through penitence, to fight once more with greater strength. For it is necessary that the soldier of Christ, if he has fallen in war, rise again as often as needed through contrition and the other remedies of penitence, to fight again, until at last, at some other time, by the mercy of God, he is able to overcome the adversary. If the just person falls seven times in a day and rises again, how shall the sinner, now penitent, not hope for pardon? Rise, therefore, to fight again, O soldiers, as often as you have fallen when the adversary has prevailed. Always renew the warfare afresh with greater strength, so that you may finally overcome by perseverance the enemy whom for the time being you are not strong enough to destroy by force. Do not despair of victory, O faithful cenobite, because you have often been conquered by temptation or have fallen into the snare of vice. Do not lie long prostrate because you feel yourself weak, but rise again at once as often as you have fallen, and trust that you have a merciful Lord, by whose help you will at last be victorious against the adversary. For no one suddenly becomes supreme, nor is victory over the enemy granted at once to inexperienced soldiers, lest, doomed to perish, they fall more gravely into pride.

be lifted up. The possession of a thing acquired with difficulty is always dearer, and a good that is obtained laboriously is guarded with greater diligence. For so long does God the loving Father permit us, defeated by the adversary’s temptations, to fall at intervals of change into the pit of sin, until, conscious of our weakness, we learn to hope in nothing in our own strength, but only in the grace of the one God. But you, man, who often break your purpose by sinning, never be slow to rise again, since even if you cannot perfectly subject the enemy to yourself, nevertheless it will be good for you if the last day, even after a fall often repeated, can find you standing and fighting. But those to whom the mercy of God has granted the power and grace to defeat the adversary, this counsel does not make lax. Nevertheless, let him who stands see that he does not fall.

On the Attentive Reformation of the Works of the First Region.

Article 4

Since, as we taught at the end of the first treatise, this middle region is next to the first from its lowest part, and in it, if the coenobite has been at all negligent and remiss, he immediately falls back again, without any interval, into the former region. And therefore whoever desires to persevere in this region while making progress should always, with attentive vigilance, strive to reform the works of the lowest region. And, lest we be too lengthy, whoever desires to exercise this reformation in himself should take up in this region works contrary to the first region in eight articles. For, as is prescribed by the teaching of physicians, contraries are cured by contraries.

Therefore the citizens of this middle region, faithful monks, are first commanded to consider this: that above all they should strive to order themselves toward God. This ordering is said to be done well when God is loved above all things, according to the law, with the whole heart.

Then the devoted coenobite should order himself toward his prelate.

Let him show humble reverence to him, strive to love him with sincere charity, and observe all the things he commands according to the Rule.

Let the ruler also of souls take care to proceed in an ordered way toward the coenobites, and to show himself a true shepherd to the sheep, not a hireling. Let him not neglect the salvation of the souls committed to him; let him not set temporal things before spiritual things. Let him hate vices, love the brothers, and show himself exemplary in all good things.

Then let the brothers cleave to one another as members of one head; let them love one another mutually in the true charity of God, and not depart from good zeal. For all of us who, through faith in Christ, trust to come to eternal life by applying ourselves to good works are members of Christ, the supreme head. But whoever persecutes his brother with evil zeal or hatred or other evil affections first separates himself from the head, and then does injury to Christ.

Next, let each one show himself ordered toward himself: let him humbly subject himself to all for the love of Christ; let him prefer others to himself through humility; and let him believe himself more unworthy than all the monks.

In the use of the monastery’s goods, let them always beware of exceeding the institution of the Rule, but strive to show themselves ordered in all things and faithful everywhere. Let them seek to have nothing against the will of the abbot; let them admit no pleasure of the spirit in the use of things.

Next, faithful coenobites should take care to order themselves, according to the institution of the Rule, to contempt of the world, so that they love nothing in this world, but truly despise all things for the love of God.

Let them not neglect to order themselves most diligently to penitence. Let them often have recourse to humble confession of their transgressions, since just as no one is believed to live in this world without sin, so penitence is judged necessary for all, even monks. Therefore the good coenobite, through the practice of compunction, should always learn to have recourse to penitence, to accuse himself humbly of his transgressions in chapter, willingly to perform the imposed penance, and faithfully to amend himself in all things.

On the Ordered Institution of True Monastic Progress and the Degrees of Humility.

Article V

The greatest virtue of a monk is humility, and the gravest crime in a cenobite is pride. For a monk who is proud with a swollen mind becomes an imitator and servant of the devil, and is stripped of all virtues, if he had any, since no virtue can subsist in a mind in which pride has come to dwell. Therefore the cenobite who desires to make progress in this middle region should learn to order himself toward the true progress of monastic institution through humility, because no one truly attains humility unless he spends time in spiritual pursuits.

True progress in regular institution, excluding all adulterous muses, arises from the degrees of humility, which are set down as twelve, by their roots, in the Rule. The roots of this progress come from the study of sacred reading, which gradually leads a person to the fear of the Lord. From reading spiritual meditation arises, from which holy compunction is generated. The more useful mode of cenobitic meditation consists in the memory of the Lord's passion and in the consideration of God's benefits. But those who, going beyond this middle region, come to tranquility of spirit render their meditations more sublime through contemplation of the divine majesty and excellence. We shall speak of these in their own place.

These two roots receive their increase from the watering of constant prayer, and grow strong into the robustness of a very firm plant. For no meditation makes progress without prayer, and study without it will not save.

From these three roots of spiritual progress arises the fear of the Lord, which is the first degree of humility; from this the other degrees, succeeding in order, are generated. But monks who neglect the saving study of the Scriptures and holy meditations, together with constant prayers, by no means reach even this first degree of humility. But one who cannot ascend the first degree of humility, how will he be able to arrive at the others? For the second is never ascended if the first is neglected. Therefore whoever neglects one ascends none.

The study of sacred reading must not be taken up for the vanity of the world, nor for the pleasure of a seduced mind, because reading never advances toward compunction when delight of the flesh or of vanity corrupts it. A monk cannot reach devotion through the study of sacred reading unless he strives to change every curiosity into a simple spirit. Therefore whoever desires to advance from the reading of the Scriptures to compunction, whoever ought to ascend to humility, must choose reading, but only that which can more fully stir the mind to the love of God.

For this purpose the reading of the body of the Lord seems to me sufficiently suitable, because through it the memory is often recalled to love of him. We also gladly admit miracles and accounts of the torments or joys of separated souls, provided they conform to the catholic faith; by these we have found that sluggish hearts are rather often stirred to compunction. Finally, the passions of the holy martyrs awaken the fervor of devotion in no small measure; in them, while we bring to mind the unconquerable charity of Christ, we are moved by the example of such great constancy and, as if touched by a certain fire of love, sigh over our own imperfection.

From reading the matter of meditation is taken, and whatever the former is like, the latter will be like as well. Not the shameful songs of poets, not the curious doctrines of philosophers, not the swollen writings of rhetoricians: rather, they suffocate fervor. Therefore if you wish to persist in good meditations, do not occupy your mind with any readings except holy and devout ones. For indeed not one good meditation is generated from such study. Let the one who studies for the knowledge of this world read those things that are suited to his learning; but let the one who seeks compunction read those things let him gather those things which kindle the soul to the love of God through fear. Therefore let frequent reading about the last things that await us take its beginning; then let the deeds of the holy fathers be read, so that the memory of future things may shake the mind with fear of God, and the exemplary way of life of the saints may kindle the desire to imitate them. For the wise man says: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” The way of life of the holy fathers is set before us as an example, and the destruction of the wicked is recounted to us for our instruction, so that virtue when rewarded may stir desire, and iniquity when punished may forbid license to sin.

Therefore the devout cenobite should always recall to memory the examples and virtues of the saints; he should consider the brief pleasure of the depraved, but their eternal torment, so that by fearing unhappiness he may deserve to escape it, and by cleaving to virtues obtain their perpetual joy. The distinct condition of the good and the evil is no slight matter, since each is described as destined to remain forever, and is ended by no limit. O eternity, always to be feared by all mortals: in it, after this life, there is no fear of consummation for the just, and no hope of liberation for the perverse. Let him who can think what eternity is think it; where there is no end, who dares imagine a boundary? And when he has found nothing in eternity except eternity, let him understand how nothing is all the time in which he lives in this world.

Indeed, once the spirit has been stripped of the flesh, it is necessarily compelled to enter the abyss of eternity; and the condition which it has once obtained according to its merits it will bear without end and will not exchange for another. For he who dies good in the love of God will obtain eternal life according to his merits. But he who is evil and, without the penance of reconciliation, once departs from this life will remain to be tormented without end with the demons in hell. From these meditations servile fear arises in the mind, through which one gradually arrives at love. But so that we may be able to lead the cenobite successively through these roots to charity, it is our pleasure to explain briefly, in order, the degrees of humility described in the Rule.

The first degree of humility, therefore, is described by Saint Benedict in the Rule as the fear of God, which is called the beginning of wisdom. The fear of the Lord is handed down under a threefold distinction: namely, servile, initial, and filial, which is also called chaste. From this threefold distinction three roots are said to proceed, according to which the beginning cenobite ought to order his meditations. For each root has its own proper meditations; and when one is rightly disposed, another, better one is always generated.

From servile fear, then, when it is assumed not only servilely but prudently and virtuously, come meditations on horror and punishments, which, restraining the soul from sin, gradually introduce filial fear. Indeed, when by consideration of punishments the mind is turned to horror, boldness in sinning is restrained, because the servant who fears blows keeps the Lord’s commands. This servile fear by itself is not sufficient for meriting the paternal inheritance; nevertheless, as an initial effect, it disposes one toward filial fear, which is sufficient.

Initial fear is placed midway between the two, and is easily changed from servile into filial. This initial fear receives meditations on the last things, and dreads both incurring punishments and losing the sweet homeland. And this step is placed in the Rule, where its roots too are described.

Filial fear, however, embraces its meditations in love, since it fears nothing except that the beloved Father may be offended. Of this fear the wise man says: “The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting, joy and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and will give gladness and joy, and length of days.” And again: “It will be well with the one who fears God at the last things, and on the day of his death he will be blessed.” This fear is also called chaste, because it detests evil not from fear of punishments, but from love alone.

From this threefold fear we see three breadths of spiritual exercises rising around the degrees of humility, and individual exercises corresponding to the individual fears. For in one way...

Servile fear carries out its exercises in one way; initial fear applies itself to the virtues in another; and filial fear proceeds in its works in yet a very different way. For just as the affections of hearts arise in various ways, so the exercises of one fear take place in different ways. The publican, mindful of his own crimes, feared the sentence of the judge in one way; Jerome said that he heard in another way the sound of the trumpet calling the dead to judgment. For the holy Gospel says of the former: “Standing far off, the publican would not lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’” But that blessed Jerome says: “Whether I drink or eat, I always think I hear that trumpet sounding in my ears: ‘Rise, dead, come to judgment.’” The compunction of both arises from fear, but each is not produced from the desire of one and the same affection. For the publican, terrified by the guilt of his sins, feared the sentence of the just judge, and therefore, pierced with compunction, said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Jerome, however, is not shaken by fear from the guilt of conscience, but, founded in charity and regarding himself as a useless servant, he reveres the abyss of divine justice.

The second degree is to relinquish one’s own will for the love of God, and to love one’s own desire in nothing contrary to the rule.

This degree arises from the first ascent of humility and raises one to the third. For truly, one who fears God and truly fears being separated from him and undergoing punishments hates nothing more than his own will. For the faithful cenobite knows that every sin arises from one’s own will alone, and therefore he detests it as the gate of hell. For that blessed man spoke truly: “Take away one’s own will, and there will no longer be hell.” For nothing burns in hell except one’s own will; nothing loses the grace of God except voluntary fault. Therefore whoever truly fears God and fears losing his grace greatly dreads his own will as the ambusher of his soul. Consideration of the danger of one’s own will makes the cenobite despise his own desire and deny himself to himself. And this denial of one’s own will and of oneself is accomplished in three ways, as will be said in what follows.

First, then, he denies himself to himself who strives to live according to the teaching of eternal wisdom and not according to his own habits, and to obey Christ in all things as he counsels him to humility. Therefore let the Savior say to the cenobite: If you wish to deny yourself to yourself and follow me, turn away your eyes, lest they see harmful things; turn away your ears, lest they hear vain things; and in place of the sweet things of this world, take up bitter things. Learn to despise the delights of your body, to love tranquillity and peace of heart, to receive all tribulations patiently and joyfully for love of me, and desire to appear vile and contemptible to all. Consequently, learn to break your own wills in all things, to mortify the desires of the flesh, to despise all earthly things, and, as far as possible, to conform your life according to your strength to the manner of life of your Savior. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. Whoever has done these things has well denied himself.

Second, the denial of one’s own will is rightly accomplished when the advantages of others are placed before one’s own. For the holy Apostle says: “Not seeking the things that are their own, but the things of others.” For according to Bernard’s judgment, the soul is laid down for the brothers as often as their advantages are preferred to one’s own benefits for the love of God.

Third, the resignation of one’s own will receives the fullness of perfection when the cenobite, pierced with compunction and wholly given over to God, desires out of love to serve him freely, without regard for reward. And this most holy resignation of one’s own will makes a person very near to God and always rests in his love.

But just as this resignation of oneself receives its substance from the second degree of humility, so too it necessarily requires an inward and complete resignation to the will of God in all things. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have not come to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me.” Perfect resignation, therefore, is that by which the human will is totally subjected to the divine will and, from whole love, is conformed he is conformed. For thus the Lord himself taught us to pray: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” And that saying of the psalmist: “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” One never lives more securely in this world than when the human will is perfectly subjected to God.

Indeed, this most perfect resignation of oneself, by which the cenobite truly subjects his own will to God, shows without intermediary the straight road to the highest good. Here there is the greatest tranquility of mind; the greatest security is present in the heart, because a soul that strives to subject itself perfectly to God will no longer be able to fear any opposition in this world except sin alone. Whatever adversity comes upon him, with the Lord’s help he has learned to overcome it; whatever advantage he desires, he understands that he possesses it in the Lord alone. He despises all adversities for love of him; he has placed all goods in love of him. For that devout man wisely said: “Let go of everything, and you will find everything. Abandon desire, and you will find true peace.”

Finally, in order that this resignation of one’s own will may receive the fullness of consummation, it implores, so to speak, the support of a threefold aid.

The first is placed in the virtue of perseverance: that the will, once denied, is never taken back. For blessed Bernard says to those who despise this aid: “Why do you again take charge of yourselves, you who once, by mature deliberation, handed over your will to us?” For the monk who has once handed over his own will to God into the hands of the abbot does not take it back without the crime of sacrilege.

The second thing required for the perfect resignation of the will is that it never be slackened. Hence in the Apocalypse the Lord says to the lukewarm soul: “I have a few things against you, because you have abandoned your first charity,” that is, your fervor.

Third, resignation of the will is perfected if it is never cut off. For the Savior says: “He who has persevered to the end will be saved.” Therefore, when you see a cenobite inquiring anxiously

E ij or moved by anger, know that the whole burden of the temptation proceeds from lack of resignation; nor will you ever cure this disease of sickness unless you first persuade him to the resignation of the will that has been denied.

The third step of humility is to subject oneself to a superior in all obedience for love of God, and to show oneself an imitator of Christ in deeds, not only in words. Concerning this the holy Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” This step takes its beginning from the second and raises its ascent up to its own third step. For just as the second mortifies one’s own will by denying it, so this one lays the foundation of a holy work through humble subjection. The former subjects the whole self to the divine will; the latter, for love of God, also obeys human beings.

The keeping of one step without the observance of the other is not sufficient in a monk; nor is the will of a cenobite subjected to the divine ordinance if it deems it beneath itself to obey the command of a superior.

Therefore the true cenobite places all his joy in the virtue of holy obedience. He considers it the greatest gain to fulfill in all things the will of his shepherd. He believes it a grave loss to the soul if he has found himself to have committed even a little thing outside obedience. For he always considers with faithful devotion what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me.” Hence blessed Bernard says to the monks: “Whatever a man commands in God’s stead must be received no differently than if God himself commanded it in person.” Therefore let the true monk prefer this subjection of obedience to every sacrifice; let him do absolutely nothing against its integrity; and let him continually say within himself what is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifice.” The Rule says: “Therefore all things are to be done according to the will of the abbot.”

But this step, as we have said, arises from the second, because he who perfectly forsakes his own will for fear of God now seeks nothing else in this world than to follow that will in all things. But because God speaks once and does not repeat the same thing, weak man cannot know the will of the Most High; therefore he has committed himself into the hands of his prelate.

he has committed himself into the hands of his prelate. Therefore let the cenobite obey, according to the Rule, the vicar of Christ, and without doubt he will fulfill the will of God.

This obedience, however, is owed strictly to prelates according to the Gospel and the monastic Rule; for although mutual obedience among brothers is good, it must never be preferred to the command of a superior. Monks are indeed commanded to render discreet obedience to one another, and, while preserving the precepts of their superiors, to anticipate one another in mutual services. And, to bring in an example from our own custom: obedience is to be given to all according to order. If a brother summons you, obey gladly; if a senior commands something else, leave aside the command of the former and obey this one. Again, if the prior of the community interposes his own command, all mutual obedience among the brothers will cease. But if the precept of the abbot intervenes, no obedience to anyone else will prevail against it. For he is believed to hold the first place in the monastery in Christ's stead, and therefore he is preferred to all.

There are, moreover, seven graded circumstances of the virtue of holy obedience, which blessed Bernard described thus. The first degree of obedience is to obey gladly, so that, evidently, you have no will of your own at all, but believe the good pleasure of your pastor to be entirely your own. The second is to obey simply, so that you do neither more nor otherwise than what has been commanded you, nor, by doing less, omit anything. The third is to obey cheerfully, so that you display serenity in your face and show sweetness in your voice. The fourth is to obey swiftly, so that the hand is not slower in the work than the command is in the voice. The fifth is to obey manfully, lest one withhold his strength from the command and pretend that he is weak and unequal to the precepts. The sixth is to obey humbly: not proudly, not haughtily, not contentiously; for unless obedience is humble, it will receive not reward but punishment. The seventh is to obey perseveringly, because obedience that is interrupted before completion is not true obedience, and he alone who perseveres to the end is rewarded.

E iij The fruit of obedience is everlasting, and is limited by no end at all. God almighty obeys our prayers only as much as we obey our superiors. Do not flatter yourself, stiff-necked monk, about your persistence in prayer, for Christ does not hear a man praying when that man despises Christ's vicar in the monastery. Humility raises prayer up; obedience commends it. For obedience, as one of the fathers said, is the salvation of all the faithful, the mother of all virtues, the finder of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens the heavens, closes the gates of hell, becomes a co-dweller with the angels, and is considered the food of all the saints. But the monk who rejects subjection to obedience runs toward death.

The fourth degree of humility is patience in adversities. Of this our holy father Benedict speaks in the Rule: if a monk under obedience embraces patience with silent conscience amid hard and contrary things, or even amid any injuries inflicted on him. This degree too takes its beginning from the third, for no one should truly be called obedient if he is found impatient. For, as that divine Chrysostom says, he cannot be pleasing to the king who has been subject to the enemy; nor is he truly subject to Christ who has been enslaved to passionate and impatient flesh. No one will be able to conquer a fierce enemy unless he has first learned to fight bravely against him. Patience is very necessary for us, because no virtue is brought to perfection lawfully if patience is lacking.

Indeed, as blessed Gregory bears witness, it is of greater merit to endure adversities patiently for God's sake than to toil in good works. And Saint Jerome says: He who believes that tribulation has come upon him for his sins summons God's mercy to himself so that he may do more good. Therefore let the cenobite learn to set the virtue of patience against all things that befall him, if he desires to triumph over his enemies. For he who suffers conquers; he who murmurs is overcome.

The virtue of patience is especially necessary in three things, and is rewarded with the highest prizes: in insults, truly In insults of words, patience preserves the purpose of humility in a prudent man who loves God; in the removal of possessions and temporal advantages, it receives increase; and in bodily injury, with conscience silent, it preserves the rule of virtue. Consider now, O faithful soul, how your most loving Savior Jesus endured these three things most patiently for your redemption; and if you believe that you love him, do not find it burdensome to bear similar things patiently for love of him.

From the three degrees immediately preceding we have established one sum of the cenobitic goal, which, as it seems to us, we reasonably call the three-degree ascent. For by three degrees, namely the second, third, and fourth, the goal of the cenobitic institution is perfected, and the denial of one’s own will is brought to completion. For where patience, the preserver of virtues, is joined to the denial of one’s own will and to obedience, every pleasure and concern of the body is mortified. Whoever has deserved to ascend this three-degree ascent has fulfilled the Lord’s command, where he says in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” through the second degree of humility; “and take up his cross,” through the third; “and follow me,” through the fourth.

The fifth degree of humility is true confession of sins. The faithful cenobite is said to ascend into it if he confesses to his abbot, with humble confidence, all evil thoughts that come into his heart, or any evils committed in secret. Indeed, if anything is committed through impatience, at the suggestion of the adversary, in the preceding three-degree ascent, it is restored in this one through contrition and humble confession. For no one is found so perfect that he does not contract some stain from earthly conduct, as Scripture says: “In many things we all offend.” For no one is clean from sin, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day. Therefore this degree necessarily follows the fourth without an intervening stage; in it all the negligences of the preceding degrees are corrected. True confession raises up the soldier falling in combat, heals him when wounded by the enemy, and strengthens the weak and fainthearted. Therefore whoever desires to stand in battle and bravely conquer the enemy should often have recourse to the defenses of true confession.

For it is impossible for one wounded by the enemy to recover health if he neglects to disclose the wound itself to the physician. You, therefore, faithful cenobite, who desire to save your soul and to be a good soldier of Jesus Christ, do not omit humble confession, because you will never be able to conquer the devil better than if you take care faithfully to disclose to your abbot all the thoughts that he suggests to you, and all your sins. It is certain to me, and proved by the destruction of many, that the cenobite who refuses to keep this degree commits himself to being conquered by many temptations of the enemy.

The sixth degree of humility arises from true confession: that the monk should consider himself base and unworthy for all things. According to the Rule, we believe him to be a true monk whom we see, from humble patience, to be content with every baseness and extremity in food and clothing. This baseness is placed in the inconveniences of ordinary use. The former gladly embraces patience in cheaper garments, foods, and any necessities of the body; the latter delights in serving the sick, lepers, and the outcast, in being put to shame, degraded, and despised in all things. Therefore the monk who is truly dead to the flesh and the world should be content with every baseness and extremity, should show himself a faithful worker in all things, and yet, because of the corruption of nature by which he offends in many things, should believe himself base and unworthy.

Indeed, whatever good is done in this world, however holy and religiously one lives in this age, it cannot suffice for anyone to merit eternal life unless God’s great mercy deigns to assist. We receive the greatest things for the smallest; we await the kingdom of God not as owed to us from our own merit, but as promised from grace. For the holy apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” For if we receive God’s justice without mercy, we are worthy of hell. We have all incurred wrath by sinning, but we receive love back from grace. No one is saved except through grace; no one is damned except through justice. Meanwhile, however, in order that we may obtain the grace of God, the zeal of our good will is required; without that grace nothing in us works toward merit. For although no one does good by his own holy powers, still no one does good unwillingly. Thus the grace of God and freedom of the will are related to one another in such a way that one without the other cannot suffice for the salvation of a human being; rather, both must necessarily come together for the working of virtue. Since, then, without the grace of God we can do nothing good, we ought to esteem ourselves vile and unworthy for all things, so that, while we submit ourselves to God in humility, we may always obtain greater things. And therefore this sixth degree of confession is meritorious, and the sole foundation of all the preceding degrees. For as long as the cenobite remains in this degree of humility, he will stand firm in the earlier ones.

The seventh degree of humility is not only to believe oneself, from the inmost affection of the heart, lower than all, but also to desire with a simple spirit that others believe and say this about him. This condition of holy humility is set on high, and in this age is loved by few monks. For the first condition of this profound humility seems to consist in this: that the monk ought from the heart to esteem himself lower than all. The second is that he rejoice to be esteemed vile and abject by all, and desire this from the inmost affection of the heart without pretense. The third condition is placed in a higher dwelling: namely, that the monk, from the same affection, delight to be treated most vilely and trampled on by all. Rooted in this humility, the cenobite loves every reproach and insult; he does not fear to be despised and cast away most vilely, because, humbly submitting himself, he places his whole self in the love of God, and hastens to insults as though to feasts, with the greatest cheerfulness. But so that you may understand the truth of this seventh degree, read the following considerations.

The first consideration directs the mind toward hope in divine love, which arises from a certain pious confidence. For although a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, nevertheless anyone can in some measure recognize, from the disposition of his own heart, what he ought to think about his state, whether good or bad.

Second, it must be considered that this good disposition of the heart, and of a will ordered toward God, is a sign of the approval of God’s love and of good works. For thus, when the Lord was born in the flesh, the angels sang: “Peace on earth to men of good will.”

Third, it must be noted that just as a good disposition of the heart always orders and rouses the mind through holy exercises toward the fear of God and the working of virtues, so the negligence of an evil disposition inclines it especially toward vices and acedia. The consideration of this difference, moreover, gives rise to conjecture.

Fourth, it must be considered that an evil disposition of the heart impedes and empties out the grace of God and merits in a person, since it makes the soul vile, ignoble, and degenerate, and always disposes it toward graver and worst things. Indeed, the root of evils of tongue and deed comes from an evil heart, as is clear in Saul and in many similar cases.

The fifth consideration is that the evil of deed and tongue is never properly examined unless the evil of the heart is first truly known. Each person, however, can examine his own heart better than another can, and consider what sort of person lies hidden within himself. Therefore it is enough for the cenobite, to whom care of another has not been entrusted, to inspect his own heart diligently, and in no way to busy himself with the scrutiny of another’s heart. But the shepherd of monks, to whom the care of souls is entrusted, is also commanded to know the face of his flock.

Sixth, it must be noted from these things that it is very rash to wish to examine another’s heart, and to judge the inner thoughts of brothers from their words and deeds. The Lord knows those who are his; nor is it granted to a human being to become a rash judge of another’s heart without the reason of office.

Seventh, it must be noted that a small evil of one’s own heart, known to the person himself, harms him more in his own heart than a great evil suspected doubtfully about another’s heart. For the former is to be wept over because it is certain and known; the latter is to be piously excused because it is unknown.

Eighth, it must be considered that, since each person sees many imperfections in his own heart that he cannot see in others...

recognize in others, on account of these, insofar as they are obstacles to grace, he ought to esteem himself lower. And insofar as they disfigure the soul, let him despise himself as more vile than others, even if he knows their public crimes. For since the root of their heart is utterly unknown to him, he cannot know how the divine election concerning them was ordained from eternity. Who would have believed that the thief crucified with the Lord was elected from eternity, if he judged him according to his works? All things turn out for good for the elect, since where sin is seen to have abounded, often, by the will of divine election, greater grace is found. For divine love regards and embraces its elect from eternity, and considers them elect not according to the misery in which they now are, but according to their future glory. Let the cenobite therefore beware of disparaging others; let him beware of judging others, if he desires to escape eternal death. For who are you, that you judge another’s servant? He stands to be judged by his own Lord alone.

The disposition of this seventh degree, moreover, because of that clause “from the innermost disposition of the heart,” possesses a threefold root of its origin: namely truth, hope, and charity. For when the faithful cenobite sees that he does not have his being from himself, he truly considers himself, insofar as he is from himself, to be nothing; and consequently, in the same respect, he considers his works, insofar as they come from himself who is nothing, to be nothing, since he is not ignorant that nothing is made from nothing. Therefore the monk greatly rejoices in the truth when, in this respect, he esteems himself and his works as nothing, because he fears falling into the vice of falsehood if he believed himself to be something great. And so, withdrawing from himself, he fails in himself, and places his being, living, and power in God alone. Secondly, this disposition is said to arise from hope of acquiring greater grace, because when a person fails in himself through humility, he comes nearer to God’s grace. Thirdly, the humility of this disposition takes its beginning from the love of God, and receives continual increase in it. For whoever loves God perfectly seeks nothing other than his honor in all things, and does not know how to exalt himself in anything, but desires to be subject to all for God’s sake. And the more he is cast down by insults and injuries, the more, rejoicing, he is glad in the Lord. For he sees that he is wretched, so that in himself he may proclaim the Lord glorious. He who truly loves his Lord seeks nothing other than his glory.

It is clear from what has been said that the perfect charity which is promised to those ascending the degrees of humility is displayed in this seventh degree. For the other five degrees that follow in the Rule add nothing to the perfection of the inner man existing in the seventh, but rather compose the outer man, lest he disturb the inner. Finally, from this seventh degree we can erect certain new ascents of humility and raise all the other degrees higher in them. For a more fervent filial fear resides in him who is able to make further progress in the breadth of the others.

Now that the common ascents of the heart to the degree of charity have been known, let the cenobite consider with what zeal, what effort, what perseverance he ought to exercise himself in these things, so that he may reach this seventh degree of love. But whoever does not always strive to advance in these degrees of humility should know that he sins against the Rule; and unless he recovers his former holy effort by repentance, he incurs the sentence of damnation. For the Rule says thus: “But if he should ever act otherwise, let him know that he will be condemned by the one whom he mocks.” So if a person making less progress in religion believes himself guilty before the divine judgment, what else does one who abandons the effort to advance deserve but to undergo the sentence of damnation? For where an account is rendered, according to the Rule, even concerning a lesser fault among those striving to advance, monks who despise every effort to advance are without doubt condemned by the sentence of the Judge. Therefore, if you do not wish to incur the danger of damnation, strive always to preserve the effort of advancing under the Rule.

Since the other five degrees of humility are said to pertain to the guarding of the inner man, let us also briefly explain them. For a monk who neglects to compose his outward conduct according to the Rule will not long remain well composed in inward things. For just as an unclothed body is corrupted, so humility without conduct is emptied.

The eighth degree of humility, then, is set down in the Rule as follows: if the monk does nothing except what the common rule of the cenobium, or the examples of the elders, encourage. In this degree, singularity of outward conduct contrary to the Rule is forbidden to monks; but inward singularity of greater charity and humility is forbidden to no one. Therefore let no one prefer his own inventions to the holy Rule; let no one put his own customs before the examples of the elders, since it is not enough for one to stand in the seventh degree if he does not keep the rule of the community.

The ninth degree of humility follows from the Rule; through it excessive talkativeness is forbidden. For it befits a monk to keep silence, especially while he is seated in the midst of the elders. Indeed, one who speaks when not questioned is deservedly regarded as a fool.

The tenth degree of humility forbids readiness to laughter and levity, since whoever delights in laughter is shown to be foolish and estranged from the fear of God.

The eleventh degree of humility enjoins modesty and maturity upon the monk, so that, when the occasion and permission to speak are granted, he should speak with humble gravity, without laughter or anger. Let the monk’s speech be rare, brief, and reasonable, because it does not befit one who wishes to please the Most High to say useless things.

The twelfth degree of humility teaches the monk to order the outward man, in appearance and dress, from a humble heart, and to show by his outward conduct also that he is inwardly devout. And although this degree is last in the order of them all, nevertheless in the practice of those beginning to make progress it is first. And therefore Bernard, describing these twelve degrees of humility, begins from this one and, ascending to the first, descends in order, so to speak. For no one easily advances inwardly to compunction of heart and the fear of God if he does not order his manners outwardly.

On the devout fitting of the powers for entrance into the third region.

Article VI

Since, by the six degrees of humility, the inner powers of a person have above all been purged, grounded, and reformed, it is now said to be very necessary in monks that they be more devoutly prepared for entrance into the third region. Now this diligence in striving toward higher things, as we have said, is necessary for the cenobite, since where the effort to make progress is laid aside, acquired virtue is altogether dissipated. No one is permitted to stand still in this second region; rather, we are all commanded to ascend to the third through continual effort. Indeed this continual motion casts every slothful and lukewarm person down into the first region of the flesh, but it gently impels the humble and those fervent in desire always toward the third, without violence.
