Therefore whoever has deserved to obtain from the Lord, through humility, the reformation of his powers is already near the third region of the spirit. In order that he may be able to enter it effectively, it is necessary that, by most diligently fitting the powers of his soul, he order them to their several operations. The intellect is then said to be rightly fitted for entrance into the third region when it is illumined for knowing the highest truth according to its capacity. Memory is ordered to the same end when it is fully absorbed in holding and cherishing the highest truth. But if the will is disposed to love the highest good, which is God, it is well prepared for the entrance of the spirit.

In order, then, that the cenobite may be able to attain purification of the intellectual powers, it is necessary that, dying to the world, he seek a mind made peaceful from every inner and outer disturbance, so that, buried within the bosom of divine love, it may remain there and never withdraw from the sweetness of inward union. Toward this rest of mind they are rooted in four ways, who, in good will, [unclear]

The first degree of good will [unclear] beginnings, which is called upright will. For the soul that, consenting to the law of God, is subjected to God through an upright will, even if it still seems weak, is ordered toward the path of virtue. For when the flesh resists, virtue brings it to completion, and how upright the will is is proved by the violence done by the spirit. Yet a will is often called upright and good even when it is found to be less strong. The good that it loves it cannot always carry out; the evil that it hates it grieves that, through weakness, it has committed. Through the weakness of the flesh it is very near the lowest region, yet by the uprightness of its intention and by the effort to make progress it is continually kindled toward the freedom of the spirit. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks many thoughts. O who could describe this battle between spirit and flesh, where the spirit itself desires to subject the flesh to itself through an upright will, and the weak flesh always resists the spirit through contrary desires?

The second degree is a will strong in uprightness, so that it both vigorously flees the evil that it hates against the impulses of the flesh, and firmly grasps, by doing it, the good that it loves, although with labor.

The third degree is a devout will, by which the mind, with enlarged heart, embraces the way of God’s commandments and delights in them as in all riches. For indeed the will does not long remain strong if it has not been devout in the commandments of God.

The fourth degree is a full will, so that it does not divide its powers at all, but continually stretches itself wholly toward its God through the renunciation of all things. For this degree three things are necessary, so that the good will may be made full in us.

The first is the complete renunciation of oneself; for a will is proved still to be weak if it is not mortified through the total renunciation of self.

The second thing required for a full good will is held to be perfect resignation. If anyone desires to apprehend it, let him fervently ascend the third degree of humility.

F ij The third member necessary for the fourth degree of good will is called the total extension of the will into God. Through it the soul, admitted into divine love and sweetly burning, is in some way transformed into that same love, and is frequently admitted into the third region.

Finally, this transformation into divine love, according to the opinion of Bernard, is love, affection, adhesion, union, charity, or fruition. No one can attain it unless he has learned to mortify all his lower affections of spirit. For the spirit of a person who has his heart lifted up to God is called a perfect will, and it is united with God in the sweetest bond. Therefore in these degrees of good will the faithful cenobite ought without interruption to direct his effort upward, and always to examine with prudent care how much he is making progress or falling short. For Saint Bernard says: Just as one who remains in a vicious will is condemned, so one who does not strive to make progress in other things is blameworthy. For where the effort to make progress is laid aside, the danger of falling away is incurred.

On the Example and Experimental Knowledge of All the Things Mentioned Above

Article VII

Although a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, nevertheless each person can, by diligently examining his conscience, recognize what he ought to think about the condition of his state. What sort of person each one lies hidden as within himself is made manifest by the testimony of his own conscience. Therefore, so that the cenobite may clearly discern the condition of his state, according to John of Kastl on the Rule he ought to observe three things in his conscience, without which no one becomes a good Christian, and no one is judged a good man or monk.

The first, then, that is required for a good man is the good testimony of conscience, namely that no mortal sin lies hidden in the conscience. For the mind that is polluted by the guilt of mortal sin is testified by conscience to have an evil state.

Therefore every monk must examine himself diligently and carefully cleanse himself of the faults he has committed according to the ordinance of the Church. But he who, on examining his conscience, has found it clean from mortal sin should offer humble praises to God and should not neglect to add the examination of the things that follow.

The second thing necessary for a good man, then, is to intend God principally in all his works, and to order all things, as far as he is able, to his praise and honor. But if, because of the multitude and variety of works, a man is hindered and cannot always actually keep God before his eyes, let him at least habitually conform his intention of living according to the most gracious will of God to this desire.

The third is that in all things he obey God, holy mother Church, and the prelates set over him, and not depart from the path of right and enlightened reason; for whoever despises this threefold obedience has denied the faith. It is therefore necessary to show equal obedience to these three in the right order, according to the ordinance of reason, so that the monk’s life may remain blameless in its actions and free from fear.

These three things, possessed with humble sincerity, make a good man and show the state of a conscience that hopes well in the Lord. But the man who lacks one of these is not perfectly good, even if he appears to be good. If, however, repenting of his sins, he has resolved henceforth to fulfill these three things, he is now made good and pleasing to God, however evil he may have been before. Moreover, in order that from a good man a good religious, or spiritual man, may be born, three other things are required, according to the aforesaid Castellensis.

The first thing required for making a good religious is that purity of heart be cleansed by the practice of discipline from every rivalry or incitement of the flesh. This purity is never better acquired than if the world, together with all its things, is contemned.

The second thing through which a good man becomes a good religious is called spiritual freedom in God. This freedom, once the phantasms of all things have been excluded, can raise itself, unencumbered, upward to God in all its exercises, and continually lift itself without impediment in thanksgiving together with devout prayers.

In the third way a good man becomes spiritually good when, through the desire of love, the spirit is united with God by grace. These last two make our cenobite spiritual and often introduce him among the citizens of the third region. Therefore whoever desires to have good confidence in the testimony of his conscience should humbly strive to exercise himself in the aforesaid things, because security is never prudently presumed when danger is not avoided. And what is so dangerous as always to live in negligence and sins, and to be unwilling to amend the errors one has committed? The confidence of the just, arising from the testimony of a good conscience, is always best, and is continually subject to God in humble service. But the impious and sinners, disturbed by their own actions, raise themselves against God and do not trust in the testimony of conscience, but rather presume vainly.

Here follow the seven roots of divine fear, which are laid fundamentally in the first step of humility.

Since this second region principally instructs the cenobite in due order through the steps of humility that proceed from the fear of God, it is necessary for him clearly to know the roots of that fear, if he wishes to reach the love of God by ascending. Therefore, so that we may be able to construct this spiritual house to perfection, we must place those roots in order in the foundation. We did not set them out in the first step of humility for this reason: that we should not confuse the order of the things to be said with excessive prolixity. There are, then, seven roots of the fear of God, through which the cenobite is led to compunction and, by making progress in true humility, is more strongly rooted.

The first root of the fear and love of God is intent meditaThe first root of the fear and love of God is intent meditation on the incomprehensible divine majesty: the more curiously it is investigated by man, the less it is comprehended. For the prophet says: Truly you are a hidden God. This meditation begets wonder at divine perfection; wonder causes reverence; from reverence arises fear of majesty; and from fear worship is produced. Meditation on the highest goodness is divided, according to our purpose, into seven considerations, which are not unfittingly adapted to the seven days of the week, or even to the seven canonical hours. And although that highest and most perfect goodness abundantly suffices for us as matter for meditation, nevertheless, because it belongs to few to be able to ascend to invisible things without visible things, we wish through known things to raise the minds of the weak to things unknown. For the holy Apostle says: The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are perceived, being understood through the things that have been made; his everlasting power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse.

First, therefore, the wondrous power of God is praiseworthy in the principal work of creation: for he who was able to bring forth all things out of nothing created, by his will alone, things so great, so solid, so varied, and so noble. From this consideration arises wonder at divine power, through which man is moved to the fear of God.

Second, the provident wisdom of God is praiseworthy, because, knowing all things, he orders the universe and governs by his providence all things that he has created. He knows all things, understands all things; by his counsel he disposes all things; by his command he contains all things. For, as a certain lover of worldly wisdom said, God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. He is within all things and is not enclosed; he is outside all things and is not shut out; he is beneath all things and is not oppressed; he is above all things and is not borne up. He includes all things, for although he is wholly everywhere, he is confined in no place; great and immense, he is bounded by no quantity. He orders all things as he wills; stable in himself and always immovable, he changes the vicissitudes of things; without passion of mind he mercifully prepares eternal rewards for the good; without disturbance he condemns the unjust in wrath. Great without magnitude, immense without quantity, he has set a limit to things; governing the world, he disposes all things.

Third, the merciful clemency of God is praiseworthy in our redemption.

It is praiseworthy because the man whom he created in his own image, fallen so wretchedly into the pit of damnation, he restored so mercifully. O what shall I, a little worm, indeed nothing in comparison with my maker, render to the supreme and incomprehensible majesty, who, when I did not exist, created me by his power, and, when I had perished, became man for me and, dying on the cross, redeemed me? What shall I repay to you, mediator of God and men, Jesus, savior of the world, who, though you are God exalted and inestimable, became man for me, the vilest, and were willing to undergo things so vile and unworthy? Behold, my heart speaks to you; all my inward parts bow toward you, because no voice can express what, concerning your most innocent passion, you grant your faithful inwardly to feel in their hearts.

Fourth, in the work of our justification, the kindly patience of God is praiseworthy, because he not only mercifully bears with sinners, but also calls those who are to be justified to repentance by the promises of eternal joys. Who could suffice to praise this clemency of the most indulgent father, who so mercifully justifies sinners returning to him, gives after a fall the grace of meriting, ordains manifold occasions for living well, and supplies his sacraments to the penitent as certain vessels of grace? Finally, for compunction, instruction, consolation, and thanksgiving, he pours the Holy Spirit himself into his faithful, making friends and sons out of enemies. He does not consider what sort of sinner a person was before; he seeks only that thereafter he remain faithful to him. Great is the clemency of divine compassion, which so mercifully receives the penitent to pardon, and even promises them great rewards after guilt.

Fifth, the deep justice of God is praiseworthy in the damnation of the reprobate, because he permits no evil to pass unpunished, depriving the sinner of the good which, by sinning, the fool does not fear to lose. Finally, to speak in our manner, the supreme purity of God is shown praiseworthy in this: it abominates every sin and vice as a putrid corpse. We have also recognized that his wisdom is praiseworthy in the damnation of the impious, which, drawing good out of evils to itself...

he compels them to serve him in punishment, though by sinning against justice they had refused to be subject to him in guilt.

Sixth, God’s abundant munificence is praiseworthy in the glorification of the blessed, since for a small merit he rewards his elect with so ineffable a recompense, and bestows on them, as immortals, a gift together with the holy angels.

Seventh, God’s incomprehensible excellence in himself is praiseworthy: he orders all things according to his providence, and, always without motion or time, remains unchangeable in his most consequent perfection. The contemplation of this seventh consideration pertains to the Sabbath of eternal blessedness, in which there is no longer the work of laborious conduct, but the happy blessedness of an eternal dwelling and of rest. For just as God, the creator of all things, is read to have completed all his work and rested on the seventh day, so in the heavenly Sabbath not work but eternal rest will be laid upon the just. Therefore, if we desire happily to reach those heavenly mansions, let us rest in God alone, in whom the rational creature is perfected by resting; and, perfected through the adherence of love, it rejoices with the Lord in ineffable union and joy.

Now, for the praising of God, let pure devotion seek nothing henceforth outside God, since almighty God himself, perfect and most wise, suffices for all as the matter of his praise, and exceeds every praise by his infinite perfections. For Scripture says: “Praise the Lord as much as you can; he will still surpass it.” For he is greater than all praise, and therefore he is to be praised by us most humbly rather in himself and for his own sake than from his creatures.

From the aforesaid considerations concerning God there arises a manifold and varied affection of devotion; through it, too, a more worthy effect of prayer is generated according to the desire of the affection. For when meditation of the heart is taken up concerning God’s majesty or power, reverent wonder is produced. But when we begin to meditate on his ineffable wisdom, confounded by our own imperfect justice, we accuse ourselves. Thus, in consequence, from consideration of God’s mercy the hope of pardon is taken up;

from his patience love of heart is generated; from his justice humility is born; from meditation on his munificence, gratitude. For just as, according to the quality of the wood, a kindled fire grows in magnitude, so, according to the various meditations on God, the ardor of devotion rises up in prayers among those who love God.

Concerning Meditation on the Work of Our Reparation in the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

Root II.

The second root of the fear and love of God is placed in meditation on our redemption, which is generated, through diligent exercise, in the life, deeds, teaching, and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Among all meditations we believe this one to be more useful for us, for in it we know that our salvation and the sum of eternal blessedness are contained. And note that the Lord’s passion, with respect to its proceedings, was unjust; with respect to its manner, shameful; with respect to its pain, bitter; and with respect to its effect, fruitful. Therefore it must always be held in memory.

First, with respect to its proceedings, it was unjust, because he who was born of a virgin neither contracted sin nor committed it, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For death is inflicted on us for sin; but he could not justly die who was always just and innocent, without any sin. Finally, a man is killed contrary to human law if a sentence of death is brought against someone neither confessed nor convicted of a crime. For before Pilate the Savior was accused on three counts: that, calling himself a king, he forbade tribute to be given to Caesar; and third, that he made himself the Son of God. The Gospel speaks about the first two, and the accusation is shown to be false. For regarding the first, the contrary was plainly established, since Christ said that his kingdom was not earthly. Nor was the falsity of the second hidden from Pilate, for he knew that Jesus had commanded that the things that were Caesar’s should be given to Caesar. When questioned by the governor concerning the third, he was silent, because Pilate could not hear the divine generation the generation of Jesus, or even his human nativity.

His Passion also was contrary to custom, because it received no delay of time. He is not, according to custom, placed in prison; nothing is deliberated in his case; but, once taken, he is at once dragged before the judge to be subjected to death. Scourged, spat upon, and afflicted with many injuries, blows, and mockeries, he is nailed to the cross. Third, it was contrary to the law of nature, and procured from the obstinate hatred of the heart. For nature forbids raging against the dead, and shudders at tearing with new wounds a body already slain. For our redeemer, dead on the cross, is pierced through with a lance; and, contrary to the law of nature, though dead, he is wounded by the impious.

Second, the Passion of Christ is said to have been ignominious as to its manner for the six causes that follow. First, because of the paltry price: for blood of incomparable worth is sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver, for which no one would deign to sell his little ass. Second, because of the shameful office: for, full of wounds and half dead, he is compelled to carry his own cross, something found to have been done to no robber. Third, because of the unworthiness of the place: for he is crucified outside the city in the place of Calvary, where robbers and criminal murderers are punished for their deserts. Fourth, because of the shameful punishment: for he is hung naked on the cross, a penalty owed only to robbers and criminal men. Indeed, as Scripture says, the redeemer of the world was condemned by a most shameful death. Fifth, because of the shameful mockery: for before the whole multitude he is hung naked on the cross, and, as if a fool and a madman, is blasphemed by all. Concerning this the psalmist says: “All the day my shame is before me.” Sixth, because of the shameful company: for, counted with criminals, he is hung in the midst of robbers. What are you doing now, O Christian soul? Behold, your savior hangs in the middle among robbers, and do you not fear to sit in the first place in council?

Third, the most holy Passion of Christ, as to its pain, was most bitter for seven reasons. First, because of the delicate vitality of his flesh, which in its natural constitution was most excellent, and therefore was more grievously afflicted in the endurance of pains. For delicate flesh suffers more than flesh coarse by natural condition. Therefore, since the flesh of Christ was subtle and delicate, he emitted a bloody sweat in the garden. Second, because of the character of those who killed him: for Christ was killed not by strangers to his own people, but by his own blood-relatives and neighbors, as he had earlier complained through the prophet: “My people, what have I done to you?” For one suffers more tolerably from strangers and enemies than from one’s own people, from whom at least friends, by reason of nearness of blood, show compassion. Third, because of the bitterness of the Passion: for he is afflicted more in those places where pain is felt more greatly because of the nerves. For, raised up on the cross, he is fastened through hands and feet; the Lord of all, thirsting, is given gall and hyssop to drink. For the psalmist says of him: “They have pierced my hands and my feet; they have counted all my bones.” Who could conceive in the mind the pain of your most holy heart, good Jesus, when the hardest nails began so cruelly to pierce your hands and feet? Would that my soul might always show itself grateful to you; would that the remembrance of your most holy Passion might not depart from my memory. I shall easily be able to obtain from you the effect of my prayers if it should befall me to delight without interruption in the exercise of your Passion. Let each person think what he can; I prefer the memory of your Passion to all exercises, through which I trust that in my prayers I shall receive whatever is fitting for salvation. Fourth, because of its duration, the Passion of Christ was most bitter: for from the hour of his capture until death he was always in most bitter torment. “All the day,” he says, “I went about sorrowful,” and “there is no health in my flesh.” Fifth, because of the generality of the Passion: for in whatever ways Christ could suffer, he suffered uniquely. For he suffered in his reputation, since, falsely accused, he is blasphemed by the impious. He also suffered in his possessions, because, naked and stripped, he is hung upon the wood;

whose garments are divided by lot among the soldiers. He suffers in his soul, because, foreseeing the bitterness of the passion, he was sorrowful even unto death. He suffered in his whole body, since from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him. He suffers in his friends, since he is betrayed by a disciple and, deserted by all, is even publicly denied by Peter. He is also afflicted in compassion for his mother, whose most holy soul is remembered as having been pierced by the sword of sorrow. He suffered from the ingratitude of many, because he foresaw that the death which he endured in compassion for all would be lost in many of the reprobate.

Finally, he suffered in all the senses, as we are taught from the Gospel. He suffers in his eyes, which, with many tears poured out, are veiled with a cloth. He suffers in his hearing, when, mocked with many insults and reproaches, he is blasphemed. He suffers in smell, since he is defiled by the foul spittle of the Jews. He suffers in touch, since he is tormented in all the members of his body. He suffers in taste, because, thirsting, he is given gall and vinegar to drink.

Sixth, because of the cause of the passion, which was solely the injury done by the Jews, since he suffered entirely without guilt. For whoever suffers unjustly is tormented all the more in spirit. But the innocent Son of God dies for our sins and is tormented for our crimes, as is read in Isaiah: Truly he himself bore our infirmities.

Seventh, because of the lack of every consolation, since Christ found no one consoling him in his passion. For he says in the Psalm: You have put friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery. Indeed, his acquaintances stood far off.

Fourth, the passion of Christ was fruitful with respect to its effect, and this is principally to be considered in three things. First, the remission of sins was accomplished; second, the bestowal of grace; third, the display of glory. These three things are indicated by the title affixed to the cross, which, as the evangelist says, contained the cause of Jesus’ passion: Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews. For Jesus, saving sinners, pertains to the first; Nazarene, bestowing the flower of grace, to the second; king of the Jews, granting the heavenly kingdom to those who confess him, to the third.

Moreover, in this second root we have arranged meditations on the passion of the Lord for the individual hours of the seven days of the week. We have placed them after the end of the third region so as not to disturb the order of what is to be said here with their excessive length. For we see that what we have now set out pertains rather to reading than to meditation, and therefore we postpone those meditations.

On Meditation on the Benefits of God. Root III.

The third root of divine fear and love is fixed in meditation on the benefits of God, through which one comes to the grace of devotion. For the beginning of devotion is placed in meditation on the benefits of God, from the memory of which love is born. Its middle, as progress in that meditation itself, desires nothing other than to please God above all things, from whom it knows that it has been anticipated in many benefits without merit. Its end loves God above all things with burning desire and pure fervor of mind, and longs to cling to him alone there continually, without intermediary.

And although merciful God has bestowed many things specially upon each one of us, nevertheless, because we are writing this synthema not for one person but for many, we ought to discuss at length, not the particular benefits allotted to individuals, but the general benefits conferred upon all. Therefore we include the more important ones under the number seven, so that through the seven days of the week, or even in the canonical hours themselves, we may have ready at hand the material for daily meditation. But if anyone is unable to ascend to that summit of contemplation, let him strive to exercise himself more fervently in these meditations on the benefits of God, so that, while he diligently continues the lower things, once purified he may ascend stronger to the higher. Therefore let the monk devoutly consider what he has received, so that he may be able to show himself grateful. Let him render to God what he has received, if he desires to be good.

For first he gave us body and soul with their ornaments; and those whom he created intellectual in his own image, he also mercifully called to the heavenly kingdoms. What more could he have given us, he who, when he had created us although we did not exist, gave himself? But what can we return to our Creator, since by our own merit we are sinners and weak? Let us return what we are; let us return what we owe: namely, faithful service for the body that we have received from the Lord, and sincere love for the soul by which we were created in the image of God. For thus the prophet admonishes us in the psalm: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.” Serve faithfully; love reverently. On the part of the body, render faithful service to your Creator; on the part of the soul, love him with all your strength. Serve him because the Lord is powerful and great; love him because he is good. His power is shown in your creation; his goodness is made clear in your restoration. Since, when you did not exist, he created you by his power, he deserves faithful service; since by his goodness he restored you when you had fallen, he deserves the affection of sincere love. For truly he is our Father through love; he is Lord through incomprehensible power.

Second, he gave us faith with the sacraments, for just as he made us without our will, so he called us to faith without our merit. For Christ says to his disciples in the holy Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” Through faith the Christian soul is led back to its beginning; we are bound to devote the sacraments that he gave with perpetual adherence, and to remain continually in his holy covenant. For in baptism we renounced the devil and all his pomps; we promised that we would cling to Christ forever, as those who raised us from the sacred font, our guarantors, stood before the Lord for us in the faith of our parents. Therefore let us always say from the heart with the prophet: “It is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.”

Third, almighty God gave us the craft of righteousness and the teachings of truth. For these we owe our Creator faithful performance and perpetual service without deceit.

Therefore we are commanded first of all to do all things to the praise of God, and in everything we do to raise our intention chiefly to his honor. For only a good intention toward God distinguishes works; only love makes them fruitful. Behold, the Lord bestowed on us the craft of nature for praising him; moreover he gave the teachings of salvation through the law; he requires from us praise and love above all things. Therefore let us exercise, to the honor of God, the craft bestowed on us, and the pure eye of intention will come about through the teaching of the law.

Fourth, the merciful Father bestowed on us the world with its necessary elements; for these he requires from us sincere contemplation of himself as due. Whatever we discern in this world ought to lead us to the memory of God and continually provoke us to love its Creator above all things. Hence Bernard, well practiced in sacred matters, says: the whole and true lover of God, wherever he turns, has the familiar admonition of his Creator; he uses things as a mirror, and thus, by reflection, is lifted up from creatures to the Creator. For concerning each thing he says: if those things that were created with time, are changed, and pass away seem good, beautiful, and sweet, what goodness, beauty, and sweetness does God their author possess, remaining forever, who has reserved for himself things incomparably better than these? By this consideration the devout man regards all human beings with the simple eye of the mind, as the likeness of the image of God, and does not curiously attend to the pleasing or displeasing form of the body in them. For in a human being he considers not what he sees outwardly, but the image of the Creator, which he knows to be a sharer in eternal happiness.

Fifth, the Son of God offered himself in torments for us, and redeemed us, lost as we were, from the destruction of perpetual death by his blood. We are commanded to devote benevolent imitation to this love of our Savior, if we desire to come to his kingdom. For the prince of the apostles says to the faithful: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps.” What shall I repay you, O good Jesus, for your benefits toward me, so great and so immense?

I shall suffer with you in heart; I shall suffer with you in deed; I shall imitate you in the affections of my mind, according to my ability.

Sixth, the Creator has bestowed on us time for meriting eternal life, and has given the necessary nourishment of the body. For here indeed we are debtors to ourselves, since in this time we owe to ourselves the acquisition of merits. Why, then, do we spend the days of salvation so negligently and without the fruit of merits, when we have nothing more precious than time? Behold, within this brief present time we can merit the joys of eternal blessedness, and yet we all dissemble when it comes to doing what is good. Woe to us, foolish and mad, who accept nothing in this world as more precious than time, and yet are accustomed to spend nothing more cheaply. For now an acceptable time is granted to us; now the days of salvation are given, in which we ought to persist in holy works with the greatest fervor, and always to have regard for the hour of death.

Seventh, God has set before us heaven, filled with all joy, and has promised himself, with all the things contained in it, as a reward. For this generosity of our Savior we ought to devote ourselves to holy works of mercy, and show ourselves imitators of God according to our strength. To this he exhorts us in his sacred Gospels: “Be merciful, just as your Father, God, is merciful.” At the end of the world also, when the day of judgment has come, by his own promise he will send the merciful into eternal life, since whoever has shown mercy will obtain mercy. And lest any monk should say, “I can show mercy to no one, since my religious life allows me to possess absolutely nothing,” let us know that among the necessary works of mercy the spiritual are the more powerful. If you wish, as a monk, to be merciful, pray to God for the wretched; give saving instruction to the ignorant.

The sum, then, of meditation on the benefits of God rests on three exercises, in which it is chiefly and wholly contained. In the first, we must attribute all things to God, not to ourselves; in the second, by remembering God’s benefits, we must exercise ourselves in the pursuit of love; in the third, for the benefits received, we must give thanks with a pure heart. But if through these exercises concerning benefits we wish to kindle our heart to the love of God, we ought to consider six conditions in those gifts just mentioned. First, consider that God’s gift is altogether noble; second, that it is especially fruitful and valuable for you; third, that it is varied, manifold, and repeated very often. These three consider the gift as ordered in itself; the two that follow have regard to the person of the giver; the last notes the condition of the receiver. Fourth, then, consider the great affection of the giver toward you; fifth, his inestimable dignity; sixth, that you, the receiver, are lowly and contemptible, and unworthy of all things, though you receive great things from the greatest one. And by these considerations of benefits, the love of God is accustomed to rise up in the mind of a devout person, and, advancing by sure steps, to lift the spirit toward contemplation.

can be, because the best does not become better, nor does the greatest become greater. God created you in his goodness, not because your condition was necessary to him, but because it was advantageous to you alone. Whoever considers this goodness of God with intent meditation rightly praises his Creator.

Second, so that you may not be lifted up into pride, O man, consider the vileness of your condition: that you were made from the mud of the earth, and after a little while, consumed by worms, you will return into the earth as dust. Why then are you proud, earth and ashes? Your conception has guilt; your birth, misery; your life, punishment; your dissolution, the distress of death. For a man born of woman, living a short time, is filled with many miseries; and then he is especially miserable when he does not recognize that he is miserable in the flesh.

Third, consider the origin of your conception, and you will find your soul stained by the foul ugliness of original sin. For we are born children of God's wrath, but, obtaining the grace of baptism in the blood of Jesus Christ, we are cleansed from the original stain. Rightly, through this consideration, we love our Savior, by whose mercy we have been cleansed from the original stain.

Fourth, faithful soul, consider how exceedingly vile you have become by repeating your ways in the act of sin, for you have shown yourself an adulteress to Christ, your bridegroom, though he joined you to himself by his own blood, wholly unstained. What are you doing, O miserable one? Why do you abandon your most beloved bridegroom, or why, foolish one, do you withdraw from your beginning? Know yourself to have been placed in the flesh, not so that you may consent to its vices and desires, but rather so that you may resist them by the command of reason. For as often as, by dissembling, you have yielded your consent, so to speak, to the disordered movements of the flesh and to things contrary to divine rectitude, so often, turned away from the highest good and from your bridegroom, you show yourself an adulteress. Beware, beware, O soul redeemed by the blood of Christ, lest the love of the flesh deceive you; for just as the first man, deceived by love for the woman who was his companion, fell into death, so any soul that consents to the pleasures of its flesh shamefully withdraws from its beginning, which is God.

But alas, miserable one, where have you fallen? You have dwelt in a foreign land; you have been defiled with the dead; you have been counted with those descending into hell. You have abandoned the fountain of wisdom; you have turned backward; you have committed adultery.

But hear my counsel, and return as quickly as possible to the guide of your youth, Jesus; submit yourself wholly and humbly to him. He is merciful. He will gladly receive you as you return to him; he will forgive your sins, and, if you ask, he will bestow the grace of his love. But you must withdraw from the affections of your flesh if you desire to come into the sight of your Savior. Therefore, if you are converted to Jesus, be converted in truth, because the highest Truth cannot love anything except what is true.

There is also another mode of self-knowledge, which is taken up with respect to God, whenever an incomparable comparison between God and man is contemplated. Concerning this mode, Bernard, clear in contemplation, says: Never does the measure of human imperfection perceive itself better than in the light of God's countenance and in the mirror of divine vision. For there, one who is more in the day and sees more clearly what is lacking in himself amends day by day, by likeness, whatever he has lost through unlikeness, drawing near to him by likeness from whom he has been made distant by unlikeness. Therefore let us raise the sharpness of the mind to the most luminous mirror of divine perfection; let us submit our affection to that immutable good, so that in God's wisdom we may be able to perceive our own foolishness, and in his power consider our own weakness.

On Keeping the Memory of One's Sins. Root V.

The fifth root of the fear of God is the memory of sins, and the foulness of sin itself when it is often contemplated. For truly, whoever genuinely understands the ugliness of mortal sin always fears the pit of this evil. But so that you may in some way recognize the gravity of sin, you must consider the seven points that follow.

First, then, consider the beauty of God's justice, to which sin is wholly contrary and therefore most to be fled. For through sin the soul is wholly turned away from the highest good, and the love that is naturally within it for its beginning is changed into hatred.

For just as all good things are from the first Good, so every love, toward whatever good it is borne, is naturally kindled by that same Good. For since our love cannot rest in any goods as in its end, it has as its end, where it will come to rest, the same good that it had as its beginning. Therefore, whenever sin is committed against the beauty of God’s justice, the soul is separated from its own beginning. For since God is charity, he demands love in the soul; peace requires peace; he loves what is like himself and hates what is unlike.

Second, consider the enormity of sin, and carefully weigh how greatly its foulness displeases God. Behold, because of pride the just God cast Lucifer, the noblest angel, out of heaven, and condemned him with his accomplices to the burning of eternal fire. He also compelled our first parents, Adam and Eve, to go out of paradise because of disobedience, and by a just judgment condemned the whole human race, in their crime, to the sentence of a double death. Finally, let us turn over the whole history of the Old and New Testament, and we shall find that what was known to have been rashly committed against God’s justice was often gravely punished by it. Therefore the gravity of the crime is easily recognized if one considers the severity of the vengeance that followed.

Third, consider what grave scandal arises from sin, especially when one sins in the presence of others. For someone who by his evil example provokes another to sin shows himself to be an adversary of God. For God, by his will and out of mercy, has determined to save souls redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son; this person, through evil example and out of aversion from God, desires to destroy them. The sin of scandal is said to be gravest with respect to guilt for this reason: because, as we have said, it opposes God. But if the person who gives occasion for harm must be considered to have caused the harm, the sinner subjects himself to as many sentences of death as he has caused people by his evil example to fall into mortal crime. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: Woe to the person through whom scandal comes. And again he says: Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it is expedient for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung around his neck, and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea. True repentance is rare in one who scandalizes the little ones, because when he neglects to restore another’s loss, he in no way attains the fruit of saving repentance.

Fourth, consider the negligence of your ungrateful heart, because, although you were created in the image of God and ought to have loved your maker above all things, you dishonor him in many ways by your sins. You ought to devote continual service of love to Christ, the Son of God, by whose blood you have been redeemed; but you do not fear to love the flesh more than Jesus your Savior. Finally, with a compassionate mind you ought daily to turn over in your mind his most holy passion, and you are accustomed to think of nothing less than that. Adopted among the sons of God by mercy alone, you ought to have shown yourself worthy of the heavenly calling as an imitator, and yet through sloth you do not fear to lie still in the lowest things. And why do I say more? Behold, you who have been marked with the Holy Spirit and counted with the angels are called to the inheritance of the sons of God; you are invited by all the saints to the feasts of paradise; you daily partake of the body and blood of our Savior Jesus Christ; and yet you do not observe the commandments of God and of the rule which you promised to keep so that you might be blessed. Examine your conscience diligently, therefore, and you will find that there are many good things you ought to do and omit, and very many evil things you ought to omit yet commit against God’s good pleasure.

Fifth, consider whom you have offended by sinning: not a human being, but God; not a creature, but the Creator. He against whom you have sinned is great and immeasurable, terrible and glorious; his majesty makes the angels tremble, and all the powers of heaven marvel at his power. To God, the highest and unchangeable Good, the beginning and end of every creature, the rational spirit ought to devote love and the desire for union beyond human understanding, and it ought to lift itself wholly, truly, to that one thing, as to its own center, scorning all phantasms; to this it can raise itself the more easily, the more leaving all other things behind, it has striven to unite itself to itself. For by the power of that One, union comes about everywhere in the one; nor are things more alike more easily united to one another for any other reason than that they are one in quality. Therefore the soul is most rightly said to be united with that one principle of things only when, having become most perfectly one in itself, it is separated from every multiplicity and, above all imagination, reason, and understanding, its unity alone escapes, enjoying through loving affection the unity of God, joining its own center, so to speak, with the center of the universe.

But when the human soul itself, wrongly yielding to its quasi-marriage with the flesh, is turned toward any animal passions, then that very unity is badly changed into a multiplicity contrary to the One alone; and it becomes as far removed from its own principle as it has been divided from itself. Finally, the soul itself contracts great difficulty in returning to that one ineffable divine One whenever, confused in itself, it falls into the sin of apostasy. Consider now how great and ineffable he is against whose honor sin is committed; and since you are wholly unable to understand the greatness of his majesty, learn humbly to fear his power.

Sixth, consider what you have lost by sinning, so that, once the greatness of the loss is known, repentance may hasten and restore through tears what has been lost. What, then, wretched one, have you lost by sinning? Hear what you have lost. You had been made like God by grace, a companion of the angels, a member of Christ, and an heir chosen for eternal happiness; you ought to have lived and rejoiced without end in the goods of the Lord with all the saints. But what happened when you sinned?

You have been compared to senseless beasts, and have been made like them. For when you were in honor you refused to understand; you abandoned the fountain of life; by sinning you became a companion and member of the devil, a whore of Antichrist, an heir of hell. You abandoned life; you chose everlasting death. If you fear the sentence, change your will, and you will find forgiveness.

Seventh, consider what you have deserved by sinning; for if eternal death is inflicted for one sin, think what one who commits many, not to say innumerable sins, deserves.

For the soul that has sinned shall itself die. Moreover, even through one mortal sin you have deserved to be the devil’s companion without end, to be deprived of all the joys of heaven, and to be burned forever in the fires of hell. These are the rewards that sin has brought you; these are the gifts it promised.

Now, therefore, from these seven considerations make a plaster for your wounded soul; take up for yourself the goad of compunction, so that you may reach the root of fear. But hurry, and do not put it off from day to day, because he who receives the humble confession of the penitent has not promised tomorrow to the one who delays. For where haste finds pardon, delay often cuts off life. Hope for a longer life draws many to destruction, because while they trust that they can live longer in this world, they make the time of repentance pass without repentance. But you, man, if you accept my counsel, do not defer repentance, because you do not know what tomorrow’s day will bring you. For he deserves to lose the time of repentance who so often does not fear to put off the pursuit of repentance.

On Present Vanity and Eternity, the sixth root.

The sixth root of fear is raised up in the mind of one meditating if the vanity of visible things and the eternity of invisible things are considered with studious intention. For all things that we behold in this world are wholly subject to vanity and corruption, and will last for only the briefest time. All mortal things hang beneath uncertain chance, and by their own mutability promise flight. Whatever you have today will perhaps leave you tomorrow, or now, while you are speaking, will cease to be yours. For we perceive nothing in this world as long-lasting and stable, but see all things changed with time.

Now, therefore, ascend the watchtower of your mind, O faithful cenobite, and consider how all things that time contains are nothing, because whatever visible thing is now perceived will be corrupted after a little while. Take from past things a consideration of present things, and see that what has passed away is not, and what now seems to be will not be after a little while. Where are the kings of the nations? Where the princes? Where the leaders? Where the rich? Where those once powerful in the world? Where are all the lovers of the world? Where the men who despised the arduous road to heaven? Finally, where are all those once known to you in the world, whom death has meanwhile snatched away while you have been in the cloister? Behold, from the origin of the world, both those who lived for many years and those who lived for few have all died in their own generation; and, according to the diversity of their merits, at the dictate of justice, they have received diverse rewards. The lovers of God, joined to the Creator of all, receive everlasting bright dwellings filled with inestimable joys; and the worshipers of the world, contemners of God's commandments, once swollen here with honors, puffed up with knowledge, immersed in riches, and devoted to pleasures and vices, have descended to hell to be tormented without end. I ask you, what harm now does the once laborious contempt of the world, contrary to the flesh, do to the saints in heaven, for which they now rejoice forever in the glad vision of God? Or what profit now is the once-enjoyed consolation of the flesh to the impious buried in hell, for which they now receive the torments of eternal damnation? Think on these things while it is profitable; meditate on these things while the opportunity of taking care is present.

Again, ascending higher, try, with the gaze of your mind, to fix yourself as far as you can in the abyss of infinite depth, and to consider how long that is which is eternal. Eternity is time that is enclosed by no end and bounded by no span. The saints of God will rejoice forever, blessed in glory; sinners will burn forever, wretched in hell. O eternity, name terrible without end: who will be able to think of you, or to speak of you, without fear? Truly, he who thinks of you will never sin forever. Eternity has no end. Hear a comparison; and when it proves insufficient for eternity, take up fear. If a heap of sand were set in the size of Mount Olympus, stretched up to heaven, from which after ten thousand times ten thousand years a small bird consumed only one grain, that mountain would by no means be said to be going to last forever, but would be subject to an end; and although after innumerable years, nevertheless it would at some point cease. Yet all that time during which some part of the mountain remained, however very long it might be, would nevertheless seem nothing in comparison with eternity. For eternity admits neither the imagination of an end, nor the hope of completion, nor a boundary.

O therefore how foolish, how witless, how insane is the man who casts away this consideration of eternity, and spends uselessly the acceptable time granted to him for meriting eternal goods. The hour will come, and already hastens near, in which the wretch, when he can no longer act better, will learn what eternity is. But you, my monk, who desire to be faithful, cast away from yourself every care of the world; place all your concern on the love of God. Do nothing, think nothing, except what can lead you to the love of your Creator, or what you know pertains to the edification of others or the pure necessity of the body. Separate yourself, I pray, from low things, so that, good as you are, you may be delighted by eternal things. Let no care of the flesh remove you from the inward tranquillity of the mind; let no pleasure corrupt you. Strive always, as much as you can, to persist in prayers with devotion, and again to raise yourself more often through the affection of love.

On Always Having Zeal for God.

The Seventh Root of Fear.

The monk is commanded to exercise himself in the seventh root of fear in no small measure. For no one tolerates calmly the injuries of his lord if he truly loves him. Therefore you, monk, who desire to be a faithful servant of Jesus Christ, do not neglect zeal for him in yourself; when you see an injury against God, do not pretend not to see it, because whoever does not at once resist those who detract from his lord is proven to love him less. Let people know you as such a lover of God and enemy of vices that they do not hear evil spoken in your presence, nor dare to do anything evil while you look on.

they should not presume to do so in your sight. Be conspicuous for uprightness of spirit, renowned for the merit of your life, venerable for your zeal. Let the upright love you as a servant of God; let the wicked fear your face as that of a judge. Let no one in your presence presume to do anything alien to good morals, since all know that you cannot tolerate injury to God. Thus Phinehas earned an everlasting priesthood, when by zeal for the law he powerfully appeased the Lord’s anger. If you see order perishing in the monastery, that is, if your brothers have begun in any way to corrupt regular observance, do not, if you are a servant of God, keep silent about their vices. Set yourself firmly and strongly on behalf of the house of the Lord; exercise zeal for God as much as you can; destroy the counsels of the malicious; resist the rashness of the proud. If you are a true lover of God, by your face alone you will scatter the gatherings of the wicked. For no one will lay bare his plan before you if he suspects your zeal to be opposed to it. But if the evil and the wicked do not fear your presence when they do wrong, then surely they recognize no zeal for God in you.

Therefore, to show yourself a true servant of Christ, you ought gladly, for love of God, to forgive the injuries inflicted on you by your brothers, and to pray to God for those very persons who injure you. But it is not yours to forgive injuries against your Lord without his will; rather, from zeal for righteousness, you must avenge them. In these matters let love of blood-kin cease; let the bond of friendship withdraw far away: zeal for God must rightly be preferred to all things. For friendship with a man is to be observed in such a way that it is never preferred to zeal for God.

Woe to monks and abbots who so boldly cast aside zeal for God, who put human familiarities before the divine command, who conceal the vices of their subjects through foolish compassion, who observe the traditions of the holy rule neither in themselves nor in others. And what shall I say? We see among cloistered monks obedience to commands despised, zeal for righteousness scorned, observance of the rule held in contempt. Two or more make a bond of carnal friendship among themselves under the name of charity; the sick entrust the diseases of their soul to those still sicker, and they in no way seek God’s friendship through purity of mind. Each one thinks his companion better than the rest, and each, deceived, loves the other not spiritually but carnally, since they do not raise their affections to God and love nothing but the consolations of the flesh. But when you see a monk seeking the friendship of weak brothers, you ought to judge him not a servant of God but a lover of the flesh. For one who truly occupies his whole heart in the love of God cares nothing for human friendship. The love of Jesus is enough for him in all things; outside him he seeks nothing further. But one who has sought the consolation of his mind in external things shows by his conduct that he does not love God with his whole heart.

The love of God loves solitude, hates the tumult of men, and does not seek conversations with friends. O good Jesus, how sweet is your love: when it pierces the heart of one who loves you, the spirit longs to see you face to face and, having you, to embrace you. Indeed, one who loves you forgets himself and meditates on nothing but your most sweet presence. There is nothing in the world that pleases one who loves you; nothing is found anywhere that the soul desires except you. O with how many sighs the mind wounded by love is distressed; with how abundant tears the face is watered in secret, because as often as it thinks on the face of the beloved reigning in heaven, so often it weeps that it is desolate on earth.

Meanwhile the languishing mind often tries to say something of its most beloved Jesus, and it also strives to provoke others to love him; but as soon as it begins to utter the most sweet name of Jesus, unwillingly, because of the greatness of love, it falls silent. For the love of Jesus is expressed by no words, but is felt with sweetness in the secret of the mind. I know who said, “My love has been crucified.” Who is your love, O servant of God? Why do you weep? Why do you groan? Ignatius: “My love has been crucified, and shall I not mourn? My Lord has died, and shall I be able to restrain my tears?” Do not weep, O faithful soul; for although your love died to redeem you from death, yet he has now risen from the dead so that in heaven he may crown you with the crown of life. Be faithful unto death, and he will give you the crown of life.

On the manner and degrees of divine love, comprising the conclusion of this second region

Since no one suddenly becomes supreme, nor can anyone by his own powers suddenly ascend to that highest summit of divine love, I now think it useful to note briefly certain manners or degrees themselves of loving God.

Therefore, to move the human heart into divine love, the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is, in my judgment, more effective than all other things, if it is diligently contemplated in a person’s mind purely, sweetly, fervently, and perseveringly. Truly, whoever often recalls to memory the life, passion, and death of our Savior, especially according to the principal articles, suffering with him and giving thanks, prepares a swift ascent of the heart to divine love. But this most holy occupation of the mind concerning the Lord’s passion we shall treat opportunely in the second principal part of this work, where we shall explain more fully the manner of spiritual exercise. As for the rationale of what has been said here, I find three manners of loving God, which I shall briefly explain in order.

The first manner commands that you love him who loves you sweetly, and join your whole self to him gently, so that your heart loves nothing apart from God and seeks nothing from elsewhere. For since God is the whole, he alone desires to possess the whole heart of the one who loves, and he removes it from dissimilar thoughts. Therefore, if you wish to love sweetly, love wholly. For the love of God accomplishes either everything or nothing. Let meditation on the passion of Jesus Christ our Savior possess your whole self, until love sweetly grows strong in you. You must despise everything that flatters in the flesh, if you desire to come to the love of God. For no one can love God sweetly in this life so long as he is convicted of loving anything in the world. Indeed, the love of the world is utterly contrary to divine love, because where the one is admitted into the inner chambers of the heart, the other is forbidden to be present. But how much sweetness, how much gentleness, and how much joy of mind the love of God generates in the heart of the one who loves, no one at all understands except the one who, having despised all the things and events of the world, has loved God alone for a long time. The heart of one who loves God loves none of the things that are in the world; it despises the riches, honors, and favors of the age; it fears no adversities to be undergone for love of its Lord. The love of God is never idle; it always desires to come to its own beginning; it refuses to endure no labors in this world. Therefore let the one who does not wish to become sluggish love.

The neighbor also must be loved sweetly on account of God, and for no reason should he be offended against God or justice. Let each person always show himself to his brother in words and deeds such as he expects others to be toward himself. For he truly loves his neighbor who exposes his property, body, and soul for him. Christ taught this; the Son of God did this for us. Truly, whoever says that he truly believes in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. He does not truly love Christ who does not keep his commandments. For he says: This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you. We are members of one head, Jesus Christ, in whom we then believe when we keep his commandment concerning love toward God and toward the neighbor. Therefore let us love our neighbor, because he is a member in Christ together with us, so that, just as one member in the body suffers with another, so a brother may humbly be helped by a brother for the love of Christ.

The second manner commands you to love wisely, and to seek nothing else in divine love than God. Extend your affection toward that Word which was in the beginning with God; raise your mind above everything that has been created, because unless you forsake yourself and all things that are in the world, you will not be able to come to him whom you love. Finally, if you desire to love God wisely, do not consider yourself to be anything, O man, because where a man considers himself to be anything, he already loves unwisely.

The third manner commands that you love bravely, and never fear to expose body and soul for the love of God.

He is not a strong lover of God who is afraid to undergo death for him. For love is strong as death. One’s neighbor is loved wisely if it is not the human being but the vice that is hated. He is loved strongly, however, if every injury is forgiven him from a disposition to do good to that same person.

Here ends the second region.

[unknown]

[unclear] Preface to the third treatise of the first part, which describes the supreme region of the spirit of cloistered persons.

As I am at last about to write, with the Lord's help, about that supreme region of the spirit, I am shaken at once by fear and by shame: for I, a small man, fear to speak of the greatest matters, and I blush deeply to teach what I have not sufficiently experienced. For what intellect of any man, however well exercised, could know the state of a mind sweetly resting in God through love? Or what speech, even of the most eloquent orator, could explain the secret sweetness of inward contemplation? Indeed, the exercise of this third region surpasses human understanding for the greater part. In it the mind of a purified man, through the fervor of divine love, is carried above itself; and, while its natural essence remains, it is lulled with wondrous sweetness and absorbed in the abyss of divine contemplation. For it is oppressed by so great a sweetness of inward majesty that it seems unable either to understand or to express its own state. Having left behind the sensitive operation, it also passes wholly beyond the intellective operation; and, what is more, leaving itself behind, without imagination, reason, or understanding, it is lifted above itself by affection to that supreme summit of divine darkness.

But when it has altogether failed from itself, it does not act but rests; nor, when it returns to itself, can it understand what it has undergone, or reveal to anyone the manner of its elevation. For this elevation of the mind into God is so profound and so sublime that not only can the inexperienced person not understand it, but even the experienced person cannot fully explain in words what it is like. But what will I be able to say about the mountain of divine darkness, which I have not yet deserved to penetrate? For the well of inward contemplation is deep, and I am weak, since I have brought no vessel fit for these waters, nor have I prepared steps suitable for ascending to heights. Composed words do not befit a fool; nor ought an unskilled and cold man to speak of the secrets of divine contemplation, one who still remains with the weak in the valleys. For only he speaks fruitfully about profound matters who is illuminated by the twofold ray of the spirit. Nevertheless, since I am a man placed under obedience to the annual chapter, I am compelled to take up the mandate of that synod and to complete, according to my powers, the work set before me. Therefore I enter upon the third region of cloistered persons under the guidance of the venerable father lord Johannes of Bursfelde, the devout abbot, so that, by reducing as far as I can into my own manner of speaking what he described in learned and truthful discourse, I may appear to have obeyed the chapter.

Here begins the third region of the soul, which is called spiritual, in which the highest tranquility of mind is possessed

The third or supreme region of the soul is called spiritual; in it the highest rest and tranquility of mind are found. This region is compared to the empyrean heaven, in which there is the true rest of all and the true happiness of souls. The spirit abiding in this region leaves behind what is below reason, and, lifted up by love, ascends wondrously into God. For whatever it does in this most holy region is judged to be wholly divine. Here the human spirit, caught up above itself, receives the divine inrush; and, lulled in the darkness of divine contemplation, withdrawn from all creatures, it sweetly rests. In this region almighty God directs the spirit of the contemplative person; and, with the intellectual powers of the soul simplified and called back from every phantasm into the inner chamber, he perfects them according to their directed tendencies. And leading the mind, stripped of every multiplicity, to himself as the one principle, he also makes it one in himself, not by nature, but by gracious participation. The citizens of this supreme region are truly spiritual persons, who, having despised all things and affections of the world, love nothing in this world except God, covet nothing inordinately, but, absorbed by inward affection by the divine spirit, thirst vehemently for God alone and burn with ineffable desire for love of him. For they are driven into God by so great a fervor of love that, lifted above themselves, they commonly leave behind all intellectual operations, and, caught up into the abyss of divine contemplation, admit nothing whatever except God. Existing there insensibly through the grace of love, they become one with God, while the property of their natures is preserved, by the gift of participation. For the holy apostle of Jesus Christ says: He who clings to the Lord is one spirit. And again he says: Those who are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God. The same apostle also shows himself to be a citizen of this most holy region when he cries out to the Philippians: But our conversation is in heaven. For as long as we are in the body we are exiles from the Lord; but we are sweetly led, as though through sleep, to our homeland when in mind and spirit we have our conversation in heavenly things. I have said “through sleep” not properly, but by a remote comparison. For in dreams we go forth amid images of things intelligible to us, with their forms preserved in the imagination; but in contemplation, beyond every imagination, we are lifted up pure in mind and spirit to God. And therefore this supreme region of the soul is called spiritual; from it all religious persons obtain the name of spirituality. Woe to us. We are called spiritual from this most blessed region, and we are named religious lovers of God, though nevertheless we desire to attain the summit of this mountain through contemplation. In this region charity holds command, wisdom the consulship; in it nothing is loved except God, nothing is committed inordinately. This most holy region, moreover, belongs to the empyrean heaven, because those whom it receives spiritually as citizens it leads to the joys of heaven.

sends them on without intermediary. For just as the lowest region of the flesh sends its citizens, when they die, to hell, and the middle region of reason sends its citizens to purgatory, so this region sends its perfect worshippers, when they depart, on to heaven. The dignity of this third and highest region is expressed by many prerogatives, and is especially commended in seven articles, as will be said in order.

That this highest region of the spirit of cloistered persons is pleasing by comparison.

Article 1

First, then, this third region of the soul is called pleasing by comparison, because it is compared to the highest empyrean heaven. For just as in the empyrean heaven all things are tranquil, so on this summit of the highest region the mind of the person contemplating God is shaken by no disturbances. Here is the highest rest of the contemplating soul; here no vicious crowd dwells; no bitterness of mind draws near at all. In the empyrean heaven, indeed, the majesty of God is seen by the holy spirits through an ineffable gift; here, in darkness, through the longing of love, it is seen above understanding. There God is all in all; here nothing among all things is pleasing except God. There it is granted to the saints to rest from their labors without end; here the mind is permitted, in rest, to taste beforehand the unspeakable sweetness of inward delight. There is no blessedness greater than that in heaven, and there is no tranquillity in the world so sweet as that in this region.

Blessed indeed are those who have deserved to ascend this mountain of divine contemplation, who love absolutely nothing in this world and long for nothing other than always to cling to God. O how secure is the conscience of such persons, how joyful their way of life, where no evil is committed and nothing is desired except that highest, unchangeable good. For the mind purified through divine love, which has truly and perseveringly ascended this region, desires nothing fleshly, nothing disordered, but raises its whole self in contemplation of the highest majesty through longing, and rests sweetly in God alone. O who could truly express the inward sweetness of the soul that loves God, where the mind recalls the powers and capacities of the soul from the dispersion of multiplicity into one, and raises them upward with fiery affections into the chamber of the spirit? Here it directs its gaze and love toward that luminous, unchangeable good, rejects entirely every created and creatable multiplicity, and gathers the soul into one, so that, being one in itself, it may rise without the hindrance of multiplicity to the principle of light, which is one. For unity alone can reach the one principle of things, because unity flees multiplicity, and unity seeks the one. For the more you cling to multiplicity, the more you withdraw from unity.

Therefore, for those dwelling in this highest region of the spirit, God is accustomed, so that he may raise them in contemplation to the principle of his love, to cast away from them every multiplicity clinging in imagination or understanding, so that, gathered in their own unity, they may be able to strive ardently toward him alone with the simple affection of love, whom they know to be above every position.

That this highest region of the spirit is sweet and lovable by its nearness.

Article 2

Second, this highest region of the spirit is sweet and most pleasant by a singular likeness of the spirit. For the citizen of this most holy region, as I might say, is separated from the citizens above by only one wall of light, because, while the spirit still dwells in the flesh, it cries out toward heaven as though through a wall. But that wall is the barrier of the flesh, from which the spirit, once freed, is about to depart and migrate to heaven when the spirit is separated from the body. But the spirit wounded by sins, which cannot raise itself to this region with the pure affection of love, is still said to stand farther away from the empyrean heaven. Those, however, who dwell in this most quiet region are very near the empyrean heaven, because, weighed down by no stains of sins, they despise all earthly and fleshly things, and always long to have their way of life in heaven in mind and spirit.

Certainly those who inhabit the empyrean heaven and those who dwell in the third region have one and the same object. But this is the difference: these contemplate God in a riddle, while those contemplate him in clear vision. In both places there is sweetness for those who contemplate: here great, there greatest; here in the desire of fervent love, there in the possession of most blessed vision.

In this supreme region of divine contemplation the rational spirit calls back its powers and faculties into its own inner chamber, where it too, free from every phantasm, is at rest; it raises itself above itself into the dense darkness of God, in which, lulled by ecstatic love, it rests sweetly. Here there is no troublesome confusion of thoughts, no imagining of phantasms; rather, the naked mind is lifted upward and contemplates without any thought or imagination. Indeed, when the mind itself again gives access to thoughts, it shows itself to be descending once more to the middle region, which is that of reason.

But since the human mind cannot always remain unmoved at the summit of divine contemplation, it must often return to the rational exercise of the second region. If, however, it has slipped down into sensual passions, then it descends again to the lowest region. Yet the spirit of the true lover of God, although because of the frailty of the flesh it cannot always remain in the delight of contemplation, nevertheless strives often, through enkindled affection, to raise itself to that region, so that it may carry out the exercise of reason in such a way that it does not entirely abandon the sweetness of inward delight. O how good it is to cleave to the Lord; how sweet it is to attend to God alone, so that the mind may thirst for the Lord Jesus above all things and may always long with burning desires to embrace him. Standing in this region, it is indeed very near the empyrean heaven, and therefore is inflamed toward it with the greatest desires of love.

O how many groans and tears the mind fervent with love is accustomed to pour forth; how ardently it sighs for heavenly things, since the nearer it is to the empyrean heaven through the secret of contemplation while standing in this supreme region, the more ardent its desire is known to be to leave the prison of the body. Hence with the holy apostle the mind, languishing with love, says in its burning sighs: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”

That This Region of the Soul Is Divine in Its Instruction. Article 4.

Third, this supreme region of the soul is said to be divine in instruction, because in it the mind, pierced by divine love, is taught not by a human being but by the Holy Spirit. For Christ said to his lovers in the holy Gospel: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” And again there is that saying of the prophet: “And they shall all be teachable by God.” For the Holy Spirit dwells in the heart of one who loves Jesus, and illuminates it by his invisible teaching.

In this region the spirit reads true wisdom, Mary’s best part, in the tranquillity of silence; mystical theology is taught in the secrecy of the divine darkness with ineffable sweetness; the mind, disposed by the fervor of most holy love, speaks with its beloved in hiddenness and is continually lifted up to him by desire. This wisdom, or mystical theology, can indeed be commended by a human being, but it cannot be taught except by divine instruction. For the work of the Holy Spirit is being done when the mind is enlightened in truth through contemplation.

But we must consider that mystical theology is acquired through the exercise of a purified affection and is taught through the fire of love. Speculative theology, however, which we call scholastic, is learned through the exercise of the intellect, while the mind, burning continually with zeal for study, is devoted to it. For the acquisition of mystical theology, the purification of affection from every entanglement is required, so that the will, depraved through aversion, may be reformed through the conversion of inward love toward its source. Indeed, unless affection has been purified from every disordered desire, it does not ascend to the height of this most sacred wisdom. But if it has cast away sensual passions, if the human will has been conformed to the divine will, the mind through enkindled by love, the mind is raised upward and is lifted by anagogical movements into the immensity of the divine darkness. No one understands the sweetness of this theology unless he receives it, and no one receives it unless he seeks it alone out of all things through the sighs of love. The psalmist sought this when he prayed to the Lord: “Would that my ways were directed to keep your justifications at all times.” For by such movements of desire the holy man was borne upward toward obedience to the divine will, so that in that same Psalm 118 he spoke scarcely any verse in which he did not set down a divine word equivalent to judgment.

The exercise of this purification is begun in the second region and is completed in this one. For no small labor is required, so that the affection may be purified from the desires of the world. But once the exercise of spiritual reformation has been taken up, the mind gradually advances in love; it longs to ascend to this region by fixed degrees; through desire it hastens to the invisible school of this theology; sighing with continual groans, it knocks at the door of divine mercy. But the mind is not admitted into the secret of this mystical wisdom unless, after the complete purification of the affection, it is stripped of every creature, unites itself to itself, and withdraws far from every reasoning or imagining of thinkable things. For unless it has withdrawn from every creature, it does not approach the Creator, who is above all things.

In this school, therefore, the Holy Spirit is believed to preside over those who learn by divine instruction. He teaches a person to love nothing in this world, and to conform himself in all things to the will of God. Happy is the one who has deserved to be the disciple of this master; happy is the one who has entered this school through the desire of love, because in mystical silence he perceives wondrous things which God has hidden from those who do not love him.

That this highest region of the spirit is founded in simplicity.

Article IV

Fourth, this most holy region of the spirit is said to be founded in simplicity, in which the mind is united to its own immutable principle, not through essence, but through the love of adherence. For, as we have already said above, that highest good, God, is one; and our soul cannot approach him unless, stripped of all multiplicity which belongs to reason, imagination, and understanding, it strives to present itself wholly united to itself.
