Finally, through meditation on the Lord’s passion, or at least on one of its more sacred articles, or on several if the opportunity of time is present, the mind of a devout person is pierced with compunction by a wonderful operation, provided that the habit of savoring meditation is possessed.

I would call meditation on the Lord’s passion “savoring” when a person, purified by true mortification, as soon as he has begun to turn over the Lord’s passion in thought, is dissolved into tears without violence, from love alone, and from the excessive desire of fervor is prepared as though for a certain transport of mind. Whoever has received this gift from the Lord will never be able to prepare himself better for celebrating than if, before the approach to the altar, he always passes over with tears at least one article of the Lord’s passion by meditating on it. Indeed, since the celebration of masses was instituted by our Redeemer himself in memory of the Lord’s passion, a person never prepares himself for it better and more fruitfully than if he is more fervently set aflame through meditation on that most bitter passion itself.

The Elevation of the Priest’s Mind to God during Celebration.

With how great reverence, devotion, and purity of mind we ought to stand before almighty God at the altar, what speech could express, or what understanding could penetrate by comprehension? For there the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are consecrated in an ineffable manner; there the Lord of majesty, truly present, is adored; there the army of angels, standing by its invisible king, rejoices together; there the whole heavenly court adores Jesus, God and man. Therefore the greatest purity of mind, the greatest reverence and humility are needed when we must stand before so great a majesty, lest the Lord Jesus, who searches the reins and the heart, be able to find anything in us that offends him. Let all worldly anxieties depart far from here; let all thoughts withdraw. Let nothing be thought here except what pertains to the consummation of so great a mystery; let nothing turn in the mind except what is fitting in the presence of so great majesty and glory. For here what is enacted is not an office of human power, but a miracle of divine majesty: the Son of God is offered to the Father; the body of our Redeemer is truly received; the mystery of our reparation is celebrated. Therefore, standing at the altar, let the priest remember that he stands before an invisible majesty, and let him beware of thinking anything whatever from elsewhere.

After celebration. Let careful custody of the mind be maintained

After the celebration, or the communion of the Lord’s body and blood, let the devout cenobite render thanks to almighty God, and throughout the whole day, by spiritual exercise, preserve himself in the purity and devotion of mind already begun. Let him direct his affections toward God with fiery rays, and not grow lukewarm from his holy purpose. Before all else, let him strive to love nothing in this world, but, with his heart entirely stripped of all earthly affections, to raise it continually to the fire of divine love. Let him always consider how, from this time onward, he may establish his life as if anew in the holy fervor of his way of life, and humbly dispose himself for the more frequent repeated reception of so great a guest.

Finally, during the day, amid the labors enjoined upon him, let him more often, with some prayer, offer himself to God the Father in the virtue and union of that sacrament, so that through the exercises of holy communion and regular obedience he may be kindled more fully in divine love. And we attain this divine love especially through the virtue of this venerable sacrament, if, in memory of the Lord’s Passion, by communicating in it more often, we are renewed through the grace of compunction. For indeed the devout human mind, through communion in this most sacred sacrament, is kindled by the effective operation of the fervor of divine love; and, wholly denied to itself, united by grace into Christ, it is transformed. Therefore, the more each person, denied to himself through true resignation, has offered himself to the Lord as a living victim in memory of the Lord’s Passion, the more disposed he will be to celebrate worthily.

After private masses. Returning to the cell.

When the celebration of masses has been completed, and the thanksgivings finished according to custom, let the monk return to his cell; and, after first saying the customary prayer, as above at Matins, let him recollect himself for a little while, and kindle himself further from his holy purpose of perseverance. Then, turned toward the Lord, let him say:

I beseech you, sweetest Lord Jesus, by the virtue of your most holy body and blood, which I have received, though unworthy: grant me the sweetness of your love, sincerity of brotherly affection, strength in temptation, purity in heart, and discipline in conduct, so that, by your gift, I may satisfy my profession and continually advance in your most holy love.

Then, until the first signal for choir, let him read something good, meditate or pray, or certainly write; and let him fervently attend to the work enjoined upon him by obedience.

At the first signal for choir, before the high mass.

When the first signal has sounded for the hour that is customarily allowed before the high mass, let the cenobite at once put aside everything he has in his hands and read the preparatory prayers for choir, as they were set out above before Matins. Afterward let him go to choir with reverence and maturity, bowing and praying according to the rite set down above.

At the high mass.

Consideration 4.

At the ringing for the high mass, you may read the appointed hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward, as much as time permits, recall to memory something from the prologue set before the private masses. For the sum of our salvation is placed in the merit of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; nor is any good work of merit believed to belong to us unless it is offered in his virtue. The memory of this Passion is enacted in the celebration of masses, where the innocent Lamb, slain for us, is offered to God the Father in an ineffable mystery. Therefore from our only Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom we believe to have suffered for us, we truly hope for salvation. And therefore whatever the Church asks in the collects, she humbly prays that it be given her by God the Father through him. This regard for the merit of the Lord’s Passion our devout cenobite should have in his heart; upon it the whole office of the mass should revolve sweetly, as upon the lower millstone. For every mass, wherever it may be that is said in God’s holy Church, is at all times referred to the merit of the Lord’s Passion.

On the Introit of the Mass.

We do not intend, however, to explain the office of the mass point by point, since each of our men can find many explanations by others; but we wish to give an occasion for meditation to devout brothers, whom we know to be inflamed with inward desires. Therefore you can reduce the first part of the introit and the verse, in meditation, to the incarnation of the Lord, and refer the repetition with the Gloria to his nativity. Nevertheless, you must diligently examine what the introit contains according to its literal sense, so that you may be able to find a suitable spiritual understanding for yourself. For nothing is done in vain in the divine office, but all things are filled with mysteries and sacred actions.

On Kyrie eleison.

Kyrie eleison is Greek, and is composed of a noun and a verb; among the Greeks these are two words. The first is from kyrios, which means “lord”; kyrie is said in the vocative. The second is from eleeo, which means “I have mercy”; eleeson, “have mercy,” is uttered in the imperative. Hence comes Kyrie eleison, that is, “Lord, have mercy,” through elision for Kyrie eleison, since a vowel before a vowel may be elided for a better sound.

Therefore Kyrie eleison is said three times to the Father, so that he who, from exceeding charity, willed his Son to be incarnate of the Virgin and to die for us may deign by his mercy to assist us in our necessities. To the Son also we say Christe eleison three times, in which we pray him to assist us. We also utter Kyrie eleison three times to the Holy Spirit, in which we humbly invoke him, through his ineffable goodness, to come to our aid.

On the Gloria in excelsis Then the Gloria in excelsis Deo is said in the singular number; in it we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one sole true God in Trinity of persons and unity of substance. Accordingly, during this angelic hymn the monk ought to be very devout, and, so to speak, attentive to each single word; in it the gift of peace is promised to people of good will, and God is humbly adored by us in various phrases.

¶ At the Collects.

When the collects or prayers are offered to God by the priest, the monk standing in choir should think of nothing else, but, listening to the words of the priest, should present his own desire to God in harmony with them.

¶ At the Epistle.

When the Epistle is read, you ought diligently to attend to everything, and with the greatest fervor of spirit give thanks to God, because, leaving behind the Jewish people, he so mercifully chose to call you and your ancestors from Gentile error to his faith.

¶ At the Gradual.

During the gradual, alleluia, sequence, or tract, consider how long a desire the holy fathers had, who before Christ’s incarnation longed for his coming. Then consider again with how many labors and injuries your Savior was wearied for you through thirty-three years in this world, he who willingly gave himself over to death for your salvation. Then call to mind the long and perilous exile of your soul in the flesh, so that still more, through this meditation on present misery, you may inflame your affection toward divine love.

At the Gospel.

During the holy Gospel, with your mind raised up in the Lord, give thanks exultantly, because the merciful Father willed that you be born of Christian parents, and because he made you a participant in his holy and most sweet doctrine.

At the Creed.

When the symbol of the catholic faith is sung, consider all the words and mysteries with humble fervor of spirit, and hasten at once to gather your whole self within yourself,

L ij so that you may be able to give thanks, without any merit of your own, to him who called you to the faith, and to lift yourself up into him through the love of the Spirit. Think, if you can, indeed as much as you can, how great, lofty, and immeasurable is the Son of God who willed to be incarnate for you, and how hard and bitter were the things he endured for you.

At the Offertory.

During the offertory, apply your mind, together with the host that is to be consecrated, to the oblation; weigh carefully what is being done there mystically.

For the host is round and white. In its whiteness, purity, innocence, and the suffering humanity of our Savior are set forth as to be offered to God the Father on our behalf against all our impurities; in its roundness, his immeasurable divinity, set before us as a reward, is offered. Therefore say to the Lord:

¶ Prayer.

I have no fitting gift to offer you, almighty God; I hand over myself to you as a sacrifice. Receive me, therefore, holy Father, in union with the most holy oblation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, as an eternal gift to you and as a perpetual servant; and give me the continual burning of your holy love, so that I may be able always to render you service pleasing to you. Through the same Christ.

¶ Prayer.

I offer to you, almighty God, the life, passion, and death of the same our Lord Jesus Christ: for my sins; for the holy Roman and universal Church; for the supreme pontiff; for our bishop; for our abbot; for all my confreres; for the unity of our observance; for our whole order also; for the salvation of all the faithful; for the conversion of unbelievers; and for the redemption of the souls of the faithful who are in the pains of purgatory. I beseech you, holy Father, receive this oblation of mine in union with that charity by which you received the same our Lord Jesus Christ as he died for us on the cross; and may it be pleasing to you.

At the Preface.

During the preface, take care to raise your mind from all earthly things to heavenly ones, and to prepare yourself to praise the Lord with the holy angels. Remember that through the merit of the Lord’s of the Passion you have been called to the fellowship of the angels; and take care that you come to it through observance of the commandments.

At the Sanctus.

With your mind raised upward when the Sanctus is sung, glorify the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God and Lord; humbly adore his majesty with the holy angels at all times.

Under the Canon.

After the Sanctus, under the Canon, you may take up meditation on the Lord's Passion, and offer it to God the Father, through its several greater and principal articles, for yourself, or for others, or for any necessity. Say, therefore, in this or a similar way:

Holy Father, I offer you the bloody sweat and tears of our Lord Jesus Christ, your most beloved Son, in that charity and union by which he voluntarily offered himself to you in death for us: for my sins, or for that brother, or for this or that necessity. And I ask you, through the pain of the wounds of your same most sweet Son, and through the shedding of his most holy blood and the power of his most innocent death: have mercy on me, or on him, or grant us this or that, etc. Through the same our Lord.

You may act similarly concerning the other articles also of the Lord's Passion, and enlarge upon them according to the intention of your affection in offering them.

At the Elevation.

If, at the elevation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your mind has not been occupied with higher things, you may pray to the Lord who is truly present in this way:

O Christ, king of glory, you are the everlasting Son of the Father. You, to deliver us, etc., to the end.

For this part of the hymn Thomas Aquinas is read to have prayed to the Lord under the elevation.

At the Agnus Dei.

When the Agnus Dei is sung, lift up your mind to the Lord Jesus with singular confidence, and humbly pray that he may receive you into perpetual peace. Direct your affection to him for whose love you have abandoned all things; seek from him, through reception of sacred communion, stable progress in your holy purpose.

At Ite, missa est

When at the end Ite, missa est is sung, see that your mind is lifted up with the holy angels returning into heaven, so that through desire you may deserve to behold the Lord Jesus presiding in majesty, whom, sent to the Father in the sacrament, you can no longer see on earth. Therefore kindle your desire through an image of desolation, in the manner of those who are unwillingly separated from their friends.

Say, therefore, in your heart:

Meditation.

Behold, my Lord has returned to the heavens; he has left me desolate on earth. What am I doing here with mortals, when I have an immortal Lord? Why do I not follow him? Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of darkness; my soul has long been a sojourner. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but who will deliver me, unhappy man, from the body of this death? O most beloved Lord Jesus, O my hope, O God and savior of my soul, draw me after you; I shall run in the fragrance of your ointments. O my sweet love, do not forget me to the end, but deign frequently to lift up my mind to you, so that, since I cannot see you bodily while placed in this mortality, at least lifted up in affection and desire in your most holy love, I may deserve often to behold you in spirit in glory. O my salvation, O heart of my heart, most beloved Jesus, do not abandon me or despise me. Be to me a gracious helper, and direct me always in your most holy will, so that I may truly be able to please you.

After the High Mass and the Following Hour.

After the end of the hour that immediately follows high mass, return to your cell with the customary reverence described above. Pour out prayers to the Lord through fervor of spirit, as we taught after matins. Spend whatever remains of the time Continue in meditations. Consider the foulness of sin: how it separates a person from God and condemns forever the one who is turned away and does not repent. Take care, therefore, to turn your will wholly to God with the firmest resolve, and, as far as you can, to avoid at all times the contagion of sin.

On the Regular Meal.

Consideration V

When the signal for the meal is rung, have heartfelt compassion for the sick, the needy, and the poor who suffer want; and when you can do nothing else for them, entreat the Lord on their behalf.

Consider that among Christians there are many far better than you whom harsh poverty oppresses in this life, to whom neither the food necessary for sustenance is offered nor even the thinnest clothing supplied for covering the body. But you, a monk, though you are a despiser of the world, are clothed in excellent garments and sit at table like a prince. Food is set before you to satiety by brothers better than you; all necessary things, even to the point of surfeit, are provided for you, an unworthy sinner, by the servants of God. Consider, therefore, what end this abundance of goods will have in a monk, since by entering religion you professed poverty, and now in religion you feast more splendidly than worldly rich men. Take care, then, not to be ungrateful for such great benefits of God. Live according to the rule which you have professed. Pray for those who contribute temporal substance to your monastery, that almighty God may mercifully grant them eternal life.

On Reading at Table.

When seated at table, be composed while eating. Do not look this way and that, but take care to eat the food set before you only for the necessity of nature, with humility and thanksgiving. Consider diligently what is read at table, so that, just as the body is refreshed by its food, so the soul may not be deprived of its own refreshment. Learn, while eating, frequently to raise your mind to heavenly things, and by the word of sacred reading, which is never lacking while we eat, sweetly to inflame it with divine compunction.

For the true and inward worshiper of God, whenever he hears anything read, even at meals, about the bitterness of the Lord’s passion, the fervor of divine love, or the kingdom of the heavenly homeland, immediately groans from excessive desire; his affection is kindled in the fire of love; compelled by exceeding sweetness, he weeps. Indeed, the mind that truly loves the Lord Jesus, as soon as it hears his name or looks upon the image of the crucified one, is dissolved in compunction and by affection is raised to his feet or to his embrace.

At Thanksgiving.

When the meal has been completed, give thanks to the Lord; and while you go to the church under the psalm, direct your mind upward. Intercede for benefactors, living and dead. If after the thanksgiving you add some particular prayer for the dead, you do well.

On Regular Reading.

On leaving the refectory for your cell, if it is not a fast day, complete the customary manner of praying; then read something good for edification, meditate, do whatever work has been assigned to you, or write. But if it is a fast day, take up the volume for your study and enter the place of regular reading. Sitting with the others, read in silence whatever you wish. But if you are asked by the presiding officer to say something good, answer humbly, briefly, and usefully, without curious citations. Use plain speech, and do not bring forward the vain curiosities of secular people. Do not entangle the brothers sitting around you, or your superiors, in your words, but express the thought of your mind simply in a few words, unless perhaps the presiding officer, for some definite reason, orders you to make a longer address.

The Monk’s Exercise after Dinner until Vespers.

Consideration VI

After the reading, when you have returned to your cell, you should always put some prayer before your works, and in everything you do ask for God’s help. While you are in your cell, do not be idle, but always do something good, especially what the obedience of the abbot has enjoined. Now write; read something good, or meditate, because the cell makes an idle monk either a beast or a demon. But we shall speak more fully of these things in their proper place below. Take care to spend your time usefully, because before long you will have to render an account to God for everything.

On Dwelling in the Cell and the Works to Be Done in It.

There are three places in which a devout monk and lover of God ought often to be found: namely, in church, in his cell, and, at the proper time, in the refectory. But he does not permit wandering about the monastery, because it is written of the wicked, the reprobate, and the gyrovagues: “The wicked walk about in a circuit.” But of the just man Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth; he will sit solitary and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself.”

There are five chief works of the cell. The first is to attend to commands; the second is to read usefully; the third is to apply oneself at suitable times to meditation; the fourth is to pray frequently; the fifth is to rest fittingly. We shall speak briefly of these in order.

In the cell, first, you should attend to commands.

First, then, while you are in the dwelling of the cell, learn to attend to commands and not to prefer your empty devotions to obedience. For Scripture says: “Obedience is better than the sacrifices of fools, and to hearken is better than to offer fat.” Therefore, if something has been enjoined on you to do in the cell, do not transgress the paths of obedience on any occasion, but strive diligently to perform the work imposed on you for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and the merit of holy obedience. Hence Hugh, a lover of quiet, says: “Be gladly in your cell, and always do something in it that may build you up, and that has been enjoined by your superior. Consider that it is not within your right to go out of it without permission, except for the necessity of nature.” You also have, concerning this, the prohibition of our most holy father Benedict in the Rule, which forbids you exit and running about without permission.

Second, in the cell one ought to read usefully.

It is especially fitting for a monk who is in his cell always to read something good, and to occupy himself usefully in all things. For sacred reading overcomes the temptations of the devil, calms the fires of the flesh, makes one despise the world, and raises the mind to heavenly things. For Jerome, lover of divine Scripture, truly said: “Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” Not all things are to be read by all monks, since one who is still weak in spirit must be instructed only in simple teachings. And Hugh says to the monk who loves simplicity: “Do not read in order to be considered more learned, nor read curiosities that do not build up, because vain reading begets vain thoughts and extinguishes the devotion of the mind.” Therefore simpler monks should read simple things, not lofty ones; devout things, not curious ones, so that those who, because of slowness of understanding, are not learned in higher matters may not become dissolved in vain things. But we do not forbid suitable studies to those who are stronger in spirit, because all things are clean to the clean, and nothing that is read harms those who are truly devout. Nevertheless, let no one claim for himself a strength of mind that he does not have, but let it be placed in the abbot’s discretion, so that he may see who is fit for freedom in reading.

Third, in the cell you should apply yourself at suitable times to meditations.

Just as a flower springs from a root, so meditation is generated from reading. If the reading has been vain, the meditation too will be fruitless and useless. For the fruit of reading is meditation, and the offspring of meditation is prayer. Therefore take care to apply yourself at suitable times to holy meditations, so that you may be able also sometimes to raise your mind, through the fervor of divine love, into contemplation. Finally, meditation itself raises the mind and commends the study of reading to the memory.

Fourth, in the cell you should pray frequently.

The holy apostle admonishes us to devote ourselves to prayer without interruption, because just as breath is always necessary for us for the life of the flesh, so continual prayer is altogether necessary for the health of the mind. For as we are instructed toward good by readings, so by prayers we are delivered from evil. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “Pray, that you may not enter into temptation.” Prayer feeds the hungry mind, extinguishes the fire of carnal desire, instructs morals, and drives away demons. If you wish always to be with God, always pray. Let your prayer be pure, simple, and clean; let it be poured out to God through the fervor of love, and it will not be able to be fruitless.

Fifth, in the cell you should rest fittingly.

He rests best who commits no evil. He rests well who despises all the occupations of the world. Be quiet in your cell, so that you do not wander here and there in any thought. Be pure and tranquil in mind, so that you may deserve to obtain tasteful wisdom. For holy Prosper says in verse: “Wisdom imbues a tranquil mind, free from cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful breast.” And again he says: “Those who are quiet can search the law in whatever way they can, if hearts free from the clamor of the world are empty. Therefore, that the mind intent on pious studies may be helped, let divine love conquer fleshly quarrels.” Remain, then, quiet in your cell, and by loving the truth you will be able to know it. For a tranquil mind cannot be receptive of divine wisdom when the body is restless. Hence Hugh says: “Be quiet in the dormitory, so that another may not be disturbed by you. Whether you are waking or wishing to sleep, let the memory of God’s goodness always come to you with thanksgiving, because he himself always watches over us, so that he may guard us from every evil as we humbly serve him.” When you go to your bed, first [unclear] of God, by thinking about him or meditating on him, so that you may be able to fall asleep sweetly amid holy thoughts. For as the occupations of a waking person have been, so will be the rest of the one who sleeps, and so too will his dreams be. For a mind fervent with divine love, whether sleeping or waking, will not be able to forget the one it loves, just as the bride says in the Song of Songs: I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.

At Vespers. Consideration VII.

When the first signal for Vespers has been heard, and after saying in the customary way, Blessed be the name of the Lord, along with the other things usually said beforehand, have compassion on those occupied in worldly business, and give thanks that almighty God has willed you to be free from those things in order to serve him. Then recollect yourself inwardly; or you may meditate somewhat on the Lord’s Passion, until, when the second signal sounds, you go to choir. For in my judgment there is no meditation better for beginners and those advancing toward compunction and devotion of mind than that which takes its beginning, through burning affections, from the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

At the Vigils of the Dead.

When, at the summons for the vigils after Vespers, you may recite the hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward think somewhat about the immeasurable charity of God by which he loves faithful souls. Then, as much as you can, consider how great is the desolation of those holy souls placed in purgatory; how great is the pain for a spirit separated from the body and longing to return to the center of its first principle, not to be able to behold the face of its Creator in friendly enjoyment, but to be compelled to wait in punishments and torments most grievous to it. For so great is the desolation, sadness, and grief of a separated soul placed in punishments and longing to come to God, that no kind of torment known to us in this world could be compared with its sorrow. Indeed, there is no comparison, in our manner of speaking, between bodily sadness and desolation and the state of a separated spirit, appointed to a delay in its return to its own principle.

Therefore, as much as you can, have compassion for the desolation of faithful souls groaning in the prison of purgatory, and pour out diligent prayers for them to the Lord. For even if the almighty and merciful Father, through his justice, delays them from the kingdom, nevertheless he loves them with inestimable charity. Therefore whatever good you now do for them by praying, you offer as a pleasing sacrifice to almighty God. And when you come there, you will receive multiplied whatever you have done here in charity for them. For Scripture says: It is a holy and wholesome thing to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins.

Passing Through the Cemetery or Cloister.

Pray for the dead.

When you pass through a cemetery, cloister, or some other place of burial for the dead, do not forget your brothers and all the dead; but, moved by charity, have compassion on them, and strive to assist them before the Lord in this or a similar manner.

Prayer

Hail, faithful souls; rest in holy peace. May he who redeemed you by his precious blood deign to free you from punishments and lead you to eternal joys, where you may rejoice and exult forever, blessed ones.

Another.

May God the Father, who created you, bless you. May Jesus Christ, who redeemed you by his most precious blood, bless you. May the Holy Spirit, who by his kindness and gift preserved you from eternal damnation, bless you. Amen.

Read the following prayer often.

I beseech you, sweetest Lord Jesus, Son of the living God, through the pain of your wounds, through the pouring out of your most holy blood, and through the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on the souls of all the faithful departed who are in the punishments of purgatory, and give them a dwelling in eternal light with all your saints.

After Vespers Until Compline. Consideration VIII

After Vespers, or the vigils of the dead, return to your cell with the customary prayers and bows; and there, on bended knees, give thanks to your most merciful preserver, because he has not only graciously rescued you from the vanities of the world, but has also guarded you in the order from many evils and dangers. Then reflect how many bodily and spiritual goods your loving Father has bestowed on you, though you have deserved nothing; and, what is greatest, how he has promised himself as a reward to you if you faithfully persevere in his love. Be grateful, and always keep watch in prayer, so that you may burn sweetly in the love of God.

But when the signal has been given for supper, prepare yourself humbly to go to it, and observe what we noted above concerning dinner. After supper you may return to your cell and devote yourself to prayer or meditation until the signal is rung for the collation.

At supper, when you hear the signal for the spiritual collation, strive to go to it at once with gravity, and to hear the last reading of the day with fervor of spirit. For the word of holy exhortation that has last been heard will cling more tenaciously to the mind throughout the whole night. But if it is a fast day, the collation has customarily been observed in the refectory while drinking. Therefore be attentive to sacred reading in every place, because when the word of holy exhortation is gladly received with attention, it cannot happen that the mind is not often lifted up.

At Compline.

When you come to Compline, beseech the Lord that he may make you always despise all worldly and carnal things, and grant you continually to remain in his most holy love, so that when the course of the present life is completed, you may deserve to enter the temple of God not made by hands, and rejoice forever in the Lord with all the saints. But at the end of Compline, when you hear the signal of the angelic salutation being rung, you shall humbly greet the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, that by her merits she may guard you through the night and continually intercede with her Son for your salvation.

After Compline.

As soon as Compline has begun, return at once to your cell; and, after the customary prayers have been said, take care to prepare yourself most diligently for the following recollection of mind.

On Recollection after Compline. Consideration IX.

Since we cannot remain wholly unmoved in one holy state of mind, it is necessary for us to renew our holy purpose frequently, so that as often as, during the day, by wandering along the byways of sins, we depart from the one beginning of our mind, the highest God, so often we may return to him through contrition and compunction, with amendment firmly resolved. Hence our holy fathers established for us that we should devote ourselves to recollection after Compline and examine ourselves concerning the negligences committed during the day, so that the purpose of holiness, which we know to be quite weak and infirm, we may renew to fervor of spirit through the continual exercise of recollection. Therefore our devout monk, wishing to recollect himself fruitfully and with useful continuance, ought chiefly to examine himself in order on five points.

The First Thing to Be Observed in Recollection.

The Rendering of Account.

The first thing to be observed is the rendering of account, by which the monk is commanded to bring back before the eyes of the mind, for correction, whatever he remembers that he has committed in the day by failing negligently, badly, or less well. And so, turned toward the Lord, he should lie before his bed with hands clasped, and say in this or a similar manner:

I give thanks to you, almighty and merciful God, for all your benefits, which you have deigned to bestow on me, an unworthy sinner with no merit at all, from my youth up to this hour.

For I, who have deserved no good, have received many and innumerable gifts of your goodness. Would that I could give worthy thanks to you, the highest and unchangeable good; would that I could praise you in your holy service with a pure heart and clean conscience. But, alas, with weakness, concupiscence, and evil habit prevailing, I, who ought to have clung to your most holy love with a pure heart and conscience, have offended you again and again by many negligences and faults; and as often as, according to the inward inspirations of your goodness, I have tried to rise to fervor of spirit, alas, so often I grieve that I have fallen again.

Behold, good Jesus, how many faults, how many negligences, how many offenses I have fallen into today alone; how many vain, how many useless, how many pernicious thoughts I have admitted in so few hours; how many useless and harmful words I have uttered; how many negligences and sins I have perpetrated in my actions this day.

Woe to me, wretched man, who could not spend even one very brief day in your most holy service without impurity of heart and negligence; I who have committed so many faults and various imperfections today. I confess to your goodness, O most gentle God, all my sins into which I have fallen from the beginning of my age. Before your feet, O sweetest Jesus, I place all the negligences that I have committed today. I ask for pardon, which I am not worthy to receive; I beg for grace, which I confess I have so often received in vain. O Jesus Christ, most loving mediator of God and men, do not cast away me, a wretched sinner, whom you willed to purchase with your own blood. I confess to you all the negligences into which I have in any way fallen today, and the faults that I have committed.

Here the monk, prostrate in mind before the Lord, should recall the more serious negligences to memory, and, humbly asking pardon, should lament his imperfection. Above all, let him consider whether he has offended anyone by word or deed; whether he has said anything against a brother; whether he has committed anything against charity and reverence; or whether he knowingly saddened someone wrongly. And in general, in whatever respect he has acted against God, against himself, against his prelate, against his neighbor, or the Rule, or the statutes of the fathers, he should take care to bring back for examination in this chapter whatever he knows he has offended in. And concerning secret matters, in tomorrow's confession; concerning public and regular transgressions, in the next chapter meeting, he should faithfully and from his heart resolve to clear himself by accusing himself. Let him grieve over what he has committed, make satisfaction for what he has repented of, and beware of what he may commit.

Next, let him consider the grave danger of offending God, whether the sin has been venial or mortal. For Jean Gerson, chancellor of Paris, says in the treatise On the Spiritual Life: "Even venial sin is so much against God that, according to his justice, he could damn a man eternally for it. But that he does not impute it to a man unto damnation proceeds not from justice but from his infinite goodness." And the holy bishop Anselm warns us that a man ought not knowingly to commit the smallest sin against God's will for the whole world. For the most blessed pontiff Augustine says: "No sin is so venial that it does not become mortal while it is pleasing." You may say: this statement cannot be true, because if a sin is venial, it can never become mortal; but if it becomes mortal, it was not venial. But listen and understand. I grant that venial sin, considered in itself, cannot become mortal. But one and the same sin, which can stand together with charity, becomes merely venial for one person by negligence and weakness alone; for another, however, through contempt and aversion from God in the same sin, it is without doubt imputed as mortal, because it is pleasing even insofar as it is sin and contrary to God. Blessed, therefore, is he who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. Whoever neglects the smallest sins when he can amend them gradually falls into greater ones.

Indeed, how much sin displeases almighty God is shown by the punishment that follows. For so often in the sacred books and in the deeds of times past we read of sinners against the Lord being gravely punished, that we rightly fear the pit of sin. How much even the very briefest thought of an averted spirit displeases him is declared to us by the fall of the first angel. For as soon as he showed himself disordered against the Lord by pride, he was cast into hell.

How contrary to the Lord idle and useless words are, the account in the Lives of the Holy Fathers about the infernal pigs appearing among those speaking useless things and gnashing their teeth warns us plainly enough.

How much evil and pernicious words offend almighty God was evident in the five-year-old boy who blasphemed; the devil snatched him alive from his father's lap and, as is believed, carried him off to hell.

How much deeds and negligence concerning one's office displease him is clear in the sons of Eli, who were negligent and less careful about the rite of sacrifice.

How much evil deeds offend God, since we can understand it from, as it were, countless histories, need not be proved by a few examples.

When, however, our monk in his devout recollections finds himself burdened by the aforesaid or by any other negligences or sins, however grave, let him assume such contrition for the past as is possible for him, a purpose of amendment by firmly avoiding them in the future, and penance for what he has committed. Therefore let him take up the counsel of the aforesaid chancellor, and, being compunct, say:

Lord my God, I confess to your most holy goodness that I have sinned in this way or that against your will. I grieve vehemently over it, and because I have offended you, who are wholly good, I humbly do penance.

¶ Truth 1: to the Lord.

Lord my God, you know all things. You know that, by your granting, I have a good purpose, and with your help I intend to amend myself according to my powers in the future.

¶ Truth 3.

Sin, however, is avoided by prayers, calling upon God for help; by punishments, inflicting penance on the body; and by flight, avoiding the occasion of sin. Therefore, for the third truth, let him say:

¶ Truth 3.

Lord my God, I have a good will to make confession of my sins, according to your command and holy mother...

of mother Church, according to place and time, and from the heart, wholly and without pretense.

Whoever has uttered these three truths to the Lord from sincerity of heart, without falsity in mouth or mind, however much he may previously have sinned, is now secure, if he should die in such a state even without confession, in the absence of a priest; yet in such a way that he must make satisfaction in purgatory for what he did not complete by doing penance. But he who, because of a will to sin in which he actually takes delight, or because of a wicked intention by which he refuses to avoid the occasions of sins, cannot truly say these same truths from a pure mind, is in a state of damnation, from which not even the pope can absolve him.

The Indication of Future Caution.

The second thing he prescribes for the monk to observe in his recollection is called the indication of future caution. Let him consider what have been for him the occasions of past transgression, and he will more easily guard himself from future danger. For the pit of sin is never better blocked up than if the occasion of sin is avoided. And Saint Bernard says: “For the coming night, indeed, an indication must be made, distributing one’s exercises according to the rule of the common institution.” In these things he duly pays every debt, if the spirit is subjected to God and the flesh to the spirit, and if anything has been omitted, neglected, or imperfect, it does not remain unrecompensed in manner, time, and place.

The Request for Suffrages.

The third thing in the recollection of a good monk is the devout request for suffrages; for he, understanding his own weakness very well, seeks help from those stronger than himself. Therefore, as soon as he has completed his recollection, he turns to the holy and undivided Trinity to ask for mercy; then he invokes the most blessed Mother of God; afterward he implores the prayers and assistance of all the saints. And here he remembers not only himself, but pours out prayers for the whole order and the Church.

The Blessing for Going to Rest.

The fourth thing in the recollection is the monk’s blessing for going to rest, by which he fortifies himself with prayers and commits himself to divine goodness to be guarded through the night. Therefore, at the sound of the signal for sleeping, or at the appointed time, going to the place of rest, let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross, and say with devotion:

The Blessing for Rest.

May the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the integrity of blessed Mary ever virgin, the sign of the holy cross, the power of the Lord’s passion, and the blessing, protection, and merit of all the saints, angels, and elect of God, stand between me and all my enemies, visible and invisible, here and forever. Amen.

Prayer

I commend myself this night and at all times into your wounds, most loving Lord Jesus, and I beg you, by the merit of your most holy passion: have mercy on me and guard me from all snares and illusions of the enemy, so that with a pure mind and a clean body I may be able to rise at the appointed hours and praise you with fervor of spirit.

Discretion for Obtaining Rest.

The fifth and last thing to be commemorated in recollection is discretion for obtaining rest: so that, just as the monk must never wholly omit this evening recollection, so also he should not wish, too indiscreetly, to prolong it to the destruction of his head. Therefore, when all things have been completed with discretion, let him raise the desire of his fervor toward God with tears, if he can, but let him not confound his mind. As he goes up to his bed, let him carry with him into memory something about the Lord’s passion, or about the love of Jesus, or certainly about the glory of the heavenly kingdom, in which, while sleeping, he may rest sweetly. For Bernard says: “When you are about to go to sleep, carry something with you in memory or thought, in which you may fall asleep peacefully; something that may also sometimes help you to dream, and that may receive you when you wake, and restore you to the state of yesterday’s intention. Thus the night will be illuminated for you like the day, and your night will be your illumination in its delights, so that you may fall asleep peacefully, rest in peace, and wake easily; and rising, you will be ready for redemption, while you return to that from which you had not wholly departed.”

Nevertheless, discretion must always be applied in all these things, lest either excessive meditation, hindering sleep, destroy the brain, or sleep taken immoderately interrupt meditation altogether. For at this hour the monk ought rather to sleep than to meditate, so that in due time so that, at the appointed time, he may be ready to rise and well disposed in cheerfulness of soul for the divine office. For an affection too greatly inflamed by meditation destroys the brain and the senses, and takes sleep from the eyes of the weak. Therefore meditation in bed should be brief, where the head does not have great strength either by grace or by nature.

On Manual Labor. Tenth Consideration.

Since our most holy father Benedict, in the Rule, commends as true monks those who live by the labor of their hands, and declares them blessed, it seemed fitting to us, after the end of the day, to say something about this most holy exercise. Indeed, we read that this work is commended in many ways by the holy fathers, and we know that in it they profited before God and human beings in no small measure. For the holy apostle says: “He who does not work, let him not eat.” What Augustine, that teacher among the most learned teachers, thought about this manual exercise he shows most clearly in the book On the Work of Monks. We also read that those ancient and most holy fathers dwelling in solitude labored not lukewarmly at the work of their hands, so that they might not incur the danger of idleness, and, living from their own labors, after the example of the most blessed teacher of the nations, burden no one. Would that we too, brothers, might deign to take up this holy exercise of laboring with the same intention and goodwill as they, so that after the end of our labor we may deserve to rest with them without end in the heavenly homeland.

There Are Four Things for a Monk to Observe in Labor.

When called to labor, a monk should strive to show himself such in all things that he does not lose the merit of bodily labor through dissolution of mind. For we see many among monks going out to labor in the wrong way, whom we see seeking nothing other than the comforts of the flesh. Some of these take up useless and less necessary labors so that, in the time of the regular fast, they may have an occasion for eating.

For they labor so that they may eat; whether it benefits or harms the monastery, they do not care. Others have been accustomed to arrange various labors so that, under this pretext, they may be able to run about here and there without the bridle of discipline. Others procure labors useless to the community so that they may freely indulge in vain talk and frivolities. Others love external labors so that, as if by a suitable opportunity and without suspicion, they may be able to see and speak with people whom I will not call seculars, known and friendly to them according to the flesh and not according to God. Others, because of instability of mind, unable to rest in the monastery, always seem to pant after labors. The intention of all those laboring in this way is not sincere, and therefore they do not attain the excellent reward of labor.

But you, brother, when you are called to labor, take care to submit your intention to the regular institution, so that you love nothing other than the honor of God, the merit of obedience, and the usefulness of the monastery, and intend nothing except the profit of the soul. While you are at labor, do not imprudently extinguish the fervor of the spirit; do not omit the exercise of spiritual conduct, but take care diligently to observe everywhere the four things that follow: in outward conduct be faithful, serviceable, and kindly; inwardly, humble and devout; in speech, sparing and edifying; in manners, composed and mature. If you keep these four things in labor, you will always return to your cell better.

Outwardly the Monk Should Be Faithful, Kindly, and Serviceable.

The first thing to be diligently observed by the cenobite in labor is that, in working, he always show himself faithful to his monastery; that he anticipate the brothers out of charity in serving and ministering, or also in carrying heavier things; and that in all words and deeds he show himself kindly and tractable. Saint Bernard, the lover of God, says: A serious and prudent soul prepares itself for every labor, yet is not dissolved in it, but through it is more intent and strives more; for it always has before its eyes not so much what it is doing as what, by doing it, it is striving for. The more truly it strives, the more fervently and faithfully also it works with its hands, subjecting to itself the service of its whole body, in in which the will makes practice, and practice supplies strength for the exercise. The devout and faithful cenobite who truly loves God does not spare himself in labor, but is accustomed to apply himself to the manual tasks imposed on him with such fervor, cheerfulness, and fidelity, as if by his labor alone he had to gather together and feed all who are established in the monastery. For the most prudent soul knows that it is devoting itself wholly to God, whatever bodily necessity for his servants it happens to labor for. For just as spiritual things cannot long endure in religion without the cooperation of temporal things, so I do not hesitate to call one who ministers bodily necessities to those serving God, for God's sake, a servant of God. Therefore whatever a good cenobite can acquire for the monastery by his labors with right intention, let him know that he is offering all that to the Lord. Nevertheless, the monk must always understand that he is to labor in such a way that he in no way omits monastic prayers, masses, and the other services of holy mother Church.

Manual work, however, undertaken out of curiosity and self-complacency is judged before the inward judge to be deprived of the merit of obedience; and work presumed as idle and without the superior's permission is held liable to account. But the good cenobite, who desires to please God alone, should say to himself that saying of Bernard in every stealthy intrusion of an idle word, deed, or thought: If you were about to die now, would you do in this way what you are now doing, thinking, or saying? But if, were you now about to die, you would not do what you are doing in the way you are doing it, you are most foolish, since, destined to die shortly, you so boldly send the works of death on ahead to death for yourself. But if, since it is necessary, you desire to die well, do at no time what you would not do if death were already present. For whatever you do now, whether good or bad, you will find after death.

Let the monk be inwardly humble and devout.

Second, in the time of labor the monk must be inwardly devout and humble, since if he abandons the progress of inward fervor, what he acquires outwardly through labor is of no help.

Therefore, so that the soul may truly profit while laboring, let him bring back to constant memory the degrees of good will written in the first section. Let him arrange meditations on the Lord's passion with fervor of devotion, in which he may conform his labors, as far as possible, to Christ's labor. Let him always be humble in heart by self-denial. Let him be devout in affection through the fervor of holy compunction, so that the labor of his hands may outwardly advance the usefulness and advantage of the community, while his mind does not withdraw from the inward sweetness of divine love. If labor wearies the working cenobite, if heat burns him, if untimely thirst oppresses him, let him call to mind what the Lord of labor endured for us, and he will bear everything lightly. And so let him say this prayer to the Lord.

Prayer of one laboring.

Most sweet and most lovable Lord Jesus, king of heaven and earth, who for my redemption were born of the most pure Virgin Mary, and for thirty-three years lived among human beings as God and man; who had great labors in walking, teaching, and preaching; and who willingly and patiently endured thirst, hunger, heat, and cold, for all of which I give thanks to you: receive, I beseech you, these very small labors of mine, however useless, which in humility of your most holy testament I offer to you in memory and honor of all your labor and of your most holy passion. And may they be pleasing to you in that union by which your most holy labors were pleasing to God the Father. Amen.

During the time of labor let our cenobite turn over in mind the chief articles of the Lord's passion: first, as though commemorating them before Christ in his passion; then, giving thanks at his knees; third, asking for mercy in himself according to the likeness of them.

Let him also recall to memory the ways of life of any holy fathers, or the passions of the martyrs, and let him consider what reward and glory they now receive in the fatherland for their labors.

Let the monk be sparing and edifying in speech.

The third thing to be observed especially by the monk in labor The third thing to be observed by the monk for progress in labor is that he speak little, and what is edifying. For Scripture says: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking.” And let no monk speak without permission, if he truly desires to be good. But when permission to speak has been given, let him speak only a few useful things, knowing that idle and scurrilous words are condemned everywhere by the rule. Let him establish for himself, everywhere and at all times, such a manner of speaking, with circumspection, that by speaking he offends no one. Let him prefer to listen rather than desire to speak; and let him not say everything that comes into his mind, if he fears the reproach of fools. For thus Hugh says to the monk: “Do not pour out everything you know, like a vessel without a lid, which as soon as it is tilted pours out whatever it contains, and lies open to every dust and impurity.”

Take diligent care that you do not seem to seek your own glory in any way, directly or indirectly; nor reveal to anyone, from a desire for boasting or otherwise imprudently, anything praiseworthy that lies hidden in you. If you are silent about yourself and conceal yourself, you will be more pleasing; if you disclose and commend yourself, you will become contemptible before all and will be mocked. Beware of idle words, because when we do not notice such things for long, we gradually slip into harmful ones; from them arise disturbances, dissipations, or grave corrosions of spiritual progress. Be such in your inner conversation that, through love of spiritual meditation, silence may please you more at every time than talkativeness.

Let the cenobite be composed and mature in conduct.

Fourth, the monk, both in labor and outside it, and everywhere, is bound to compose his conduct and to show himself mature before men in all things, both in deeds and in words. Let him be clean and humble in heart; let him be kind and useful in speech; let him be modest and grave in his gait; let him be mature and exemplary in his whole way of life. The whole person is easily brought into conformity with the norm of discipline, if the effort to make progress is held firmly in the soul at all times. For truly, when a monk desires daily to advance toward better things, he avoids every dissolution and disorderly way of life. For a firm effort to make progress has this as its own property: that it makes the mind of the one striving very circumspect in all things. But one who does not have a firm effort to make progress toward the better cannot truly be called composed, although he may seem mature to men. For feigned maturity quickly dissolves into open dissolution of mind where the root of discipline does not have the fear of God. Therefore, so that our cenobite may always be able to be composed both inwardly and outwardly, let him strive to be truly rooted in the fear of the Lord. For one who fears God neglects nothing. And the love of God is not idle.

What the monk’s conduct ought to be toward other people. Consideration XI.

Since, then, we have begun to speak about the maturity and composure that a monk must preserve before men, it seems useful to us now to say briefly how he ought to show himself to individual persons. For he is instructed to show himself in one way to his prelate, and is commanded to show himself in another way to his brothers and to secular persons. To his ruler, in the place of Christ, he ought to show reverence; to his brother, charity; to those who injure him, meekness; to secular persons, modest piety. Therefore let the monk render to each what is his own, and he will truly be composed before God and men. What he owes to God, and what to himself, has been sufficiently said above; now let us pursue what has been proposed to us.

Let his conduct be reverential toward the prelate in the place of Christ.

First, the monk’s conduct ought to be reverential toward the prelate, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me.” For the monk who withholds due obedience and reverence from his abbot does injury to almighty God. For as our most holy father says in the Rule, the abbot is shown to hold the place of Christ in the monastery. Therefore whoever Therefore whoever despises the vicar of some king has without doubt despised the king himself. But tell me, good brother: why do you withhold due reverence from your prelate, whom you hear is Christ’s vicar? Perhaps you think him evil and wholly unworthy of such an office, and for that reason you think it is permissible for you to despise him. Not so, brother, not so. Rather, consider whose place it is in which Christ’s vicar presides, and know that you honor the sender, not the one sent. If you wish to be Christ’s disciple, always consider why you have come, and you will never deny reverence even to an unworthy prelate. For why have you come? Surely so that, according to the Gospel and the Rule, you may deny yourself for God’s sake; so that under another’s command you may serve Christ as a soldier; so that with patience you may await the eternal reward for these things. Therefore do not, brother, do not lose the crown of eternal blessedness prepared for you in heaven because of one man’s displeasing conduct, a crown you ought not exchange for the whole world.

Remember that you have nothing except from God, to whom you owe wholly what you are and what you know, so that you may fulfill his will and live according to his ordinance. But since you cannot understand God’s will by your own consideration, you must humbly obey your rector as his vicar, to whom you have subjected yourself; nor must you examine either his life or his command, since it is not permitted you to judge your shepherd. Indeed, in your profession you swore that you ought not carry out your own will, but that you wished to obey the abbot in all things according to the Rule. Therefore the abbot is lord of your will, not by his own assumption, but by the ordinance of God, whose vicar he also is. But handling another’s property against the owner’s will is theft, and you know that thieves will have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

Thus the monk who has been professed according to the Rule to God and to his abbot no longer thereafter has lordship over his own will. If afterward he usurps that will for himself, he commits theft and sacrilege. Nor will permission obtained save the presumptuous man, if it has been obtained by threats and insults. Your abbot, O brother, is God’s vicar; to him you must render the obedience promised, not as to a human being but as to God, and show humble reverence in God’s place. For whatever is given by subjects to the ruler is without doubt referred to God, whose vicar he is. Therefore, since you have subjected yourself to your prelate for God alone and for no other cause, strive at all times to present yourself toward him in such a way that he may freely be able to command you to do or leave undone whatever seems expedient to him, and that he may have no fear at all of any insolence or disturbances of your spirit. For if your abbot is compelled to fear you, his monk, the order of justice is violated; and where a disciple strives to be above the master, he sins against the Gospel.

Take care, therefore, lest you withhold reverence and honor from prelates; take care lest by saddening them you offend the Lord. Rather, see to it that, whatever sort of men they may be, you meet them reverently and obey their commands in all things according to the Gospel and the Rule. Believe me, brother, because the fault committed by a subject against a prelate will be punished most severely, either in the present life or in the life to come. For it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones.” Whatever your prelate commands you, you must receive with such trust that you believe God has inspired it in him.

Let the monk’s conduct toward his brothers be charitable.

Second, the conduct of a monk toward his brothers is commanded to have charity, through which alone peace and concord are maintained in the monastery. Let our faithful cenobite always think, and turn over in his heart, the common joy of souls in eternal blessedness; and let him continually direct the eye of the mind toward the equal condition of souls, so that his thought may not withdraw from love of their future fellowship. If a brother has offended you in any way by word or deed, if he has been troublesome or opposed to you in some matter, do not weigh the disorderly movement of sensuality from this; do not consider his present weakness, but lift the eyes of your mind to the nobility of his soul, and consider what kind of fellowship in eternal blessedness he is to have with you. To this end you ought often to recall to memory the chapter of the Rule on the good zeal of monks, so that you may more easily rouse yourself.

you may be able to rouse yourself. Above all, take care not to admit displeasure against your brother, because he who is frequently angry with his neighbor plainly proves that he does not love God. For whoever loves God with his whole heart does not admit displeasure against his faithful brother. The monk, indeed, ought to be established in such elevation of mind that, whatever a brother may have committed against him, by weighing the nature of that brother’s soul he cannot be moved.

Let the monk’s conduct toward those who injure him be gentle.

Third, the monk’s conduct toward those who injure him ought to be gentle, because only then is it well done, if regard is always had for the common future happiness and companionship. To attain this gentleness of soul, let our cenobite learn often to recall to mind the conduct of the holy fathers, and faithfully consider with how much joy they received injuries. Let him strive above all, as far as possible, to imitate our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who not only endured the injuries and insults of the wicked with a most gentle heart, but also prayed to the Father for his persecutors, that they might not perish. Imitating this example of the Savior, the holy fathers were accustomed, for the love of God, to receive injuries patiently and gently, and, what is more, to love those who injured them. To this end let the cenobite recall to mind the degrees of gentleness, which are briefly contained and included in these verses:

Adapt. Strengthen. Being gentle, bear contrary things. Preserve. Restrain. Rest wholly within yourself. Correct prudently. Be merciful. Give wisely. Pray by setting yourself there, by desiring martyrdom.

For if humility has possessed the mind of the cenobite, it makes him love injuries. The degrees of humility, however, are contained in these words:

The twelve degrees of humility.

The first of the degrees of the righteous fears the Almighty. The second puts reins on the enticements of the flesh. The third reverently subjects himself to the abbot.

The fourth, with insults despised, patiently obeys. The fifth reveals the secrets of his heart to the abbot. The sixth judges himself vile and unworthy. The seventh believes himself to be inferior to all. The eighth does nothing that the rule of the cell does not allow. The ninth does not speak until another asks him. The tenth banishes laughter and condemns guffawing. The eleventh speaks few words of reason. The twelfth always looks at the ground with head bowed.

On the same, otherwise.

Look upon God, and do not do your own will; let another govern you. Bear hard things; hide nothing in your heart, but also seek the lowest things. Be a cleansing refuse; do not wander alone; stop your tongue. Let laughter be sparing, speech weighty, gestures humble.

Note: Peripsema ought to be read and written, not peripsima, as the unlearned read in the Epistle to the Romans; and it is said to mean the filings and purging of all things.

Let the monk’s conduct toward secular people be modest.

Fourth, the monk’s conduct toward secular people ought to be modest, so that neither his familiarity with them is excessive nor his withdrawal indiscreet. Hence Hugh says: With respect to people, as far as lies in you, avoid everything that can be a bad example to them, just as it befits a faithful servant of God to advance the honor of his Lord in all things, and to guard against dishonoring him. And do not be familiar with any woman, even a holy one. For if they are discreet, you will please them more by this; but if they are importunate, they are all the more to be avoided. Do not be suspicious. Be attentive to the weak, humble in acts of service; be very truthful in words. Let your words be as an oath, and you will edify others. Love poverty. Be chaste in all things, and everywhere fearful of God.

But in founding all virtues and good morals, set before yourself that most brilliant and most perfect example of all brightness, of the life and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent from heaven for this, that he might lead us on the way of virtues and teach us by his own example, just like himself. Therefore, the more a monk has taken care to conform himself to him by imitation on the way of virtues, the more like and nearer to him he will doubtless be in the glory of eternal happiness. Whatever you do, always look to him, and see how he conducted himself in all things according to the Gospel and your estimation. For since he is best, he conducted himself best in all things. Say, then, to yourself: If my Lord Jesus were present, what do you think he would do in this matter, or what would he now say? Surely he would both act and speak in the best way; and I ought to imitate him in all things according to my strength.

General conclusion of all spiritual exercises.

Consideration XII

Wishing at last to put an end to this work, we say that the completion of all spiritual exercises consists in two things. First, in the knowledge and feeling of one’s own imperfection, so that the monk may always be conscious of his weakness and remain rooted in humility. Second, in the desire and effort to come to a higher conduct, so that he may always desire to advance in spirit toward better things and not withdraw at all from this effort. Toward this effort of advancing, every cenobite ought to extend his mind at every moment; if he ever sets it aside, he incurs transgression of his vow and very grave danger to his soul. But let the monk take care that consideration of his own weakness does not cast down the effort to advance; let him take care that the effort itself does not despise the consideration of imperfection. Rather, let these two so cling mutually to each other that they never withdraw from one another. But if excessive consideration of one’s own imperfection has tempted the mind toward despair of God’s mercy, let him recall to memory what the holy abbot Bernard said: Let us breathe again, brothers, because although we are nothing in our own hearts, perhaps something in us may lie hidden in the heart of God. These two considerations, of our weakness and of divine estimation, stir up great devotion in us. Thus the Psalmist said: I am poor and sorrowful. Behold the first. Your salvation, O God, has received me. Behold the second.

Finally, it is necessary for one who wishes to occupy himself profitably in these spiritual exercises to have a joyful and free heart, alien to every anxiety and to the cares of the world. For the Holy Spirit is a spirit of freedom and joy: he loves a free heart, joyful in God, and, so to speak, applauds one like himself. For just as a bird tied to the earth cannot lift itself up to heaven by flying, so a mind occupied with perishable things cannot raise itself to heavenly things. Nor should the spirit be cast down by too much frequent practice; otherwise the brain too is confused, and one labors in vain through dry habit. Therefore let the cenobite, fervent in spirit, learn always to persist in these things with moderation, and by his intention continually refer the purpose of every exercise to God, who is the beginning and end of all goodness. Let him faithfully direct his effort toward fear and love of him, and fix his mind in profound humility, since one who is rooted in love is not easily abandoned by God.

Here ends the spiritual exercise of cloistered persons, by Peter of Friedberg, in the noble city of Mainz, on the eighth Ides of August, in the year of salvation M.cccc.xcviii.

The Compendium of the Spiritual Exercise Begins. Johannes Trithemius.

Although this formula of spiritual exercise, published by us for the edification of cloistered persons, might appear very brief to any devout persons who have leisure, nevertheless we fear that to those occupied with household affairs it may seem rather lengthy. For when their thought is stretched by continual concern in arranging the necessities of their subjects, the mind is easily wearied even by very brief spiritual exercises. Therefore, lest our monks who are either devoted to exterior matters, or are less devout in spiritual conversation, be able, by occasion of its length, to take refuge in their customary excuse, we have been ordered to abbreviate the same instruction, so that the fervent may keep the longer one in their devotion, and the lukewarm may not omit the shorter.

The Practice of the Spiritual Exercise Follows.

Before each and every hour, in general, the devout cenobite should strive to direct his effort toward this end: that with all his strength he may desire to magnify God in his heart, by the root of his benefits. Let there be in him so great a most fervent ardor of devotion, so great a compunction, and finally so great an outpouring of tears, that whoever sees him chanting psalms may be moved by his example to magnify the Lord. Secondly, let him remember that he can be stirred to charity toward his neighbor, since love is directed toward God in vain if one’s neighbor is hated. Therefore, when all the thorns of displeasure have been expelled, let the most devout cenobite, turned toward the Lord, pray.

Prayer

Almighty, eternal God, who, instructing us for the exercise of your love through the manifold creation of things, commanded us to love you above all things with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves for your sake: graciously grant me the grace of your most holy love and of love for my neighbor, so that, with every movement of displeasure, aversion, and anger restrained, Another Prayer.

I beseech you, holy Father, almighty, eternal God, by the power of the most holy passion of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: enlighten the eyes of my heart, so that, pierced in spirit, I may see how often I have offended in your commandments; and, cleansed by your mercy from every stain of sin, may never offend you hereafter.

After Matins

When Matins has been completed, while still remaining in the church, or also when placed in your cell, take up for yourself the disposition of true resignation, praying thus.

Prayer

O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who at the hour of Matins, placed in the greatest anguish of your most holy heart, after your threefold prayer resigned yourself most fully to the will of God your Father: grant me, by the power of that charity of yours, perfectly to despise my own will in all things for love of you, and truly to resign myself at every time to the ordering of your will and of those whom you have set over me. Who lives and reigns.

After Prime.

After Prime, when, leaving the choir, you enter the chapter place, in memory of your most innocent Savior accused before Pilate, you shall form your disposition toward humble confession, praying thus to the Lord.

Prayer

Most loving and sweetest Lord Jesus, who at the hour of Prime, falsely accused before Pilate, truly confessed yourself to be the Son of God: have mercy on me and grant me, through your innocence, the virtue of true confession, so that I may humbly endure any words of accusation against me, and may not withdraw from the inward tranquillity of mind on account of any reproaches. You who live and reign with God the Father.

After Terce.

After Terce you shall call to mind how many reproaches, how many mockeries and derisions the most innocent Lord Jesus endured for your redemption. In memory of this, take up for yourself the desire for the sixth degree of humility, praying thus.

Prayer

Sweetest Lord Jesus, who for us were pitiably scourged, mocked, derided, crowned with thorns, and spat upon at the hour of Terce: grant me, by the power of all your passions, through the outpouring of your most holy blood, always to be content for love of you with every baseness and extremity, so that, in view of my sins, I may humbly regard myself as your unworthy servant, and yet may in no way grow lukewarm in your holy service.

After Sext.

After Sext, consider the Lord Jesus carrying his cross before all and then hanging miserably upon it, together with the other articles of his sufferings; and, inflamed with desire for the seventh degree of humility, pray to him with fervor of spirit.

Prayer

Sweetest Lord Jesus, who for us wretched sinners, after the countless sorrows of your passion, while your most sorrowful mother looked on, carried your cross to the place of your death; on which, cruelly fastened, with gall and vinegar to drink and mocked in many ways.

You were given gall and vinegar to drink and were mocked in many ways: I beseech you, by the pain of your wounds, grant me forgiveness of all my sins, the grace of holy compunction, a fountain of tears, the profound virtue of humility, and continual remembrance of your most bitter Passion, so that all that I am and can do may always serve you, and my mind may continually burn with your love.

After None.

After None, be mindful of most sweet Jesus dying on the cross; and, falling in spirit at his knees, with tears and with as much devotion as you can, give thanks and pray.

Prayer

I adore and hold you, most sweet Lord Jesus Christ, king of heaven and earth, dying on the cross for me, wretched as I am; and I humbly give you thanks for your holy Passion and most innocent death. O most loving Savior, what shall I repay you for all the things you have repaid to me? Behold, I offer myself to you; I long continually to dwell in your most holy wounds. I beseech you, by the virtue of your most innocent death: have mercy on me as you know how; pierce my flesh with fear of you; restrain in me all disordered movements, so that, inflamed with the fervor of your most holy love, I may love you with a pure heart, confess you worthily with my mouth, and follow you in deed, as far as I am able, with a humble manner of life. I beseech you, most merciful Lord Jesus, by that anguish of your most holy heart which you endured on the cross when your most holy soul departed from your body: have mercy on my soul at its departure.

The first hour after dinner.

At the first hour after dinner, unless you are occupied with higher exercises, you shall pray to the Lord in this or a similar way, to obtain knowledge of your own frailty.

Prayer

Lord God, whose great kindness created me, in my first parent, from the mud of the earth, so that, mindful of my humble condition, I might glorify you, my creator, in true humility: grant me, I beseech you, to know my frailty truthfully at all times, so that, when I consider how vile I am and almost nothing by my own merit, I may deserve to please you by your gift. Through Christ.

The second hour.

At the second hour after midday, let our devout cenobite briefly recall to memory the gravity of his sins by which, especially while living in holy religion, he has sinned against the Rule; and, turned to the Lord, let him pray thus.

Prayer

Almighty, everlasting God, who by the incarnation and death of the only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, out of your mercy alone, deigned to bring us wretches, dead in sins, to life: grant me, by the virtue of his most innocent Passion, pardon for all my sins, so that henceforth I may deserve to serve you with a pure conscience. Through the same our Lord.

The third hour.

At the third hour after dinner, let the faithful cenobite remember his vows which he promised to the Lord, and especially the renunciation of all ownership, namely in possessions, judgments, and will; and, moved to compunction, let him pray to the Lord in fervor of spirit thus.

Prayer

Almighty and merciful God, who with gracious favor sanctify and receive the vows of your servants offered to you from faithful devotion: grant me to render all the things promised to you through the virtue of humility, chastity, obedience, and poverty with such purity of mind that, by your mercy, I may deserve to come to your kingdom promised to the poor in spirit. Through our Lord.

After Vespers

After Vespers, let our good cenobite consider how vain all visible things are; and, with his mind lifted up to love of invisible goods, let him cry to the Lord with as much devotion as he can.

Prayer
